teile.einleitung: A heartbeat consists of two phases: systole, in which the heart ejects blood, and diastole. In diastole the ventricles relax and fill with blood again.
wichtigste: In diastole the ventricles relax and fill with blood.
The blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.
The semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles are closed at this time.
The second heart sound marks the start of diastole.
At rest, diastole lasts longer than systole.
The Greek word diastole means expansion.

abschnitte.text: The heart works like a pump in time. In **systole** the ventricles contract and press blood into the arteries. In **diastole** the ventricular muscle relaxes, and the ventricles fill anew. The word comes from Greek and means **expansion**: the ventricles widen and take in blood.

During diastole the **atrioventricular valves** between the atria and the ventricles open. In this way blood flows from the **atria** into the ventricles. At the same time the **semilunar valves** at the exits of the ventricles are closed. They prevent blood from flowing back from the **aorta** and the **pulmonary artery**. When the aortic and pulmonary valves close, the **second heart sound** arises, which marks the start of diastole.

In a calm heartbeat, diastole makes up about **two thirds** of the heartbeat. In this way the ventricles have enough time to fill. If the heart beats faster during **sport**, it is mainly diastole that becomes **shorter**. The ejection phase, by contrast, stays almost the same length.

The heart muscle itself needs blood too. It gets it by way of the **coronary arteries**. In systole the tensed muscle squeezes the small vessels in its wall shut. That is why the left ventricle is supplied with blood mainly **during diastole**. Only in the relaxation phase can the blood flow well there.

When **blood pressure is measured**, you get two numbers, for example “120 over 80”. The upper one is the **systolic** value, when the heart pumps. The lower one is the **diastolic** value. It shows the pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes and fills.

gewusst: The heart of an adult beats about 60 to 80 times a minute at rest, and each time there is a diastole.
The typical double sound of the heart can be heard well with a stethoscope.

teile.einleitung: A medical specialist has specialised in a particular field after studying medicine. So there are specialists for the heart, skin, eyes, lungs and many other areas. Often the family doctor sends patients to a specialist when a closer examination is needed.
wichtigste: A **cardiologist** treats heart diseases.
With a skin rash you go to a **dermatologist**.
The **neurologist** treats diseases of the brain and nerves.
ENT stands for ear, nose and throat.
An **oncologist** treats cancers.
In Switzerland, several years of further training are needed after studying.

abschnitte.titel: The path to becoming a specialist
abschnitte.text: First you study **medicine** at a university. After that you work for several years in hospitals and practices and get to know a field thoroughly. In Switzerland you finish this **several-year further training** with an exam. Then you receive a **federal specialist title**. The family doctor is also a specialist, namely in general internal medicine.

The **cardiologist** is responsible for heart diseases. Diseases of the lungs are treated by the **pulmonologist**. An **oncologist** deals with **cancers** and plans, for example, treatments with medicines. Many specialist names end in **-logy**, which comes from the Greek word for study. Cardio means heart, pneumo means lung.

The **neurologist** treats diseases of the brain and nerves. With a severe skin rash you go to a **dermatologist**. The specialist for eye diseases is called an **ophthalmologist**, and in everyday speech an eye doctor. **ENT** stands for **ear, nose and throat**. An ENT doctor therefore helps with earache or problems with the tonsils.

An **orthopaedic surgeon** is responsible for **bones, joints and muscles**, for example after a sports accident. The **radiologist** reads **X-ray images** and other pictures of the inside of the body. These also include ultrasound and magnetic resonance. Often several specialists work together so that a patient gets the best treatment.

gewusst: There are special doctors for children: children's doctors, technically called paediatricians.
In Switzerland there are several dozen different specialist titles.

teile.einleitung: The thumb is the shortest and strongest finger on our hand. It is especially mobile and can touch the tips of all the other fingers. That is why we can grasp, hold and write with it, and it also appears in many sayings.
wichtigste: The thumb has only **2 finger bones**.
It can touch the tips of all the other fingers of the same hand.
A thumbs up usually means “well done”.
Anyone who **keeps their fingers crossed** for someone wishes them luck.
Anyone who has **green fingers** makes plants grow well.
**Thumbelina** from the fairy tale is only as big as a thumb.

abschnitte.text: The other fingers have three finger bones, the thumb only **two**. In return it is especially mobile. A special joint at its base, the **saddle joint**, makes this possible. In this way the thumb can touch the tips of all the other fingers **of the same hand**. Experts say it is **opposable**, that is, it can be set against the other fingers.

Without a thumb, much would be difficult. We need it to hold a pen, do up a button or open a bottle. Together with the index finger it forms a kind of **pincer** for small things. Monkeys also have opposable thumbs, but in humans the grip is especially fine. When counting on their fingers, many people in Switzerland start with the thumb.

If someone shows a **thumbs up**, it usually means: well done, all in order. At the roadside, a **hitchhiker** uses an outstretched thumb to show that they want a **lift**. And anyone who **keeps their fingers crossed** for someone wishes them **luck**, for example before an exam. In German you do it by clenching your hands into fists with the thumbs inside, and calling it “pressing thumbs”.

Of someone with whom plants grow especially well, people say: they have **green fingers**, in German a “green thumb”. A **flick book**, in German “Daumenkino” or thumb cinema, is a small booklet with many pictures. If you let the pages run past quickly with your thumb, the pictures seem to **move**. And anyone who does something “over the thumb”, as the German saying goes, is only estimating it roughly.

Many **babies** like to suck their **thumb**. It calms them and helps them to fall asleep. In the fairy tale by **Hans Christian Andersen** there is **Thumbelina**, a tiny girl who is only as big as a thumb. She has many adventures with animals before she finds a happy home.

gewusst: The thumb contributes a great deal to the strength of the hand: without it you can grip much less firmly.
The thumb is moved by several muscles of its own, which form the large ball of the hand.

teile.einleitung: A chilblain is a red, itchy swelling on the skin. It appears when you are out for a long time in cold, damp weather.
wichtigste: A chilblain is a red, itchy swelling.
Chilblains often appear on toes and fingers.
Cold, damp weather makes them more likely.
The skin is red to bluish, and it itches and burns.
Chilblains are not frostbite, because the skin is not frozen.
Warm, dry socks and gloves protect against them.

abschnitte.text: A **chilblain** is a **red, itchy swelling** on the skin. The medical term for it is **pernio**. It often appears on **toes and fingers**, sometimes also on the ears or nose. These parts of the body are far from the heart and cool down quickly. Chilblains usually heal by themselves after a few days to weeks.

Chilblains are made more likely by **cold and damp** weather, for example with wet snow just above freezing point. In the cold, the small blood vessels in the skin contract. If the hands or feet then warm up quickly again, the vessels react wrongly. A slight **inflammation** results, and the skin swells.

With a chilblain, the skin is often **red to bluish**. The spot **itches and burns**, especially when it gets warm. You should **not scratch** an itchy chilblain, or the skin can be damaged. Chilblains are **not the same as frostbite**. With a chilblain, the skin is **not frozen**, while with frostbite it is.

Against chilblains on the feet, **warm, dry socks** and good shoes protect you. Anyone who has played in the snow with **wet gloves** should put on **dry gloves**. You warm up cold fingers and toes slowly, not with hot water. Exercise helps the blood to flow well. If chilblains come up often, a doctor can help.

gewusst: Chilblains usually do not appear in freezing cold but in cold, wet weather.
Chilblains have nothing to do with bumps from knocking yourself, because they are a reaction of the blood vessels.

teile.einleitung: Epilepsy is a disease of the brain in which seizures keep occurring. It is one of the most common diseases of the nervous system and can affect people of any age. With the right treatment, many people who have it live quite normally.
wichtigste: In a seizure, many nerve cells send signals at the same time and excessively.
Epilepsy is not contagious.
The **EEG** is used to measure the electrical activity of the brain.
Medicines against seizures are called **antiepileptics**.
In a convulsive seizure, nothing should be put in the person's mouth.
If a seizure lasts longer than five minutes, you call 144 in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In the brain, billions of **nerve cells** work and communicate with electrical signals. Normally these signals are well ordered. In an **epileptic seizure**, very many nerve cells suddenly discharge at the same time and excessively. It is a little like a thunderstorm in the head. Depending on which part of the brain is affected, the seizure looks quite different.

The best known is the **grand mal seizure**: the person loses consciousness, falls down and twitches all over the body. Grand mal is French and means “great illness”, and in medical terms it is called a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Quite different is the **absence seizure**, which occurs mainly in children. The child stares into space for a few seconds and does not respond, but does not fall down. Afterwards the child carries on as if nothing had happened.

To detect epilepsy, an **EEG**, an electroencephalogram, is often done. Electrodes are stuck on the scalp and record the brain currents. Treatment is usually with **antiepileptics**, which lower the excitability of the nerve cells. Many people become free of seizures with them. In some people, certain triggers set off seizures, for example **rapidly flickering light** in light-sensitive epilepsy.

In a convulsive seizure, you stay calm and stay with the person. You protect them from injury, move hard objects away and put something soft under the head. You do not hold them down and you push **nothing between the teeth**, because that can break teeth or block breathing. After the seizure, you put them in the recovery position. If the seizure lasts longer than five minutes, you dial **144** in Switzerland.

gewusst: Epilepsy has been known since ancient times and was often misunderstood in the past.
Thanks to medicines, many people with epilepsy go for years without any seizure.

teile.einleitung: In **gas exchange** in the lungs, oxygen from the air we breathe gets into the blood. At the same time, the blood gives off carbon dioxide into the air, which we then breathe out.
wichtigste: Gas exchange takes place in the air sacs of the lungs.
A human has around 300 million air sacs or more.
Together they have an area of about 100 square metres.
The gases pass into and out of the blood by diffusion.
The wall between air and blood is thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre.
Exhaled air still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the finest airways lie tiny **air sacs**, also called **alveoli**. An adult human has an estimated **300 million** of them or more. Spread out, they would have an area of about **100 square metres**. That is roughly the floor area of a large flat. In a small space, this creates a huge surface for the exchange.

The air sacs are wrapped in a net of the finest blood vessels, the **capillaries**. Their wall lies close against the wall of the sacs. The dividing wall is thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre. The shorter the way, the faster the gases get through. At rest, a red blood cell spends less than a second at one sac, and that is still enough.

The gases travel by **diffusion**. This means that particles move by themselves from a place with a lot to a place with a little. In the air sacs there is more oxygen than in the arriving blood, so it flows into the blood. With **carbon dioxide** it is the other way round, and it goes from the blood into the air. In the blood, the red blood pigment **haemoglobin** carries the oxygen on.

On the inside of the air sacs lies a thin film, the **surfactant**. It lowers the **surface tension**. Without this film, the tiny sacs would collapse when we breathe out. This way they stay open and can easily fill again when we breathe in.

The lungs take only about a quarter of the oxygen out of the air, which is why exhaled air still contains about **16 per cent** oxygen. **Carbon monoxide**, a poisonous gas with no smell, is dangerous. It binds much more strongly to haemoglobin than oxygen does and takes its place. The blood can then hardly carry any oxygen. That is why there are carbon monoxide alarms.

gewusst: Fresh air contains about 21 per cent oxygen.
Because exhaled air still contains a lot of oxygen, mouth-to-mouth resuscitation works in first aid.

teile.einleitung: Epithelial tissue is a tissue that covers the inner and outer surfaces of the body. It forms the outer layer of skin, for example, and lines the airways, gut and bladder. It protects, takes in substances and gives off substances.
wichtigste: Epithelial cells lie tightly next to each other and sit on the **basement membrane**.
Epithelial tissue contains no blood vessels.
The outer layer of skin consists of stratified keratinised squamous epithelium.
The bladder is lined with stretchy **transitional epithelium**.
Cilia in the airways carry mucus with dust to the throat.
A malignant tumour of epithelial tissue is called a **carcinoma**.

abschnitte.text: Epithelial cells lie close together like paving stones and form a closed layer. They sit on a thin layer, the **basement membrane**, which separates them from the tissue below. A typical feature is that epithelial tissue contains **no blood vessels**. Nutrients and oxygen therefore reach the cells from the connective tissue underneath. Special cell connections, the **tight junctions**, close the gaps between the cells so tightly that hardly any substances get through.

Epithelia are classified by the shape of the cells and by the number of layers. Flat cells form a **squamous epithelium**, but there are also cube-shaped and tall cells. The outer layer of human skin is a **stratified keratinised squamous epithelium**, which protects well against friction and drying out. The alveoli of the lungs, on the other hand, are lined with **single-layered squamous epithelium**. Because it is so thin, oxygen and carbon dioxide can pass through quickly.

The bladder is lined with **transitional epithelium**. It adapts when the bladder fills and stretches a lot, and becomes flatter as it does so. In the airways, the epithelium carries tiny **cilia**, the kinocilia. They beat constantly and move mucus with dust and germs towards the throat. This keeps the lungs clean.

Epithelial tissue protects the body, takes up nutrients in the gut and makes substances such as sweat or saliva in glands. Because epithelial cells are often renewed, they divide frequently. Mistakes can sometimes occur in the process. A malignant tumour that starts from epithelial tissue is called a **carcinoma**. Many common types of cancer belong to this group.

gewusst: The outer layer of skin is renewed all the time, and old keratinised cells flake off unnoticed.
The word epithelium comes from Greek.

teile.einleitung: Football is one of the most popular sports in the world. Two teams try to shoot the ball into the opponents' goal, and that keeps the body fit too.
wichtigste: A football team has 11 players on the pitch.
Only the goalkeeper may catch the ball with his or her hands.
A normal match for adults lasts 90 minutes.
The yellow card is a warning, and the red card is a sending-off.
The Swiss national team is often called “Nati” for short.
The world football association FIFA has its seat in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: In **football**, two teams play against each other. Each has **11 players** on the pitch. The aim is to shoot the ball into the opponents' **goal**. You play the ball with your feet, your head or your body, but not with your hands. Only the **goalkeeper** may catch the ball with his or her hands in the penalty area.

A normal football match for adults lasts **90 minutes**. It is divided into two halves of 45 minutes each. In between there is a break. For children, the matches are shorter, and often fewer children play on a smaller pitch. The team with more goals wins.

The **referee** makes sure that everyone keeps to the rules. After a foul he or she can show a **yellow card**, which is a **warning**. The **red card** means a **sending-off**: the player has to leave the pitch. After a foul in the penalty area, there is a penalty kick. This is simply called a **penalty**.

The Swiss national football team is often called the **Nati** for short. It regularly takes part in World Cups and European Championships. The world football association **FIFA** has its seat in **Zurich**. The European football association **UEFA** is also based in Switzerland, in Nyon on Lake Geneva. In almost every municipality there is a football club for children.

In football you run a lot, sprint and stop. This strengthens the **heart**, **lungs** and **leg muscles**. You also train skill, balance and quick reactions. Because you play in a team, you learn to work together. Before the match you should warm up so that you do not get injured.

gewusst: A professional footballer often runs around 10 kilometres during a match.
Switzerland hosted the football World Cup in 1954.

teile.einleitung: Reproduction means that living things have offspring. In humans, a new life begins when an egg cell from the woman joins with a sperm cell from the man. After that the child grows for about 40 weeks in the mother's womb.
wichtigste: Humans reproduce sexually.
Sperm cells are made in the testes, and egg cells ripen in the ovaries.
Fertilisation usually takes place in the fallopian tube.
The egg cell and the sperm cell each contain 23 chromosomes.
The X or Y chromosome of the sperm cell decides the biological sex.
Through the placenta, the unborn child is supplied with nutrients and oxygen.
A pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks.

abschnitte.text: **Reproduction** makes sure that life goes on. In humans, it needs a female and a male reproductive cell. Because the child receives genetic information from both parents, every child is unique. This is called **sexual reproduction**.

In men, **sperm cells** are made in the testes, millions every day from puberty onwards. In women, one **egg cell** usually ripens in the ovaries once a month. Both reproductive cells contain only 23 chromosomes, half as many as other body cells. The egg cell is one of the largest cells in the human body.

Fertilisation usually takes place in the **fallopian tube**. Only a single sperm cell can get into the egg cell. The genetic material then merges, and the fertilised cell again has 46 chromosomes. If the sperm cell brings an X chromosome, the child is usually a girl, and with a Y chromosome, a boy.

The fertilised egg cell divides and settles in the womb. Through the **placenta**, the child gets oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood. After about eight weeks, all the organs have been formed, and from then on it is called a foetus. A pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, counted from the last period.

At the end of the pregnancy, the muscles of the womb tighten in **contractions**. They push the child out through the birth canal. Sometimes a child is also born by Caesarean section. In Switzerland, around 78,000 children were born in 2024.

The ability to reproduce begins with **puberty**, roughly between the ages of 9 and 16. Hormones then make the body mature. In girls, periods begin, and in boys, sperm production starts. These changes are normal and happen at each person's own pace.

begriffe.erklaerung: An egg or sperm cell that merges with another during reproduction.
The merging of an egg cell and a sperm cell.
An organ in pregnancy that supplies the child, also called the afterbirth.
The organ in which the unborn child grows.

gewusst: A sperm cell is one of the smallest cells in the body, while the egg cell can just about be seen with the naked eye.
Identical twins arise when one fertilised egg cell splits into two parts.

teile.einleitung: Dentine is the hard substance that forms most of a tooth. It lies under the hard enamel and surrounds the soft pulp. In German it is also called “Zahnbein”.
wichtigste: Dentine lies under the enamel and forms most of the tooth.
The German word for it is **Zahnbein**.
It is softer than enamel, but harder than bone.
Fine **tubules** run through the dentine.
It is formed by the **odontoblasts**.
**Ivory** consists mainly of dentine.

abschnitte.text: A tooth consists of several layers. Right on the outside of the crown lies the **enamel**, the hardest substance in the body. Under it follows the **dentine**, which forms most of the tooth. Right on the inside lies the **pulp** with nerves and blood vessels. In German, dentine is also called **Zahnbein**.

Dentine is **softer than enamel**, but **harder than bone**. It consists for the most part of minerals, above all **hydroxyapatite**, a compound with calcium. In addition there are protein and water. As a result, dentine is a little elastic and does not break so easily. Its colour is **yellowish**, which is why it shows through when the enamel is thin.

The dentine is run through by countless **fine tubules**. They run from the pulp outwards. In them lie fine extensions of the **odontoblasts**, the cells that form the dentine. If the dentine is exposed, for example at the neck of the tooth, cold or sweet things can trigger a stimulus through these tubules. Then the teeth feel **sensitive**.

Unlike enamel, dentine can be newly formed throughout life. The odontoblasts slowly lay down new dentine on the inside. That is why the space for the **pulp** gets **smaller** in the course of life. In response to stimuli too, for example from tooth decay, the tooth can form extra dentine as protection.

The **tusks** of elephants are very large teeth. Their material, **ivory**, consists **mainly of dentine**. In the past, jewellery, piano keys and figures were made from it. Because many elephants were hunted for this reason, the trade in ivory is now strongly restricted internationally. Switzerland, too, keeps to these rules to protect elephants.

gewusst: The tusks of walruses and the long tooth of the narwhal also consist of dentine.
Because dentine is yellowish, teeth with thin enamel never look quite white.

teile.einleitung: The canine teeth are the pointed teeth at the corner of the dental arch. They stand right next to the incisors and help with holding and tearing food.
wichtigste: The canine teeth stand next to the incisors.
In the permanent set of teeth there are four canines, two at the top and two at the bottom.
Canine teeth are pointed.
You use them for holding and tearing.
The upper canine has the longest root of all teeth.
The upper canines are also known as eye teeth in everyday language.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the mouth are the **incisors**. Right next to them, at the **corner of the dental arch**, come the **canines**. There are two at the top and two at the bottom, so **four** altogether. Behind them come the molars. Children's **milk teeth** also already include four canines.

A canine tapers to a **point** at the top. With it you can **hold** and **tear** tough food well, for example a piece of bread crust. The incisors bite off, and the molars grind the food. So each type of tooth has its own job.

The **upper canine** has the **longest root** of all human teeth. That is why it sits very firmly in the jaw. Its root reaches far up towards the eye. That is why the upper canines are also called **eye teeth** in everyday language. Because they are so sturdy, they often stay in place into old age.

Many **predators** have very large, long canines. The **tiger** uses them to seize its prey. In **dogs** and **wolves**, the long canines are called **fangs**. In some animals, canines have grown into huge tusks, for example in the walrus or the wild boar.

gewusst: An adult's permanent set of teeth has 32 teeth including the wisdom teeth, and the milk teeth have 20.
The tusks of elephants are not canines but greatly elongated incisors.

teile.einleitung: Detoxification means that the body breaks down harmful substances, makes them harmless and gets rid of them. The most important detoxification centre is the liver.
wichtigste: The liver is the body's most important detoxification centre.
It lies in the upper right of the abdomen, under the diaphragm.
The portal vein brings blood from the gut straight to the liver.
The liver turns poisonous ammonia into urea.
The liver makes bile, which is stored in the gallbladder.
In an adult, blood alcohol falls by only about 0.1 to 0.2 per mille per hour.
The liver can grow back.

abschnitte.text: The **liver** lies in the **upper right of the abdomen**, directly under the diaphragm. It is partly protected by the ribs. It breaks down many poisons, **medicines** and **alcohol**, or makes them harmless. After that, the substances can be removed through the kidney or the bile. The blood from the stomach and gut flows through the **portal vein** to the liver first. This lets it check and process substances that have been taken in.

When protein is broken down, poisonous **ammonia** is formed. The liver turns it into harmless **urea**. It travels with the blood to the **kidneys**, which get rid of it in the urine. If the liver no longer works properly, ammonia can build up in the blood and disturb the brain.

The liver makes **bile** every day. This carries waste products into the gut. Bile also helps with the **digestion of fat**. It is stored temporarily in the **gallbladder** on the underside of the liver. There it is thickened and released into the duodenum when you eat a meal rich in fat.

The liver breaks down alcohol slowly and steadily, in an adult at about **0.1 to 0.2 per mille per hour**. Coffee or cold showers do not speed this up. Years of heavy drinking can cause **cirrhosis of the liver**. In this, healthy liver tissue is gradually replaced by **scar tissue**. The liver can then carry out its tasks less and less well.

The liver is especially good at **regenerating**. If a part is removed, the remaining tissue grows back. That is why even a **partial donation** of the liver from a living person is possible. In severe damage such as advanced cirrhosis, however, this ability is no longer enough.

gewusst: The liver is the largest gland of the human body and weighs about 1.5 kilograms in an adult.
A healthy body does not need drinks or cures that supposedly “detox”, because the liver and kidneys do that.

teile.einleitung: An electron microscope magnifies tiny things much more strongly than a light microscope. Instead of light, it uses a beam of electrons.
wichtigste: Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll from 1931.
Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986.
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, which gives higher resolution.
Inside the machine there is a high vacuum, so that air does not scatter the electrons.
Magnetic fields from coils focus the electron beam.
The Swiss scientist Jacques Dubochet received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017 for cryo-electron microscopy.

abschnitte.text: How finely a microscope shows details depends on the **wavelength**. Light microscopes reach a limit of about 200 nanometres. Fast **electrons** have a wavelength of only a few picometres. That is why the **resolution** is much higher. This makes it possible, for example, to see **ribosomes**, which measure only 20 to 30 nanometres.

Inside the machine there has to be a **high vacuum**, because even a few air molecules would deflect the electrons. Glass lenses do not help with electrons. Instead, **magnetic fields** from **coils** with a current running through them focus the beam. They act as electromagnetic lenses. The image appears on a fluorescent screen or a sensor.

In a **transmission electron microscope** (TEM), the electrons pass through wafer-thin slices. Biological samples are often given contrast with **heavy-metal salts** such as uranyl acetate, which make structures show up dark. The **scanning electron microscope** (SEM), on the other hand, scans surfaces with a fine beam. It produces images that look three-dimensional, for example of the head of a fly. In **freeze-fracture**, flash-frozen samples are split open to show the inside of membranes.

The German physicist **Ernst Ruska** developed the first electron microscope from 1931 with **Max Knoll** at the Technical University of Berlin. It was not until **1986** that Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. The Swiss biophysicist **Jacques Dubochet** of the **University of Lausanne** was honoured with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **2017**. He shared it with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.

Dubochet found a way of freezing samples in a flash in **glass-like ice**. No ice crystals form that would destroy the sample. This makes it possible to look at proteins and viruses in their natural state. This **cryo-electron microscopy** now helps, for example, in developing medicines.

gewusst: More than 50 years lay between the building of the first electron microscope and Ruska's Nobel Prize.
Modern electron microscopes can even make single atoms visible.

teile.einleitung: Fever means that the body is warmer than usual. Usually it is a sign that it is fighting germs such as viruses or bacteria.
wichtigste: In a fever, body temperature is raised, and people usually speak of fever from about 38 degrees Celsius.
Fever often helps the body defend itself against germs.
When a fever rises, you often feel cold and shiver.
When a fever falls, you usually sweat.
With a fever, you should drink plenty and rest.
If a child seems very ill, you go to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Normally, body temperature is about **37 degrees Celsius**. In a **fever**, it is clearly higher. The brain then sets the inner “thermostat” higher, rather like a heating system. Usually an **infection** lies behind it, for example flu or a cold. The warmth helps the body's own defences fight the germs.

When a fever rises, the body wants to get warmer. That is why you feel cold even though you are already warm, and you shiver. This is called **chills**. Shivering makes warmth in the muscles. When the fever falls again, the body gives off the warmth, and you **sweat** heavily.

abschnitte.titel: How you can tell it is a fever
abschnitte.text: In a fever, the forehead often feels **hot** and the cheeks are flushed. Many sick people are tired, have no appetite and do not feel like doing anything. Headaches or aching limbs are also common. You only know for certain when you measure with a **clinical thermometer**.

Someone with a fever loses a lot of water by sweating. That is why it is important to **drink** a lot, for example water or tea. Rest and sleep give the body strength. In a high fever, an adult can give a child a **fever medicine**, in the right amount for their age. If a child seems very ill, is very young or the fever lasts a long time, you go to the doctor.

gewusst: Many animals also get a fever when they are ill.
Lizards, which do not make heat themselves, lie in the sun for longer when they have an infection and warm themselves up that way.

teile.einleitung: Everybody farts, and that is perfectly normal. A fart is gas from the gut, and the medical term for it is flatulence.
wichtigste: A fart is made of gas.
All people fart, and that is normal.
A healthy person often farts more than ten times a day.
After beans, you often have to fart more.
Farts smell bad because of gases containing sulphur.
Another word for a fart is a “trump” or “wind”.

abschnitte.text: A fart is made of **gas** that escapes from the gut through the bottom. The medical term for it is **flatulence**. A healthy person often farts **more than ten times** a day. That is quite normal, because **all people fart**.

Some of the gas is **air** that you swallow while eating and drinking. If you eat in a hurry or drink a lot of fizzy water, you swallow more air. Most of the gas, however, is made in the **large intestine**. There live billions of tiny **bacteria**. They break down leftovers of food that the body could not digest, and this makes gases.

After some foods you have to fart more, especially after **beans**, lentils, cabbage or onions. They contain substances that only the gut bacteria can break down. This produces a lot of gas. That is no reason to avoid these foods, because they are healthy and contain plenty of fibre.

Most of the gases in a fart have no smell at all, for example nitrogen or carbon dioxide. Farts smell bad because of **gases containing sulphur**, such as **hydrogen sulphide**. It smells of rotten eggs. Even a tiny amount of it is enough for you to smell it.

Farting is natural, but it can still be unpleasant for other people. If a fart slips out in company, it is polite to say **excuse me**. You do not need to feel ashamed. If someone often has tummy ache and bloating, a doctor can help.

gewusst: Many animals fart too, for example dogs and horses.
In one day, a person gives off roughly half a litre to one and a half litres of gut gas.

teile.einleitung: The **cardiac conduction system** makes sure the heart beats at the right rhythm. It produces electrical signals and passes them through the heart in a fixed order. This makes the atria contract first and then the ventricles.
wichtigste: The **sinus node** is the heart's natural pacemaker.
The excitation travels from the sinus node via the AV node, the bundle of His and the Tawara branches to the Purkinje fibres.
The system consists of specialised heart muscle cells.
The heart can produce excitation itself, which is called **automaticity**.
The bundle of His is named after a doctor from Basel.
The sympathetic nervous system raises the heart rate.

abschnitte.titel: A heart with its own rhythm
abschnitte.text: The heart does not need an order from the brain to beat. It can **produce excitation itself** without any outside trigger. This ability is called **automaticity**. The cardiac conduction system, which consists of **specialised heart muscle cells**, is responsible. These cells hardly contract at all, but mainly produce and pass on electrical signals.

The **sinus node** in the wall of the right atrium is the primary pacemaker of a healthy heart. From there the excitation spreads across the atria to the **AV node**. From there it goes on into the **bundle of His**, then into the **Tawara branches** and finally into the **Purkinje fibres**. These distribute the excitation through the muscle of the ventricles. The AV node briefly slows the excitation, so that the atria can first pump the blood into the ventricles.

Between the atria and the ventricles lies the **cardiac skeleton** made of connective tissue. It electrically insulates the atria and ventricles from each other. That is why the excitation normally reaches the ventricles only through the AV node. If the sinus node fails, centres lower down can step in. Tertiary centres in the ventricles, however, have a natural rate of only about **20 to 40 beats per minute**.

The **bundle of His** is named after the doctor Wilhelm His junior, who was born in **Basel**. The Tawara branches are named after a Japanese researcher, the Purkinje fibres after a Czech one. The autonomic nervous system can adjust the rhythm. The **sympathetic nervous system** raises the heart rate, for example during sport or excitement. The parasympathetic nervous system lowers it again.

gewusst: An artificial pacemaker takes over the job when the cardiac conduction system is not working properly.
The **ECG** can be used to record the electrical excitation of the heart.

teile.einleitung: Intestinal villi are tiny, finger-shaped outgrowths of the lining of the small intestine. They enlarge the inner surface of the intestine enormously. In this way the body can take up many nutrients from the food.
wichtigste: Intestinal villi are found in the **small intestine**.
They are tiny, **finger-shaped** outgrowths.
A villus is about **1 millimetre** tall.
Their purpose is to enlarge the **surface**.
On their cells sit even smaller **microvilli**.
In **coeliac disease**, the villi are damaged by gluten.

abschnitte.text: If you look at the inner wall of the **small intestine** under the microscope, it looks like a thick velvet carpet. This carpet consists of millions of **intestinal villi**. These are tiny, **finger-shaped outgrowths** of the lining. A single villus is about **1 millimetre** tall. With the naked eye you can hardly see them.

The most important task of the intestinal villi is to enlarge the **surface**. The larger the surface, the more nutrients can be taken up at the same time. For this there are even smaller outgrowths: on the cells of the villi sit the **microvilli**. They form a fine border that is called the **brush border**. In addition there are large folds of the intestinal wall on which the villi stand.

In every intestinal villus run fine blood vessels, the **capillaries**. Sugar and amino acids that are taken up by the villi pass **into the blood**. By way of a large vein, this blood first flows to the **liver**. The liver checks and processes the substances before they reach the whole body.

Fats take a different route. In the middle of each villus lies a **lymph vessel**. It takes up mainly the **fats**. By way of the lymph system they reach the blood only later. In this way each villus has two transport routes for different nutrients.

In **coeliac disease**, the body cannot tolerate the sticky protein **gluten**, which is found in wheat, spelt, rye and barley. The immune system then attacks the lining of the intestine, and the intestinal villi become **flatter**. The intestine can then take up fewer nutrients. The treatment is a **gluten-free diet**, after which the villi usually recover. In Switzerland, gluten-free products are often marked with a symbol.

gewusst: The cells on the surface of the intestinal villi are renewed about every few days.
Without folds, villi and microvilli, the small intestine would have only a small part of its inner surface.

teile.einleitung: In an endoscopy, doctors use a thin instrument to look inside the body. This lets them see organs without cutting much open.
wichtigste: An endoscope is a thin tube or hose with a light and a camera.
Endoscopy means “looking inside”.
A look into the stomach is called a gastroscopy, a look into the bowel a colonoscopy.
In an arthroscopy, a joint is examined.
In a bronchoscopy, the airways are looked at.
Tissue samples can be taken through the endoscope.
Glass fibres guide the light round the bends.

abschnitte.text: An **endoscope** is a thin, often flexible tube with a **light source** and a **camera**. The word comes from Greek: “endon” means inside, “skopein” means to look at. In flexible instruments, **glass fibres** guide the light. Inside the fibres, the light is reflected back again and again from the wall, which is called **total internal reflection**. This is how it gets through curved tubes too.

Depending on the organ, the endoscopy has its own name. In a **gastroscopy**, the endoscope is pushed through the mouth into the gullet and stomach. A **colonoscopy** examines the large intestine. In a **bronchoscopy**, the doctor looks into the windpipe and bronchi. An **arthroscopy** shows a joint, as “arthron” means joint. It is often done after sports injuries to the knee.

Fine tools can be passed in through a channel in the endoscope. In this way a small **tissue sample**, a **biopsy**, can be taken, for example. It is examined in the laboratory. In a colonoscopy, small growths called **polyps** can be removed straight away. Many procedures are possible like this without a large cut.

In a **capsule endoscopy**, you swallow a small capsule with a built-in camera. It travels through the digestive tract and takes many pictures on the way. This even makes it possible to examine the long **small intestine**, which is hard to reach with normal endoscopes. The capsule is passed out again naturally afterwards.

gewusst: A camera capsule is about as big as a large vitamin tablet.
As early as the 19th century there were the first rigid endoscopes, lit by candles or lamps.

teile.einleitung: The electronic patient record, EPR for short, is a digital collection of a person's important health documents in Switzerland. Doctors, hospitals and pharmacies can store and read reports in it, if the patient allows it.
wichtigste: The Federal Act on the Electronic Patient Record (EPRA) came into force in 2017.
For the public, opening one is voluntary so far.
The patient grants the access rights themselves.
Health insurers and employers have no access.
You open the EPR with a certified core community.
Hospitals have had to take part since 2020.
eHealth Suisse is the coordination body of the Confederation and the cantons.

abschnitte.text: The **electronic patient record** collects information that is relevant to treatment. This includes, for example, **discharge reports** after a stay in hospital, **medication plans** or vaccination details. In an emergency or when changing doctor, professionals can then quickly get the important data. Duplicate examinations and mistakes with medicines should become less frequent.

The **Federal Act on the Electronic Patient Record** (EPRA) came into force in April **2017**. After that, the providers first had to be certified. For the public, the EPR has so far been **voluntary**. In a law revision now under way, people are discussing whether it should in future be opened automatically for everyone. Supporters hope for more benefit, while critics worry about data protection and self-determination.

The **owner** of the record decides for themselves which healthcare professionals may see documents. They can change the access rights at any time. The law expressly excludes **health insurers** and **employers** from access. This is meant to keep the health data protected. You can also upload documents yourself.

You open an EPR with a **core community**. These are certified providers that manage the records and access rights. Since **2020**, **hospitals** have had to join an EPR community. Care homes and newly licensed doctors' practices followed later. **eHealth Suisse** is the coordination body of the Confederation and the cantons. It prepares the groundwork and informs the public.

gewusst: In the EPR you can also store documents yourself, for example an emergency card.
By law, insurers may not look at the EPR, even if they pay for the treatment.

teile.einleitung: We feel pressure every day: when a shoe pinches, when we dive or when the doctor measures blood pressure. Pressure arises when a force acts on a surface.
wichtigste: Pressure arises when a force presses on a surface.
The smaller the surface, the greater the pressure.
When diving you feel the water pressure on your ears.
Blood pressure shows how strongly the blood presses against the arteries.
Firm pressure on a wound slows bleeding.

abschnitte.text: If a **shoe is too small**, it squeezes the toes and foot. You feel this as unpleasant **pressure**. A **sock band** that is too tight also presses into the skin for a long time. Afterwards you see **red marks**, which soon disappear again. Our skin has many small sensory cells that sense pressure.

How great the pressure is depends on the **force** and on the **surface**. If you stand on a **pointed stone**, the whole weight presses on a tiny point. That is why it hurts more than on a flat stone. Conversely, a large surface spreads the pressure: with **snowshoes** or skis you sink less deep into the snow. Pressure is measured in **pascals** or **bar**.

In a **bicycle tyre** there is air under pressure. If you press on it with your thumb, a well pumped-up tyre hardly gives way. If it is soft, it needs more air. Water presses too: the **deeper you dive**, the more water lies above you. In the swimming pool you feel this especially on your **ears**.

The heart pumps blood through the arteries. With an inflatable **cuff** on the upper arm, the doctor measures the **blood pressure**, that is, how strongly the blood presses against the walls of the arteries. Pressure can also help: with a **heavily bleeding wound** you press firmly on it with a clean cloth. This slows the bleeding. Afterwards you quickly get help, in Switzerland by the number **144**.

gewusst: The air around us also presses on us all the time, we just do not notice it.
On high mountains the air pressure is lower than in the valley, which is why water boils there at under 100 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Fibrin is a protein that forms during blood clotting. In a wound it forms a fine mesh of fibres and so helps to stop bleeding.
wichtigste: Fibrin is made from the plasma protein fibrinogen.
Fibrinogen is made in the liver.
The enzyme thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin.
Fibrin threads form a mesh in which blood cells get caught.
In fibrinolysis, the mesh is dissolved again later.
A clot in a blood vessel is called a thrombus.

abschnitte.text: In the liquid part of the blood, the **plasma**, a dissolved protein called **fibrinogen** floats. It is made in the **liver**, together with many other substances for clotting. The clotting factors are numbered with Roman numerals, and fibrinogen is **factor I**. As long as no vessel is injured, it stays dissolved and the blood flows freely.

When a blood vessel is injured, a chain of steps starts, the **clotting cascade**. One factor switches on the next, like falling dominoes. At the end, the enzyme **thrombin** is formed. An enzyme is a protein that speeds up chemical processes. Thrombin splits fibrinogen, and it becomes insoluble **fibrin**.

The fibrin threads join together to form a dense **mesh**. Red blood cells and platelets get caught in it. This makes a firm plug that closes the wound. On the skin, you later see it as a **scab**. Underneath, the skin can renew itself in peace.

When the wound has healed, the body breaks the mesh down again. This process is called **fibrinolysis**, and the most important enzyme for it is called **plasmin**. Sometimes a clot forms inside a vessel, which is called a **thrombus**. It can, for example, block a vein in the leg. Because the liver makes the clotting substances, clotting can be disturbed in liver diseases.

In operations, surgeons use **fibrin glue**. It copies the last step of clotting. A firm clot forms on the wound, which stops bleeding and sticks tissue together. This makes it possible to seal wounds without having to sew everywhere.

gewusst: The name fibrin comes from the Latin word “fibra”, which means fibre.
A scab on a grazed knee consists to a large extent of fibrin and blood cells.

teile.einleitung: Fluoride is a substance that protects teeth from tooth decay. That is why it is in toothpaste and, in Switzerland, often in table salt too.
wichtigste: Fluoride comes from the chemical element fluorine.
It hardens tooth enamel and protects against tooth decay.
Fluoride helps to put minerals back into tiny spots of decay.
It also slows the acid production of bacteria.
In Switzerland, table salt is widely enriched with fluoride.
Basel added fluoride to its drinking water until 2003.

abschnitte.text: **Fluoride** comes from the chemical element **fluorine**. Fluorine itself is a very reactive, poisonous gas. Fluoride, by contrast, is a form found in minerals, in water and in some foods. In small amounts it is good for the teeth. That is why almost every **toothpaste** contains fluoride.

Fluoride is built into the **tooth enamel** and makes it harder. This means acid can attack it less easily. In early, still small spots of decay, fluoride helps to **put minerals back**. This process is called **remineralisation**. In addition, fluoride **slows down** the **acid production of bacteria** in dental plaque.

After brushing your teeth, it is recommended to only **spit out** the foam and not to rinse out vigorously. This way more fluoride stays on the teeth and can work for longer. At the dentist's, the dentist sometimes puts **fluoride varnish** straight onto the teeth. It sticks for a while and gives off fluoride. Children need a children's toothpaste with the right amount.

In Switzerland, **table salt** is widely enriched with fluoride. The packet then carries a note such as “with fluoride”. The city of **Basel** went a different way for a long time and added fluoride to its **drinking water**. It stopped doing so in **2003** and switched to fluoridated salt.

As with many substances, the amount matters. If children take in too much fluoride while their teeth are developing, **white spots** can appear in the tooth enamel. This is called **dental fluorosis**. That is why children should not swallow toothpaste and should only use the recommended amount.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Black tea also naturally contains some fluoride.

teile.einleitung: Decibel, abbreviated dB, is the unit used to say how loud a sound is. The scale runs from the quietest audible sound to noise that hurts in the ears.
wichtigste: Decibels are used to give the sound level, that is, how loud something is.
0 dB is roughly the quietest sound that a healthy young ear hears.
A whisper is about 30 dB, a normal conversation about 60 dB.
From about 120 to 130 dB, sound hurts in the ears.
The “A” in dB(A) means a weighting that is adapted to hearing.
Loud and long sound can damage the hair cells in the ear.

abschnitte.text: Decibels give the **sound level**, that is, how loud a sound is. The **pitch**, by contrast, is measured in **hertz**. The unit is named after the inventor **Alexander Graham Bell**, “deci” means a tenth. **0 dB** does not mean complete silence. It is roughly the **threshold of hearing**, that is, the quietest sound that a healthy young ear can just still hear at 1000 hertz.

The decibel scale is not an ordinary scale like on a ruler. It is **logarithmic**: if 10 dB are added, ten times as much sound energy is behind it. To our ear, a sound that is 10 dB louder seems about **twice as loud**. That is why even a few decibels more make a big difference for hearing.

Quiet **whispering** is at around **30 dB**. A normal **conversation** at a distance of one metre has about **60 dB**. A vacuum cleaner, at around 70 to 80 dB, is clearly louder. The **threshold of pain** is at about **120 to 130 dB**, as loud as a jet aircraft from close by. Often you see **dB(A)**: the A-weighting weights the tones the way the ear hears them, because we hear very low and very high tones less well.

In the inner ear sit fine **hair cells** that turn sound into nerve signals. For damage, the **sound dose** counts, made up of loudness and time. Even from about **85 dB** over a longer time, the hair cells can suffer, and broken hair cells do not grow back. That is why you should not turn **headphones** up too loud and should wear **ear protection** at concerts.

In Switzerland there are rules for loud **events** such as concerts or parties. A federal ordinance, the **V-NISSG**, limits the sound level, averaged over an hour, depending on the event to 93, 96 or at most **100 dB(A)** (as of 2025). At the loudest events, organisers have to offer ear protection, for example.

gewusst: Because the scale is logarithmic, two equally loud devices together give only about 3 dB more, not double.
Bats call with sounds so high that humans cannot hear them at all.

teile.einleitung: **Gastrin** is a hormone of the stomach. It makes sure that the stomach produces hydrochloric acid when we eat.
wichtigste: Gastrin is made mainly in the G cells in the lower part of the stomach.
It increases the production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
Protein building blocks and a stretched stomach wall stimulate its release.
Somatostatin from the D cells slows the release of gastrin.
Gastrin works through the CCK2 receptor.
John Sydney Edkins described gastrin in 1905.

abschnitte.text: Gastrin comes mainly from the **G cells**. They lie in the **antrum**, the lower part of the stomach before the exit to the gut. The G cells release gastrin into the **blood**. Through the blood it reaches its target cells in the lining of the stomach. A **hormone** is therefore a chemical messenger that works through the blood.

**Protein building blocks** in the stomach, that is, peptides and amino acids, have an especially strong effect. The **stretching** of the stomach wall after eating also stimulates the G cells. In addition, the **vagus nerve**, an important nerve from the brain to the abdominal organs, promotes the release.

The most important effect of gastrin is more **hydrochloric acid** in the stomach. It stimulates the **parietal cells**, which make the acid. A large part works indirectly: gastrin makes the **ECL cells** release **histamine**, and histamine then activates the parietal cells. Gastrin binds to the **CCK2 receptor** in doing so. It also promotes the growth of the stomach lining.

If the stomach becomes very acidic, the **pH value** falls. Then the **D cells** release the hormone **somatostatin**. It inhibits the G cells and so slows acid production. This is called **negative feedback**. If people take **proton pump inhibitors** against acid for a long time, this brake falls away, and the gastrin level rises.

The British physiologist **John Sydney Edkins** described in **1905** a substance from the antrum that stimulates acid production. He called it gastrin. In **Zollinger-Ellison syndrome**, a tumour, a **gastrinoma**, makes gastrin without control. The constant flood of acid causes serious, often recurring stomach ulcers.

gewusst: Gastrin and the gut hormone cholecystokinin are related to each other.
The name gastrin comes from the Greek word “gaster” for stomach.

teile.einleitung: An echo is a sound that bounces off a hard surface and comes back to us. In the mountains, this is how you hear your own shout a second time.
wichtigste: An echo happens when sound bounces off a hard wall.
The wall has to be far enough away for you to hear the shout separately.
Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air.
In Switzerland, you can often hear an echo in the mountains.
Bats and dolphins find their way using echoes.
The name comes from the nymph Echo in a Greek legend.

abschnitte.text: If you shout across to a **rock face**, the shout comes back. The **sound** bounces off the hard surface like a ball off a wall. That is why you often hear an echo in the **Alps**. But the wall has to be **far enough away**. If it is too close, the sound comes back so quickly that it blends with your own shout.

Sound is fast, but not infinitely fast. In air it travels about **340 metres per second**. That is faster than a passenger plane, but much slower than light. The sound has to travel to the wall and back again. That is why you hear the echo **a little later** than your own shout. If the wall is 170 metres away, it takes about one second.

In an **empty gym**, the sound bounces off the hard walls, the floor and the ceiling. It rings out, almost like an echo. **Soft things** such as curtains, carpets or cushions swallow the sound. That is why an empty room sounds much louder than a furnished one.

**Bats** call out very high sounds that we cannot hear. From the echoes, they can tell where **obstacles** and **insects** are, even in the dark. This is called **echolocation**. **Dolphins** also use echoes: they send out clicking sounds and so recognise fish and rocks. Ships do something similar: with an **echo sounder**, they measure how deep the water is.

The word comes from a **Greek legend**. In it, the **nymph Echo** could no longer speak for herself, but could only repeat the last words of others. The echo is named after her, because an echo also only repeats what we shout.

gewusst: In water, sound travels more than four times as fast as in air.
Some rocks and valleys in the Alps are known among hikers for their especially good echo.

teile.einleitung: Endocrine glands are hormone glands. They release their messengers, the hormones, straight into the blood and so control many processes in the body.
wichtigste: Endocrine means “releasing inwards”, hormone glands release their substances into the blood.
The sweat gland is not a hormone gland, it releases sweat to the outside.
A hormone only works on cells with matching receptors.
Hormones work more slowly than nerves, but often for longer.
Ghrelin from the stomach triggers hunger, leptin from fatty tissue signals fullness.
The parathyroid glands control the calcium level in the blood.
Endocrinology is the field that deals with hormones.

abschnitte.text: A gland is an organ that makes and releases substances. **Exocrine** glands release their substances to the outside through a duct. One example is the **sweat gland**, which brings sweat onto the skin. **Endocrine** glands have no such duct. They release their **hormones** straight into the blood. Endocrine means “releasing inwards”. Examples are the thyroid gland, the pituitary gland and the adrenal glands.

The word **hormone** comes from the Greek “horman”, which means to drive on. Hormones set processes going in the body. They travel everywhere with the blood. But they can only work on cells with matching **receptors**. A hormone fits like a **key** into a particular lock. Cells without a matching receptor do not react.

Nerves and hormones are the two great control systems of the body. **Nerve signals** reach their target in fractions of a second. **Hormones** have to travel through the blood and so work more slowly. In return, their effect often lasts longer. Hormones control, for example, growth, blood sugar and metabolism.

Organs that you do not think of as glands also make hormones. When the **stomach** is empty, it releases **ghrelin** into the blood. The brain then signals hunger. **Fatty tissue** makes **leptin**. The more fat stores there are, the more leptin tells the brain that enough energy has been stored.

Behind the thyroid gland there are usually four small **parathyroid glands**. They are only about as big as lentils. Their hormone, **parathyroid hormone**, raises the calcium level in the blood. The body needs calcium for bones, muscles and nerves. **Endocrinology** deals with hormone glands and their diseases.

gewusst: The parathyroid glands were only discovered in the 19th century, as the last larger organs of the human body to be found.
The pancreas is both: it releases digestive juice into the gut and insulin into the blood.

teile.einleitung: A fragrance is a smell that we find pleasant, for example from flowers, fresh bread or perfume. We smell fragrances with the nose, and they can awaken memories.
wichtigste: A fragrance is a pleasant smell.
Scent particles float in the air and get into the nose.
Many flowers smell in order to attract insects.
Lavender and roses are known for their strong scent.
Fragrances can easily awaken memories.
In warmth, scent substances evaporate faster than in cold.

abschnitte.text: Scent particles are tiny and float in the **air**. We breathe them in, and they get into the **nose**. Up there sit the **smell cells**. They recognise the particles and send a message to the brain. In this way we know whether it smells of roses or fresh bread. If the nose is blocked in a cold, we smell much less.

Many flowers smell in order to attract **bees** and other **insects**. The insects carry **pollen** from flower to flower, and in this way the plants can reproduce. The **rose** is famous for its scent and often has thorns on the stem. From its flowers **rose oil** is made. The purple **lavender** also smells strongly. Dried, it is put into little bags for the wardrobe.

In the morning, at the **baker’s** it smells of fresh **bread**, because many scent substances arise during baking. A **perfume** is a scented water that you spray on the skin. It contains scent substances from flowers, woods or from the laboratory. Herbs such as peppermint or thyme also smell when you rub them between your fingers.

In the brain, smells quickly reach areas for **feelings** and **memories**. That is why a scent can suddenly remind us of earlier times, for example of holidays or of grandmother’s kitchen. In winter we smell less outdoors than in summer: in the **cold**, scent substances evaporate more slowly, and fewer scent particles float in the air.

gewusst: Dogs have many more smell cells than humans and therefore smell much better.
A large part of what we perceive as taste when eating is actually smell.

teile.einleitung: DNA is the substance that our genetic material is made of. It looks like a twisted rope ladder and contains the building instructions for every living thing. It was a researcher from Basel who first discovered this substance.
wichtigste: DNA is the abbreviation for deoxyribonucleic acid.
It has the shape of a double helix, a twisted rope ladder.
The building blocks are called nucleotides and consist of phosphate, deoxyribose and a base.
There are four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
Adenine always pairs with thymine, guanine always with cytosine.
Friedrich Miescher discovered nucleic acid in Basel in 1869.
James Watson and Francis Crick published the double helix model in 1953.

abschnitte.text: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the carrier of **genetic information** in almost all living things. In it is stored how proteins are to be built. In humans it lies packed in the chromosomes in the cell nucleus.

DNA looks like a twisted rope ladder, the **double helix**. The rails consist alternately of phosphate and the sugar deoxyribose. The rungs are formed by two bases each. Together with the sugar and the phosphate, each base forms a **nucleotide**.

The four bases are called adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine, abbreviated A, T, G and C. They always form fixed **base pairs**: A with T and G with C. Between guanine and cytosine there are three hydrogen bonds, between adenine and thymine two. The order of the bases is like a text in which the genes are written.

The Basel doctor **Friedrich Miescher** found a new substance in pus cells in 1869, which he called nuclein. Only much later was it recognised that this was DNA. In 1953 **James Watson and Francis Crick** published the model of the double helix. Important X-ray pictures for it came from the researcher Rosalind Franklin.

Before a cell divides, the DNA has to be copied. This process is called **replication**. In it the rope ladder opens like a zip. To each half, matching new bases are added, so that two identical DNA strands arise.

With DNA tests you can prove relationship or convict offenders. Medicine uses DNA analyses to recognise hereditary diseases. With the gene scissors CRISPR, DNA can be changed in a targeted way. In 2003 the human genetic material was deciphered almost completely for the first time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of DNA, like a letter in the alphabet of the genetic material.
A basic building block of DNA made of phosphate, sugar and base.
The shape of DNA, which looks like a twisted rope ladder.
The copying of DNA before a cell division.

gewusst: The human genetic material consists of around three billion base pairs.
Humans and chimpanzees agree in about 98 to 99 per cent of their DNA.
In Basel a research institute is named after Friedrich Miescher.

teile.einleitung: Inflammation is a defence reaction of the body to a harmful trigger, for example bacteria or an injury. It is meant to limit the damage and start the healing.
wichtigste: Inflammation is a defence reaction to germs, injuries or foreign substances.
There are five classic signs of inflammation.
The spot becomes warm and red because more blood flows through it.
It swells because fluid leaks from the vessels into the tissue.
Histamine widens the blood vessels in inflammation.
If an inflammation lasts for months, it is chronic.
Many inflammations have names ending in “-itis”.

abschnitte.text: **Inflammation** arises when the body reacts to **germs**, **injuries** or foreign substances. One example is a splinter in a finger. The body sends defence cells to the spot to fight the intruders. After that the repair begins. An **acute** inflammation begins suddenly and usually dies down after a few days. If it lasts for months or years, it is called a **chronic** inflammation.

In medicine there are **five** classic signs of inflammation. Their Latin names are **rubor** (redness), **calor** (heat), **tumor** (swelling), **dolor** (pain) and **functio laesa** (reduced function). The first four were already described by the Roman doctor **Celsus**. The fifth sign was added later.

abschnitte.titel: Why it gets warm and swells
abschnitte.text: In inflammation, the blood vessels **widen**. More warm blood flows into the spot, which therefore looks red and feels warm. The walls of the small vessels also become more permeable. Fluid and defence cells get into the tissue, which as a result **swells**. An important messenger substance here is **histamine**, which is released by mast cells, among others.

Many medical names for inflammations end in **-itis**. Examples are **bronchitis**, an inflammation of the bronchi, or **arthritis**, an inflammation of a joint. **Appendicitis** is inflammation of the appendix. Strictly speaking, it is the appendix, the worm-shaped extension of the caecum, that becomes inflamed. The ending “-oma”, on the other hand, often stands for a growth and “-algia” for pain.

gewusst: Fever can also be part of the defence, because many germs grow less well at a higher temperature.
Antihistamines work against histamine, and people take them for hay fever, for example.

teile.einleitung: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor. In 1796 he carried out the first scientifically tested vaccination, against the dangerous disease smallpox. That is why he is often called the father of vaccination.
wichtigste: Edward Jenner was a country doctor from Berkeley in England.
He developed the first vaccine, against smallpox.
On 14 May 1796 he vaccinated a boy called James Phipps.
For this he used the harmless cowpox.
The word “vaccination” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow.
Jenner is regarded as the father of vaccination.

abschnitte.text: **Edward Jenner** lived from 1749 to 1823. He was a **country doctor** in **Berkeley** in the county of **Gloucestershire** in England. In his time, **smallpox** was one of the most feared diseases. Many people died of it, and survivors often had scars on their faces.

In the countryside it was well known that **milkmaids** who had caught the harmless **cowpox** did not catch real smallpox. In humans, cowpox is mild. Jenner took this observation seriously and wanted to **test it scientifically**. He suspected that cowpox prepares the body for the dangerous smallpox.

On **14 May 1796**, Jenner took material from a blister on a woman who had cowpox. He passed it on to eight-year-old **James Phipps**, the son of his gardener. It later turned out that the boy was **protected** against smallpox. Today, an experiment like this on a child would no longer be allowed, but back then these rules did not yet exist.

Jenner's method quickly spread all over **Europe**. The word **“vaccination”** reminds us of this: it comes from the Latin **“vacca”**, cow. Jenner's smallpox vaccine laid the foundation for all later **vaccines**. That is why he is often called the **father of vaccination**. Thanks to vaccinations around the world, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in **1980**.

gewusst: To this day, smallpox is the only human disease that has been completely wiped out.
The French scientist Louis Pasteur later suggested calling all vaccinations “vaccination” in honour of Jenner.

teile.einleitung: Erythrocytes are the red blood cells. They give blood its red colour and carry oxygen to all the cells of the body. Many trillions of them float in your blood.
wichtigste: Erythrocyte is the technical word for a red blood cell.
Red blood cells carry oxygen.
Their red colour comes from the iron-containing haemoglobin.
They have the shape of a disc dented on both sides.
In humans, mature erythrocytes have no cell nucleus.
They are made in the red bone marrow and live for about 120 days.

abschnitte.text: The name **erythrocyte** comes from Greek and means red cell. Red blood cells are the most common cells in the blood. An adult has about 25 trillion of them in all. A single drop of blood already holds many millions.

An erythrocyte is round and dented on both sides in the middle, a bit like a doughnut without a hole. It is only about 7 to 8 thousandths of a millimetre across. It is very flexible and can squeeze through the narrowest **capillaries**. In humans, a mature erythrocyte has no **cell nucleus**, which leaves more room for carrying oxygen.

Every erythrocyte is packed full of **haemoglobin**. This red pigment contains iron, to which oxygen binds. In the lungs the red blood cells take up oxygen and give it off again in the body. They also help to bring carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

Red blood cells are made in the red **bone marrow**, for example in the breastbone, pelvis and vertebrae. About two million new ones are made every second. An erythrocyte lives for about 120 days. After that it is broken down mainly in the spleen and the liver.

At great height, for example in the mountains, the body makes more red blood cells over time. This is controlled by the hormone **EPO** from the kidneys. If you have too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin, it is called anaemia. In sickle-cell disease, the erythrocytes have a wrong, sickle shape.

begriffe.erklaerung: The red, iron-containing pigment that binds oxygen.
Soft tissue inside the bones in which blood cells are made.
A hormone that stimulates the making of red blood cells.
A lack of blood, when there are too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin.

gewusst: If you laid all the red blood cells of one person side by side, they would cover an area of several thousand square metres.
Birds, reptiles and fish have red blood cells with a nucleus.
Some endurance athletes have used EPO illegally as a doping substance.

teile.einleitung: Frostbite is an injury caused by severe cold. The skin and tissue freeze, usually on the fingers, toes, nose or ears. In winter, when skiing or in the mountains, good protection against the cold is therefore important.
wichtigste: In frostbite, the skin and tissue freeze.
Fingers, toes, nose and ears are most likely to be affected.
Frostbitten skin is often white or grey and feels numb.
You never rub frostbitten skin with snow.
You warm it slowly, for example with body heat.
If the whole body cools too much, it is called **hypothermia**.

abschnitte.text: In severe cold, the body narrows the blood vessels in the hands and feet to keep the inside warm. As a result, fingers, toes, nose and ears get less warm blood. If it gets too cold, **skin and tissue freeze**. These parts of the body are furthest from the trunk or stick out freely. That is why they are most likely to freeze.

Frostbitten skin often looks **white or grey** and feels hard. At the spot, you feel **almost nothing**, as it is numb. This is exactly what makes it dangerous, because the frostbite is then easy to overlook. As it thaws, it can tingle and hurt. In severe frostbite, blisters form, and then you need a doctor.

First, you take the person somewhere warm and take off wet clothes. The frostbitten spot is warmed **slowly**, for example with body heat, such as under the armpit. You must **not rub it with snow**, because this injures the skin further. Hot water or a stove are also wrong, because you cannot feel the heat properly. Warm drinks help the whole body.

In winter, **warm gloves**, a hat and good shoes protect you. Several layers of clothing keep you warmer than one thick one. In **wind**, the cold feels much stronger, because the wind takes more warmth from the body. If the whole body cools too much, it is called **hypothermia**. It is dangerous, and you then call 144.

gewusst: The term “wind chill” describes how cold the air feels when there is wind.
Wet clothes cool the body down much faster than dry ones.

teile.einleitung: The set of teeth is all the teeth in the mouth together. With it we bite and chop up food, but it also helps with speaking. In a lifetime, a person gets two sets of teeth: first the baby teeth, then the permanent teeth.
wichtigste: A child's set of baby teeth has 20 teeth.
An adult has 32 teeth, counting all the wisdom teeth.
There are incisors, canines, premolars and molars.
Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
From about the age of 6, the changeover of teeth begins.
Tooth decay arises when bacteria turn sugar into acid.
Brushing your teeth twice a day protects against tooth decay.

abschnitte.text: The **set of teeth** consists of all the teeth in the upper and lower jaw. The teeth sit firmly in hollows of the jawbone. With the teeth we bite, chew and grind our food. Without teeth, speaking sounds such as S or F clearly would also be difficult.

At the front sit the **incisors**, with which we bite off pieces. Next to them come the pointed canines for holding and tearing. At the back lie the premolars and the **molars**, which grind the food. A complete adult set has 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars, so 32 in all.

From about the age of 6 months, babies get their first teeth. The complete set of **baby teeth** has 20 teeth. From about 6 years, the baby teeth fall out one after another, and the permanent teeth grow in. The rearmost molars, the **wisdom teeth**, often come only between 17 and 25 years or not at all.

The visible part is called the crown, and the part in the jaw is called the root. On the outside, the crown is covered by **tooth enamel**, the hardest substance in the body. Underneath lies the dentine. Right at the centre is the pulp with nerves and blood vessels.

Bacteria in dental plaque turn sugar into acid, which attacks the tooth enamel. This is how **tooth decay** comes about, that is, a hole in the tooth. You should brush at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste. In Switzerland, schoolchildren regularly visit the school dentist, and school dental hygienists show the right way to brush in class.

Animals have sets of teeth that suit their food. Predators such as the wolf have large canines and sharp carnassial teeth. Cows have broad molars for grinding grass, but no incisors at the top front. The incisors of rodents such as the beaver keep growing all their life.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard, shiny protective layer on the outside of the tooth.
Rotting of the tooth, in which acid eats holes into the teeth.
The first 20 teeth of a child.
The rearmost molar, which often only comes through in adults.

gewusst: Sharks can lose and replace thousands of teeth in the course of their lives.
In some people, the wisdom teeth never develop at all.
School dental care has been a tradition in Switzerland for decades and has greatly reduced tooth decay in children.

teile.einleitung: Choking means that a person can no longer get air. It often happens when a piece of food or a small object gets into the airways. Someone who knows what to do can save a life in such a moment.
wichtigste: Someone who is choking often grabs their throat and cannot speak.
As long as someone can cough strongly, they should keep coughing.
If an adult can no longer cough effectively, you give firm blows between the shoulder blades.
For back blows, a baby lies face down on your forearm, with the head lower.
If the person becomes unconscious, you call the emergency number and begin resuscitation.
When oxygen is missing, the lips turn **bluish**.

abschnitte.text: When we swallow, a small lid, the epiglottis, closes the windpipe. Sometimes this goes wrong, for example when you laugh or talk while eating. Then something gets into the airways. When foreign objects or liquid get into the airways, it is called **aspiration**. A strong cough reflex usually helps to bring the foreign object back out.

A person who can no longer get air **grabs their throat** and cannot speak. They look frightened and breathe with a whistling sound or not at all. If oxygen is missing for longer, the **lips turn bluish**. If the person can still **cough strongly**, you encourage them to keep coughing. Coughing is then the best thing they can do.

If an adult can no longer cough effectively, you first give **firm blows between the shoulder blades**. The person leans forward as you do this. If that does not help, there are other techniques, which you learn in a first-aid course. For a **baby**, back blows are given with the baby lying **face down on your forearm**, with the head lower than the body. If the person becomes **unconscious**, you lay them down, call the emergency number 144 and begin **resuscitation**.

Even if everything has turned out well, the person should be **examined by a doctor**. Pieces might have got into the lungs, or injuries might have occurred. For small children, **peanuts and marbles** are an especially common danger. Small, hard things should therefore be kept out of reach. When eating, it helps to sit calmly and chew well.

gewusst: Small children put many things in their mouths because that is how they explore their surroundings.
In Switzerland, the Samaritans' Association and other organisations offer first-aid courses, including for teenagers.

teile.einleitung: Electrolytes are substances that break up into electrically charged particles in water. In the body they are essential for nerves, muscles, the heart and the water balance.
wichtigste: An electrolyte breaks up into ions in solution and then conducts electricity.
Outside the cells, sodium is the most common positive ion.
Inside the cells, potassium is the most common positive ion.
Chloride is the most important negative ion outside the cells.
In the blood, normal levels are about 135 to 145 mmol/l of sodium and 3.5 to 5 mmol/l of potassium.
The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in.
About 99 per cent of the calcium is stored in the skeleton.

abschnitte.text: If you dissolve **table salt** in water, it breaks up into charged particles, the **ions**. Positively charged ones are called **cations**, negatively charged ones **anions**.
