Such substances are called **electrolytes**. Their solutions conduct electric current. In the body, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate are especially important.

Outside the cells, **sodium** is the most common cation. It largely decides how much water is held there. In the blood, it is normally about **135 to 145 mmol/l** and is controlled very tightly. Deviations can affect the brain. **Chloride** accompanies sodium as its counter-ion and is about 100 mmol/l in plasma, and bicarbonate is about 24 mmol/l.

Inside the cells, **potassium** is the most common cation. There its concentration is about 30 times higher than in the blood. This is important for the **resting membrane potential**, the electrical voltage at the cell wall. In the blood, potassium is normally **3.5 to 5 mmol/l**. Even small deviations can disturb the **heart rhythm**.

To keep these differences in place, the **sodium-potassium pump** works in every cell. In each cycle it uses up one **ATP**, the cell's energy carrier. In doing so it moves **three sodium ions** out and **two potassium ions** in. A large part of the energy the body needs at rest goes into these pumps.

About **99 per cent** of the **calcium** is in bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite. The small remainder in the blood is essential for blood clotting, muscles and nerves. When there are disturbances, doctors have to be careful: if a long-standing, severe sodium deficiency is corrected too quickly, brain cells suddenly lose water. This can damage the protective sheaths of the nerve fibres.

gewusst: When you sweat, you lose not only water but also electrolytes, mainly sodium.
The term electrolyte goes back to the English scientist Michael Faraday.

teile.einleitung: Breakfast is the first meal of the day. After the long night without food, it fills up the energy stores again. A healthy breakfast gives you strength for school, sport and play.
wichtigste: Breakfast is the first meal after getting up.
A healthy breakfast gives you energy for the day.
It can help you to concentrate better in the morning.
Wholegrain products, dairy products and fruit are good.
Heavily sugared breakfast cereals are more of a sweet.
Bircher muesli is a Swiss invention.
Every country has a different kind of breakfast.

abschnitte.text: **Breakfast** is the meal in the morning. The word means breaking the fast. At night, you eat nothing for many hours. In the morning the body therefore needs new energy.

The brain needs a lot of energy, above all in the form of sugar. A balanced breakfast supplies this energy slowly and evenly. Many children can then **concentrate** better at school. Someone who is not hungry at all in the morning can also take a healthy **mid-morning snack** (called “Znüni” in Swiss German) for break.

A good breakfast combines several food groups. These include **wholemeal bread** or oats, milk, yoghurt or cheese, and a piece of fruit. A glass of water or unsweetened tea completes the meal. Wholegrain keeps you full for longer because it contains a lot of **fibre**.

Many breakfast cereals contain a great deal of sugar. Sweet spreads, pastries and sugary drinks also supply a lot of sugar but few nutrients. Afterwards, hunger often comes back quickly. Such foods are more for special days.

A typical Swiss breakfast consists of bread, butter, jam and cheese, with milky coffee or Ovomaltine. On Sundays, many families have a **“Zopf”**, a plaited loaf. Around 1900, the doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner invented **Bircher muesli** in Zurich. It consists of oats, grated apple, nuts and milk or yoghurt.

In England, people like to eat eggs, bacon and beans. In Japan there is often rice, fish and miso soup. In France and Italy, by contrast, breakfast is small, for example a croissant and coffee. Every culture has its own breakfast habits.

begriffe.erklaerung: Parts of plants that keep you full for a long time and help digestion.
Grain in which the whole kernel with its husk is used.
Swiss German word for a small snack in the middle of the morning.
The sugar in the blood that supplies muscles and brain with energy.

gewusst: Bircher muesli was originally invented as a healthy evening meal for patients.
Ovomaltine was put on the market in Bern in 1904.

teile.einleitung: The fingertip is the soft, round end of a finger. It is one of the most sensitive spots on our body and helps us to feel things.
wichtigste: The soft end of a finger is called the fingertip.
With the fingertips you can feel most finely.
Blind people read Braille with their fingertips.
After a long bath, the fingertips become wrinkly.
On the upper side of the finger lies the fingernail.
A thimble protects the fingertip when sewing.

abschnitte.text: The **fingertip** is the soft, round end on the inner side of the finger. On the upper side, directly above, lies the **fingernail**. It supports the fingertip from above, so you can grip better. On the skin of the fingertip you can see fine lines that form the **fingerprint**.

In the fingertips there are especially many **touch receptors**. These are tiny sensory cells that feel pressure and touch. That is why no other part of the hand can feel so finely. Blind people use them to read **Braille**. It consists of raised dots that you feel with the fingertips.

You operate a **phone screen** best with the fingertip. The screen senses the conductive skin, and with the fingernail it mostly does not work. When sewing, you put on a **thimble** so that the needle does not prick the fingertip. People who often play the **guitar** get **hard skin** on their fingertips over time. It protects against the hard strings.

After a long bath, the fingertips look **wrinkly**. Researchers have found that this is controlled by the nervous system. The blood vessels under the skin contract, and the skin falls into folds. This probably helps you to hold on to wet objects better, rather like the tread of a tyre.

gewusst: Braille was invented by the Frenchman Louis Braille, who was blind himself.
In people whose hand nerves are injured, the fingertips do not go wrinkly in water.

teile.einleitung: Phagocytes are defence cells of our body. They take in germs and digest them, like tiny refuse collectors in the blood and in the tissue.
wichtigste: Phagocytes take in germs and digest them.
Phagocytes are also known as “eating cells”.
They belong to the white blood cells.
The process of taking in is called phagocytosis.
Large phagocytes in the tissue are called macrophages, and they develop from monocytes.
Ilya Metchnikoff discovered phagocytes and received the Nobel Prize in 1908.

abschnitte.text: Our body is constantly attacked by **germs** such as bacteria. To defend itself, it has various **white blood cells**. An important group of them are the **phagocytes**, which are also called “eating cells”. The word comes from Greek and means “cells that eat”. Their main job is to **take in and digest** germs.

When a phagocyte meets a germ, it wraps its cell membrane around it. Then it takes it into its inside. This process is called **phagocytosis**. Inside the cell, the germ is broken down with strong substances. Phagocytes also clear away dead cells and specks of dust.

Especially large phagocytes are called **macrophages**, which means “big eaters”. They live in the **tissue**, for example in the lungs, the liver or the skin. They develop from **monocytes**, a kind of white blood cell. When monocytes move from the blood into the tissue, they develop into macrophages.

Macrophages do not only eat, they also pass on information. After eating a germ, they show **pieces of the germ** on their surface. Other defence cells recognise these pieces and so get to know the enemy. Then the body can make **antibodies** in a targeted way. This is how different parts of the defence work together.

Phagocytes were discovered by the Russian researcher **Ilya Metchnikoff**. In the 19th century he watched starfish larvae under the microscope. In them he saw moving cells that wrapped themselves around foreign bodies. For his research he received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine in **1908**, together with Paul Ehrlich.

gewusst: Pus consists to a large extent of dead phagocytes and germs.
Macrophages in the lungs also eat the dust that we breathe in.

teile.einleitung: A pivot joint is a joint in which a bone turns around its own long axis. Thanks to such joints we can turn the head and turn the hand over.
wichtigste: In a pivot joint, a bone turns around its long axis.
Pivot joints are also called wheel joints or trochoid joints.
The first neck vertebra turns around the tooth of the second.
Between the radius and the ulna there are pivot joints.
Supination: palm up, pronation: palm down.
An annular ligament holds the head of the radius in place at the elbow.

abschnitte.text: In a **pivot joint**, a bone turns around its own **long axis**, like a wheel around its axle. That is why it is also called a **wheel joint** or **trochoid joint**. Other joints move differently: the **hinge joint** in the knee folds like a door, the **ball-and-socket joint** in the shoulder allows movements in many directions.

The first neck vertebra is called the **atlas**, the second the **axis**. The axis has a peg pointing upwards, the **dens** or tooth. The atlas turns together with the head around this peg. In this way we can look left and right, for example before we cross a road.

In the forearm lie two bones, the **radius** and the **ulna**. The joints between them are pivot joints. When the hand is turned over, the ulna stays almost still, and the **radius** turns around it and takes the hand with it. At the elbow, an **annular ligament** wraps round the head of the radius like a ring. In this way the radius can turn in it without slipping out.

If you turn the forearm so that the palm points upwards, this is called **supination**. You can remember it by thinking of carrying a bowl of soup. The opposite movement is called **pronation**: the palm points to the floor, for example when typing on a keyboard. We need both movements all the time, for example when unlocking a door with a key.

gewusst: The atlas is named after a figure from Greek myths who carries the sky. The neck vertebra carries the head.
When turning a screwdriver, you mainly use the pivot joints between the radius and the ulna.

teile.einleitung: The elbow is roughly in the middle of the arm. There you can bend the arm and straighten it again.
wichtigste: With the elbow you bend and straighten the arm.
It works roughly like a door hinge.
In German, it takes its name from the forearm bone, the Elle.
At the elbow lies the “funny bone”, a nerve right under the skin.
The ell used to be a unit of length.
“Using your elbows” means pushing your way forward without consideration for others.

abschnitte.text: With the **elbow joint** you bend the arm and straighten it again. This is how you bring a spoon to your mouth or throw a ball, for example. The elbow folds the arm mainly in one direction, like a door on its **hinge**. In addition, the forearm can rotate. This is how you turn your palm up or down.

In German, the elbow, Ellenbogen, gets its name from the **Elle**, the ulna, a long bone in the forearm. Its upper end forms the hard **tip** of the elbow. The ell, which has the same name in German, was also once a **unit of length**. It was roughly the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. Because arms differ in length, the ell was not the same length everywhere.

If you knock your elbow at a certain spot, it tingles all the way to your fingers. This spot is called the **funny bone**. In German it is the “Musikantenknochen”, the musician's bone, or the “Mäuschen”, the little mouse. It is actually not a bone at all. There a **nerve** lies right under the skin, the ulnar nerve. When it is knocked, it sends a tingling signal all the way to the little finger.

Someone who “**uses their elbows**” pushes in front and thinks only of themselves. This is a saying for inconsiderate behaviour. An old **table rule** says: elbows do not belong on the table when eating. Hands, on the other hand, may rest on the table. When cycling or skating, pads protect the elbows in a fall.

gewusst: In German, the funny bone is called the “Musikantenknochen”, the musician's bone.
You feel the tingling in the little finger and the ring finger, because the ulnar nerve runs to them.

teile.einleitung: An electrocardiogram, ECG for short, records the electrical activity of the heart. Electrodes on the skin measure tiny voltages that arise with every heartbeat.
wichtigste: An ECG measures electrical voltages on the skin in the millivolt range.
The P wave shows the excitation of the atria.
The QRS complex shows the excitation of the ventricles.
The T wave shows the excitation fading in the ventricles.
A standard resting ECG has 12 leads.
Willem Einthoven received the Nobel Prize in 1924 for the ECG.
ST segment elevation is a typical sign of a heart attack.

abschnitte.text: Before the heart muscle contracts, it is excited electrically. This **excitation** produces electric fields in the body. **Electrodes** on the skin measure the resulting voltage differences in the **millivolt** range. A machine records them as a curve. In this way you can see how the excitation travels through the heart.

The **P wave** appears when the excitation spreads from the **sinus node** across both atria. The large **QRS complex** shows the excitation of the ventricles. The **T wave** shows how the excitation fades again in the ventricles. The fading in the atria cannot be seen, because it happens at the same time as the much larger QRS complex. The **PQ interval** measures the conduction from the atria to the ventricles, and the normal range is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

ECG paper usually runs at 25 millimetres per second. If two R spikes are 20 millimetres apart, one beat lasts 0.8 seconds. 60 seconds divided by 0.8 gives **75 beats per minute**. A **standard resting ECG** has **12 leads**: 6 on the arms and legs and 6 on the chest wall, called V1 to V6.

The Dutch physiologist **Willem Einthoven** developed the string galvanometer, a very sensitive measuring device. With it he created the modern ECG. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in **1924**. The names P, Q, R, S and T for the waves also go back to him.

The ECG is used to detect heart rhythm disorders and other heart problems. A typical sign of an acute **heart attack** is **ST segment elevation**. This is then called a STEMI. Rescue services in Switzerland therefore have ECG machines in their vehicles.

gewusst: The first ECG machines weighed several hundred kilograms, and the patients put their hands and feet into basins of salt water.
Today some smartwatches can record a simple ECG.

teile.einleitung: Endorphins are messengers that the body makes itself. They can dull pain and bring a good feeling, for example after long exercise.
wichtigste: Endorphins are peptides, that is short chains of amino acids.
The name means “the body's own morphine”.
They are among the body's own opioids.
They were discovered in the 1970s.
They are made mainly in the brain, in the pituitary gland and hypothalamus.
Long endurance sport and laughing together release endorphins.

abschnitte.text: Endorphins are **peptides**, that is short chains of **amino acids**. They are cut out of a larger precursor protein. The name is made up of “**endogenous**” (made inside the body) and “**morphine**”. Endorphins are among the body's own **opioids**. These are substances that bind to certain docking sites in the nervous system, the opioid receptors.

**Morphine** is a very strong painkiller. It is obtained from the milky sap of the capsules of the **opium poppy** and needs a prescription. Endorphins work in a similar way in the body: they dull pain and can lift the mood. Unlike medicines, the body makes them itself and in small amounts.

In the **1970s**, researchers wanted to understand why morphine works in the brain. They found matching **receptors** on nerve cells. From this they concluded that the body must make similar substances itself. Soon afterwards they discovered the endorphins. They are made mainly in the **brain**, in the **pituitary gland** and in the **hypothalamus**.

After long **endurance sport** such as running or cycling, some people report a feeling of elation. It is called the “**runner's high**”. Researchers also found signs that endorphins are released when **laughing with friends**. Studies from Finland and England showed this. Laughing together probably also strengthens the sense of belonging.

gewusst: Morphine is named after Morpheus, the god of dreams in Greek legend.
Endorphins probably also help the body to feel less pain for a short time after injuries.

teile.einleitung: “Five a day” is a simple rule for healthy eating: every day we should eat five portions of vegetables and fruit. The rule helps us to get enough vitamins, minerals and fibre.
wichtigste: Five portions of vegetables and fruit are recommended every day.
About three of them should be portions of vegetables and two portions of fruit.
A portion is roughly a handful, so a little less for children.
Frozen vegetables count too.
Whole fruit is better than fruit juice.
Potatoes do not count towards “five a day”.

abschnitte.text: A **portion** is about as much as fits into your own hand. Children have smaller hands, so their portions are smaller too. This way the rule suits every age. An apple, a handful of berries or a bowl of salad is one portion each.

The recommendation is: **three portions of vegetables** plus fruit. Vegetables should therefore make up the larger part. Fresh vegetables are good, but **frozen** vegetables count too. They are frozen shortly after harvest and keep many good substances. **Potatoes**, by contrast, belong in the food pyramid with bread, rice and pasta and do not count.

A whole apple is healthier than a glass of apple juice. The Swiss nutrition recommendations of 2024 therefore focus on **whole fruit**. It contains more **fibre**, that is, plant parts that are good for digestion. Whole fruit also keeps you full for longer. Juice contains a lot of sugar and is drunk quickly.

Vegetables and fruit come in many colours: red tomatoes, orange carrots (called “Rüebli” in Swiss German), green broccoli, blue blueberries. Each colour points to different **plant compounds** and vitamins. Someone who eats colourfully therefore gets a little of many good substances. A plate with several colours is not only pretty but also healthy.

abschnitte.titel: How to manage it in everyday life
abschnitte.text: “Five a day” is easiest when **every meal** includes some vegetables or fruit. At breakfast, berries go well in muesli. For a **mid-morning snack** or an **afternoon snack**, apple slices, carrots or pieces of cucumber are suitable. Crisps, biscuits and gummy bears do not count. At lunch and dinner, there is salad or vegetables as a side dish.

gewusst: The idea of “five a day” exists in many countries, including Switzerland.
Frozen vegetables can sometimes contain more vitamins than vegetables that have lain for a long time in the fridge.

teile.einleitung: The **food pyramid** shows in a simple way how to eat a balanced diet. At the bottom are the foods you should eat plenty of, and at the top those you need only a little of. In Switzerland, the Swiss Society for Nutrition publishes these recommendations together with the Confederation.
wichtigste: The pyramid is wide at the bottom because you should eat the most of these.
The base is made up of drinks, with vegetables and fruit directly above.
3 portions of cereals, potatoes or pulses are recommended every day.
On top of that come 2 to 3 portions of dairy products a day.
You should eat meat at most 2 to 3 times a week.
At the very top are sweets and salty foods.

abschnitte.text: The pyramid is built in levels. At the bottom it is **wide**, because you should eat and drink the most of these. It gets narrower and narrower towards the top. At the very tip are **sweets and salty foods**, which you should enjoy only in small amounts. No food is forbidden, it is the amount that counts.

The bottom level is made up of **drinks**, ideally water or unsweetened tea. Directly above are **vegetables and fruit**. Several portions of these a day, in different colours, are recommended. They provide vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre.

The next level is cereals, potatoes and pulses. The Swiss pyramid recommends **3 portions** of these a day, for example bread, pasta or rice, ideally wholegrain. Above them come dairy products and sources of protein. Of **dairy products** such as milk, yoghurt or cheese, **2 to 3 portions** a day are recommended.

You need about **1 portion** a day of meat, fish, eggs or tofu, and you should vary them. You should eat **meat** at most **2 to 3 times a week**. Further up are oils, fats and nuts. About **2 tablespoons of vegetable oil** a day are recommended, especially **rapeseed oil**, because it contains valuable fatty acids. You need butter and cream only sparingly.

gewusst: The Swiss nutrition recommendations were revised in 2024.
Exercise is also part of a healthy lifestyle, not just food.

teile.einleitung: For many people, showering is part of their daily washing routine. You wash off sweat and dirt and feel fresh afterwards. With a few tricks, you can also save water.
wichtigste: A short shower usually uses less water than a bath.
After sport, you wash off the sweat.
Before swimming in an indoor pool, you have to shower.
You can turn the water off while you soap yourself.
The shower water should be pleasantly warm, not too hot.
A rubber mat protects against slipping.

abschnitte.text: When playing and doing **sport**, you sweat. If the **sweat** stays on your skin, it soon starts to smell, because bacteria break it down. Showering washes off sweat and dirt. For washing you use **shower gel**, a liquid soap for the skin. Washing-up liquid, on the other hand, is meant for dishes. The water comes out of the **shower head**, which has many small holes.

At an **indoor pool**, you shower **before swimming**. This keeps sweat, skin cream and dirt out of the pool water, and the water stays cleaner. The pool water contains **chlorine**, which kills germs but can dry out the skin. That is why you also shower **after swimming**, to rinse off the chlorinated water.

The water should be **pleasantly warm**. **Water that is too hot** can scald the skin and dries it out. Wet tiles are very **slippery**. That is why many showers have a **rubber mat** with little bumps, so that you stand safely. After showering, you dry yourself well, also between the toes.

A full **bath** needs a lot of water. A **short shower** usually needs much less. You save even more if you **turn the water off** while you soap yourself. Because warm water first has to be heated, showering for less time also saves **energy**. A water-saving shower head helps as well.

gewusst: A water-saving shower head mixes air into the water, so that less water flows through and it still feels powerful.
Showering too often or for a very long time can dry out the skin.

teile.einleitung: The double helix is the shape of DNA, the carrier of genetic information. Two strands wind around each other like a spiral staircase.
wichtigste: DNA consists of two strands that form a double helix.
The backbone of each strand consists of deoxyribose and phosphate.
Hydrogen bonds between the bases hold the strands together.
One turn of B-DNA comprises about 10 base pairs.
The double helix is around 2 nanometres thick and right-handed.
Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51” was an important clue to the helix.

abschnitte.text: **DNA** consists of two long strands that wind around each other. The “banister” of each strand, the **backbone**, consists alternately of the sugar **deoxyribose** and **phosphate**. The **bases** point inwards and form the steps. Two always fit together: **adenine with thymine** and **guanine with cytosine**. They are joined by **hydrogen bonds**.

The common form is called **B-DNA**. Its base pairs lie about **0.34 nanometres** above one another. A full turn comprises roughly **10 to 10.5 base pairs**. The helix is about **2 nanometres** thick and so far too thin for a light microscope. B-DNA is wound **right-handed**. There is also a left-handed form, Z-DNA, but it is rare.

The sugars of the two strands do not lie exactly opposite each other. As a result, two grooves of different width arise on the surface, the **major** and the **minor groove**. There many **proteins** bind to the DNA, for example those that switch genes on and off. Besides the hydrogen bonds, **stacking forces** between the bases lying on top of one another also stabilise the helix.

**Rosalind Franklin** and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling took the famous picture **“Photo 51”** with X-rays. Its X-shaped pattern pointed to a helix. In 1953 **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** presented their model of the double helix. In 1962 they received the Nobel Prize together with Maurice Wilkins. Franklin had already died in 1958.

gewusst: DNA as a substance was discovered as early as 1869 by the Basel researcher Friedrich Miescher.
The DNA of a single human cell, stretched out, would be about two metres long.

teile.einleitung: The **gall bladder** is a small organ under the liver. It stores bile and releases it when we eat something rich in fat.
wichtigste: The gall bladder lies in the upper right abdomen on the underside of the liver.
It is pear-shaped and about 8 to 10 centimetres long.
It holds about 30 to 50 millilitres of bile.
It stores the bile and thickens it.
After a fatty meal, it contracts.
You can live well even without a gall bladder.

abschnitte.text: The gall bladder lies in the **upper right abdomen**, directly on the underside of the liver. It is a small, **pear-shaped** hollow sac about 8 to 10 centimetres long. It is connected to the liver and the small intestine by ducts. The bile flows in and out again through these ducts.

The liver makes bile all the time, even between meals. During this time the gall bladder **collects** it. In doing so, it takes **water** out of the bile, so that it becomes concentrated. Although the gall bladder only holds about 30 to 50 millilitres, it can take in this much bile fluid.

When fatty **food pulp** enters the small intestine, cells in the gut wall release the hormone **cholecystokinin**. A hormone is a chemical messenger in the blood. It makes the gall bladder contract. Then a lot of bile flows into the gut and helps with the digestion of fat.

Sometimes components of the bile clump together and become hard. This is how **gallstones** form. Many people do not notice them. Gallstones can, however, cause strong pain in the upper abdomen. Then the gall bladder is often removed in an operation.

A person can **live well** without a gall bladder. The liver goes on making bile. It then releases it directly and continuously into the gut. Removal of the gall bladder is one of the most common operations on the abdomen.

gewusst: Some animals, for example horses, have no gall bladder at all.
The hormone cholecystokinin carries the gall bladder in its name: “chole” means bile in Greek, and “kystis” means bladder.

teile.einleitung: The **Eustachian tube** is a narrow passage that connects the middle ear with the back of the nose and throat. It is also called the **auditory tube**. It makes sure that the air pressure in the ear is the same as outside.
wichtigste: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear and the back of the nose and throat.
It serves mainly to **equalise the pressure** in the middle ear.
It is named after the anatomist Bartolomeo Eustachi.
In adults it is about 3.5 cm long.
Swallowing or yawning opens it and helps when flying.
In small children it is shorter and flatter.

abschnitte.text: Behind the eardrum lies the **middle ear**, a small space full of air. From there the Eustachian tube leads down to the **back of the nose and throat**, that is the space behind the nose. In adults it is about **3.5 cm** long. Usually it is closed and opens only briefly, for example when you swallow. Its name recalls the Italian anatomist **Bartolomeo Eustachi**, who lived in the 16th century.

For the eardrum to vibrate well, the air pressure has to be the same on both sides. The Eustachian tube takes care of this **pressure equalisation**. When a plane **comes in to land** or on a fast drive down a mountain, the air pressure outside rises. Then your ears feel pressure. **Swallowing or yawning** opens the tube, and with a soft click the pressure is equal again.

When diving, the pressure rises quickly underwater. Divers often equalise it with the **Valsalva manoeuvre**. They hold their nose shut and carefully blow air in. This pushes air through the Eustachian tube into the middle ear. You learn this on a diving course, because blowing too hard can harm the ear.

With a bad **cold**, the lining of the auditory tube swells. Then the ear feels dull and blocked, because no pressure equalisation is possible. In **small children** the auditory tube is shorter and flatter. Germs therefore get more easily from the back of the nose and throat into the middle ear. That is why children get **middle ear infections** more often than adults.

gewusst: The technical term for the auditory tube is tuba auditiva.
On a plane, a bottle or a sip of water often helps small children, because swallowing clears the ears.

teile.einleitung: **Evidence-based medicine** wants to base treatments on the best available evidence. Doctors are not supposed to decide only out of habit, but to check what good studies show.
wichtigste: It combines the best available study results, clinical experience and the wishes of patients.
At the very top of the evidence hierarchy are systematic reviews of randomised trials.
A **meta-analysis** combines the results of several studies statistically.
The **Cochrane** network is known for systematic reviews.
**David Sackett** of McMaster University in Canada is regarded as an important founder.
With **publication bias**, studies with positive results are more likely to be published.

abschnitte.text: When deciding on a treatment, evidence-based medicine combines three things. First, the **best available study results**, that is what good research shows. Second, the **clinical experience** of the doctor. Third, the **wishes and values of the patient**. Only all three together make a good decision.

Not every piece of evidence is equally strong. At the very top are usually **systematic reviews** of **randomised trials**. In a randomised trial, chance decides who gets which treatment, so that the comparison is fair. Combining the results of several studies on the same question statistically is called a **meta-analysis**. The opinion of a single expert **without study data**, on the other hand, counts as rather weak evidence.

One of the most important founders is regarded to be the doctor **David Sackett**, who worked at **McMaster University** in Canada. The term became well known in the early 1990s. The international network **Cochrane** produces systematic reviews of medical treatments. Professional societies sum up the knowledge in **guidelines**. These are recommendations for how to treat particular diseases.

A useful figure is the **number needed to treat**, NNT for short. It says how many people have to be treated for one of them to benefit. If a medicine lowers the risk of a heart attack from 10 % to 5 %, the difference is 5 percentage points. You work out 100 divided by 5 and get an NNT of **20**. Care is needed with **publication bias**: studies with positive results are more likely to be published, so a treatment can look better than it is.

gewusst: The Cochrane network is named after the British doctor Archie Cochrane.
The smaller the NNT, the more people benefit from a treatment.

teile.einleitung: Loneliness is the distressing feeling of having too few real relationships with other people. It can affect anyone, older people just as much as teenagers.
wichtigste: Being alone can be pleasant, but loneliness is a painful feeling.
Social isolation means that someone really has hardly any contacts.
Loneliness that lasts a long time acts like constant stress and can harm health.
Besides older people, many young adults also feel lonely.
Clubs, groups and hobbies help you find new contacts.
Online contacts do not fully replace real meetings.

abschnitte.text: Many people like being **alone** from time to time, for example when reading or hiking. They still feel connected with others. **Loneliness** is something different: you feel misunderstood or have too few close relationships. You can even feel lonely in the middle of a group. When someone objectively has hardly any contacts, this is called **social isolation**.

Almost everyone knows short phases of loneliness. If it lasts a long time, it means lasting **stress** for the body. Studies show links with **cardiovascular diseases** and **depression**. That is why loneliness is now seen as an important health issue. It is worth taking seriously.

In January 2018, the politician Tracey Crouch was given responsibility for the issue of loneliness in **Great Britain**. In this way loneliness was recognised as a problem for society. In Switzerland, too, it is being researched and discussed. Surveys show that besides older people, many **teenagers and young adults** also feel lonely.

Someone who feels lonely can join a **club**, a sports group or a course. There you meet people with the same interests. Volunteering also brings contacts. **Social media** can connect people, but does not replace meeting in person. Someone who keeps comparing themselves with others can even feel lonelier. Talking with people you trust or with advice centres also helps.

If a classmate often stands alone at break, a small step can make a big difference: **speak to them and invite them**. Often the person is just waiting for it. A friendly question or a game together can be the start of a friendship.

gewusst: In 2018, Great Britain was one of the first countries to give a member of the government responsibility for the issue of loneliness.
You can feel lonely in the middle of many people and be happy on your own.

teile.einleitung: A **bicycle helmet** protects the head in a fall. It can prevent or lessen serious head injuries. That is why you should wear it on every ride, even on short trips.
wichtigste: You wear a bicycle helmet **on every ride**.
The foam in the helmet cushions the impact.
The strap is fastened under the chin.
About one finger fits between the chin and the strap.
After a hard fall, you replace the helmet.
In Switzerland, a helmet is compulsory on the fast e-bike.

abschnitte.text: A bicycle helmet consists of a hard shell on the outside and **foam** on the inside. In a fall, the foam is squashed and **cushions the impact**. This means less force reaches the head. Because the foam is damaged in the process, it protects less well next time. That is why you have to **replace the helmet after a hard fall**, even if you cannot see anything from the outside.

The helmet has to fit well and sit straight on the head, so that it protects the forehead. It is fastened with a strap **under the chin**. There should be room for **about one finger** between the chin and the chin strap. If the strap is too loose, the helmet can slip in a fall. Many helmets have a little wheel at the back for adjusting the size.

In Switzerland, a helmet is not compulsory for cyclists. For the **fast e-bike**, which assists up to 45 km/h, a helmet is required. Experts still recommend a helmet to everyone, **on every ride**. A fall can also happen slowly and on the way to school.

A helmet in **bright colours** such as yellow makes you easy to see in traffic. Many helmets also have reflectors or a small light. Light-coloured clothing also helps, especially at dusk. Someone who is seen well travels more safely.

gewusst: A helmet can age over time, even if it has never been in a fall.
Bicycle helmets are tested against standards before they are sold.

teile.einleitung: Fluoridated table salt is cooking salt with fluoride mixed in. It is meant to help prevent tooth decay and has been widely used in Switzerland for decades.
wichtigste: Fluoridated table salt is used to prevent tooth decay.
In Switzerland it was introduced in the 1950s.
It contains around 250 mg of fluoride per kilogram of salt.
In tooth enamel, fluoride turns into hard fluorapatite.
Fluoride also promotes the remineralisation of early damage.
For decades, Basel fluoridated its drinking water instead of the salt.

abschnitte.text: **Fluoridated table salt** is ordinary cooking salt with a small addition of **fluoride**. It is used for the **prevention of tooth decay**, that is, to protect teeth from holes. The idea behind it: almost everybody eats salt every day. This way the whole population gets a small amount of fluoride without having to do anything special.

Tooth enamel consists mainly of a mineral called **apatite**. When fluoride is built in, **fluorapatite** forms. This is harder and resists acids better. In addition, fluoride promotes **remineralisation**: early, small damage in the enamel is filled up again with minerals.

In Switzerland, fluoridated table salt was introduced in the **1950s**. Switzerland was thus one of the first countries to do so. Today it contains around **250 mg of fluoride per kilogram** of salt. The city of **Basel** fluoridated its **drinking water** instead of the salt for decades. In 2003 it stopped doing so.

You can tell whether table salt contains fluoride from the note **“with fluoride”** or **“fluoridated”** on the packet. Often the same salt also contains **iodine**, which is important for the thyroid gland. There is also salt without additives. Every family can choose for itself which one it buys.

Fluoride only works well in small amounts. Taking in too much while the teeth are developing can cause **dental fluorosis**. This produces **white spots** in the tooth enamel. That is why experts make sure that salt, toothpaste and other sources together do not add up to too much.

gewusst: A kilogram of fluoridated salt contains only about a quarter of a gram of fluoride.
Besides Switzerland, other countries such as Germany also use fluoridated table salt.

teile.einleitung: Thanks to the finger joints, we can grip, write and make a fist. Each finger has several small joints that make it flexible.
wichtigste: An index finger has three joints, not counting the wrist.
The thumb consists of two finger bones.
The joint at the front is called the end joint, the one at the back the knuckle joint.
Finger joints bend well towards the palm.
In the cold, muscles and tendons become stiff.
The bumps on the back of the hand when you make a fist are called knuckles.

abschnitte.text: A finger is made of small bones, the **phalanges**. The index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger each have three. The **thumb** has only two finger bones. A **joint** is the movable connection between two bones. An index finger therefore has three joints, if you do not count the wrist.

The joint where the finger meets the hand is called the **knuckle joint**. In the middle of the finger lies the **middle joint**. Right at the front by the fingertip sits the **end joint**. When you make a fist, you see hard bumps on the back of the hand, the **knuckles**. These are the heads of the metacarpal bones at the knuckle joint.

There are almost no muscles in the fingers themselves. The force comes from muscles in the **forearm** and in the hand. They pull on the finger bones through long **tendons**, like strings. The finger joints bend well **towards the palm**. In the other direction, they only move a little. In great cold, muscles and tendons become stiff, which is why the fingers are harder to move then.

When playing ball games, you often sprain a finger. This happens when the ball hits the **fingertip** head-on. The joint is then pushed in too hard, swells and hurts. Cooling and rest usually help. If the finger is crooked or cannot be moved at all, a doctor should look at it.

gewusst: A hand has 27 bones, counting the wrist, the palm and the fingers.
The crack when you crack your fingers is caused by gas that forms in the joint fluid.

teile.einleitung: The fovea centralis is a tiny pit in the retina of the eye. We see sharpest there, which is why we always point our eyes so that the image falls exactly on this spot.
wichtigste: The fovea centralis is also known simply as the fovea.
It lies in the macula, the yellow spot of the retina.
In the fovea there are almost only cones.
Its diameter is about 1.5 mm.
Here sight is sharpest, because the cones are hardly linked together.
With fast jumps of the gaze, called saccades, the eye brings objects onto the fovea.

abschnitte.text: At the back of the eye lies the **retina**. It contains sensory cells that turn light into nerve signals. In its centre lies the **macula**, also called the **yellow spot**. In the middle of the macula is the **fovea centralis**, which means “central pit”. It has a diameter of **about 1.5 mm**.

The retina has two kinds of sensory cells: **rods** for seeing in dim light and **cones** for colours and sharp sight. In the fovea you find **almost only cones**, packed close together. There, each cone is connected almost singly to a nerve cell. Because the cones are **hardly linked together**, **sharpness of sight** is greatest here.

abschnitte.titel: A clear path for the light
abschnitte.text: Normally, light first has to pass through several layers of nerve cells before it reaches the sensory cells. In the fovea, these **inner layers of the retina are pushed aside**. This is how the small pit comes about. The light thus reaches the cones especially **without obstruction**.

abschnitte.titel: Jumps of the gaze and the blind spot
abschnitte.text: Because only the fovea sees so sharply, the eyes move constantly. With fast jumps of the gaze, the **saccades**, they bring important things exactly onto the fovea. When reading, too, the gaze jumps from word to word like this. Somewhat towards the nose, beside the fovea, lies the **blind spot**. There the optic nerve leaves the eye, and there are no sensory cells at all.

A disease that is common in old age is **age-related macular degeneration**. In it, cells in the macula are damaged. Those affected see blurred or a dark spot in the middle of their field of vision. **Central vision** is disturbed, while at the edges they can often still see. Regular check-ups at the eye doctor are therefore important in old age.

gewusst: Many birds of prey even have two foveae in each eye and so see especially sharply.
We do not notice the blind spot in everyday life, because the brain fills in the gap.

teile.einleitung: Bones form in the body in two ways. In desmal ossification, bone is formed directly from connective tissue, without a detour through cartilage. This is how mainly the flat bones of the skull arise.
wichtigste: Desmal ossification means direct bone formation from connective tissue.
There is no cartilage precursor.
This is how mainly the flat bones of the skull vault arise.
Many bones of the face and for the most part the collarbone also arise in this way.
Ossification begins in ossification centres.
First woven bone arises, later lamellar bone.

abschnitte.text: **Ossification** means the formation of bone. In **endochondral ossification**, a model made of cartilage arises first, which is later replaced by bone. In **desmal ossification** this detour is missing: the bone arises directly from connective tissue. The name comes from the Greek word **“desmos”**, which means band or fetter.

At the start there is a loose connective tissue called **mesenchyme**. At certain places, the **ossification centres**, cells gather and become **osteoblasts**. These are cells that form bone substance. They build up fine bony struts, and from there the ossification spreads outwards. First disordered **woven bone** arises, which is later remodelled into firm **lamellar bone**.

Typically formed by the desmal route are the flat bones of the **skull vault**: the frontal bone, the parietal bones and parts of the occipital bone. They are also called **membrane bones**. In addition there are many bones of the face, such as the **upper jaw**, the **cheekbone** and the nasal bone. The **collarbone** too arises for the most part by the desmal route, only its ends arise by way of cartilage. Vertebrae, ribs and the bones of the arms and legs, by contrast, have a cartilage model.

Even in long bones such as the thigh bone, the desmal way plays a part. Around the cartilaginous shaft lies a sheath, the **perichondrium**. From it come osteoblasts that form a **bony collar** directly around the shaft. This **perichondral ossification** works in principle like a desmal ossification.

gewusst: The collarbone is the first bone of the body to begin to ossify.
In babies the skull bones have not yet grown completely together. The soft places between them are called fontanelles.

teile.einleitung: Enzymes are tiny helpers in all living things that speed up chemical reactions. Without them, digesting your food would take years. Each enzyme has a very particular job.
wichtigste: Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions in the body.
They are not used up in the process.
The substance an enzyme converts is called the substrate.
The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.
According to the lock-and-key principle, only a particular substrate fits a particular enzyme.
Most human enzymes denature at temperatures well above 40 °C.
Amylase in saliva begins the digestion of starch.

abschnitte.text: An **enzyme** is a biological catalyst, that is a substance that makes a chemical reaction run faster. Most enzymes are proteins. After the reaction they are unchanged and can get straight back to work. The body has thousands of different enzymes.

The substance an enzyme works on is called the **substrate**. It binds at a special spot, the **active site**. Only a matching substrate fits in, just as only a particular key fits a lock. This is called the **lock-and-key principle**.

Digestion already begins in the mouth: the **amylase** in saliva breaks starch down into sugar. If you chew bread for a long time, it therefore tastes slightly sweet. In the stomach, the enzyme pepsin splits proteins, and works best at a very acidic pH of about 2. In the small intestine, more enzymes from the pancreas help.

Enzymes only work well under suitable conditions. Most human enzymes work best at about 37 °C. If it gets much warmer than 40 °C, their shape changes and they **denature**, which means they are ruined. The pH also has to be right, and each enzyme has its favourite range.

Enzymes can be slowed down. In **competitive inhibition**, a similar substance occupies the active site, so that the substrate can no longer bind. Many medicines work in this way. Some poisons also block vital enzymes.

Washing powders contain enzymes that remove stains made of protein or fat. In cheese-making, also in Switzerland, the enzyme rennet makes the milk curdle. Enzymes also help in baking and brewing beer. Many enzyme names end in -ase, for example lactase.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance that an enzyme converts.
The spot on the enzyme where the substrate docks.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A protein being ruined when it loses its shape.

gewusst: Some enzymes manage thousands of reactions per second.
People who cannot digest milk well often have too little of the enzyme lactase.
Bacteria from hot springs have enzymes that work even at over 70 °C.

teile.einleitung: Depression is a serious mental illness. Those affected feel low for a long time, lose their joy and have hardly any drive. Depression is not a weakness, and it can be treated well.
wichtigste: Depressions are described as an illness in the WHO’s **ICD**.
A main symptom is the **loss of interest and joy**.
The symptoms must last for at least about **two weeks**.
In **bipolar disorder**, depressive and manic phases alternate.
Antidepressants often act only after a few weeks.
Against winter depression, **light therapy** often helps.

abschnitte.text: Everyone is sad sometimes, that is normal. In a **depression** it is different: the low mood stays for a long time and cannot simply be shaken off. Many of those affected lose **interest and joy** in things they used to like. The inability to feel joy is called **anhedonia**. In addition there are often tiredness, sleep problems and difficulty concentrating.

The World Health Organization WHO describes illnesses in the **ICD**, the international classification of diseases. Depression is listed there too. According to ICD-10, low mood, **loss of interest and joy** and reduced drive are among the main symptoms. For a **depressive episode** to be diagnosed, the symptoms must last for at least **about two weeks**. The diagnosis is made by doctors or psychologists after a detailed conversation.

There are different forms. In **bipolar disorder**, depressive phases alternate with **manic** phases, in which someone is excessively wound up and full of energy. **Dysthymia** is a milder, chronic depressive mood that lasts for years. In **seasonal affective disorder**, the “winter depression”, the complaints appear mainly in the dark season.

A depression can be treated well. **Psychotherapy**, that is, conversations with a professional, is very important. Often **antidepressants** help in addition. Commonly prescribed are **SSRIs**, which act mainly on the messenger substance **serotonin** in the brain. Their mood-lifting effect typically sets in **only after a few weeks**. In winter depression, **light therapy** with a very bright lamp is often used.

Anyone who feels low for a long time should talk to someone about it, for example their parents, a teacher or the family doctor. In Switzerland, children and young people can call Pro Juventute’s number **147** free of charge around the clock. For adults there is **Die Dargebotene Hand** (The Helping Hand) on the number **143**. For friends with a depression, it helps if you listen and take them seriously.

gewusst: Depressions are among the most common illnesses in the world.
Exercise in the fresh air and a regular daily routine can support treatment.

teile.einleitung: Frederick Banting was a Canadian doctor and researcher. With his team he discovered the hormone insulin in 1921, which still saves the lives of millions of people with diabetes today.
wichtigste: Banting and his team discovered insulin in 1921.
He worked on it together with the young student Charles Best.
They obtained the insulin from the pancreas.
In 1922, Leonard Thompson became the first person to be treated with insulin.
In 1923, Banting received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with John Macleod.
He is still the youngest winner of the prize for medicine.
The discoverers sold the patent for a symbolic sum.

abschnitte.text: Frederick Banting was born in **1891** in the Canadian province of Ontario. He became a doctor and served as an army doctor in the First World War. Afterwards he turned to the illness **diabetes mellitus**. In **type 1**, the body no longer makes **insulin**. Insulin is a **hormone**, that is, a chemical messenger that carries sugar from the blood into the cells. Without treatment, this illness was deadly at that time.

In 1921, Banting began research at the **University of Toronto**. Professor **John Macleod** gave him a laboratory. The young student **Charles Best** helped him with the experiments. The two obtained insulin from the **pancreas** of animals. In 1922, the biochemist **James Collip** purified the extract so that it could be used safely on humans.

In **1922**, 14-year-old **Leonard Thompson** in Toronto became the first person to be treated with insulin. He was seriously ill, and after the treatment he was clearly better. Soon many more sick people could be treated. **Type 1 diabetes mellitus** could thus be treated for the first time.

Already in **1923**, Banting and **John Macleod** received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine**. Banting was 32 years old at the time and is still the **youngest winner** of the prize for medicine. He thought it unfair that Best was not honoured, and shared his prize money with him. The discoverers sold their **patent** to the university for a **symbolic sum**. They wanted insulin to stay affordable for everyone.

gewusst: World Diabetes Day on 14 November is Banting's birthday.
Banting was also a gifted painter and painted Canadian landscapes.

teile.einleitung: Dopamine is an important messenger substance in the body. In the brain it helps to control movements and plays a part in motivation and reward.
wichtigste: Dopamine is made from the amino acid tyrosine.
It belongs to the catecholamines, like noradrenaline and adrenaline.
In the body, noradrenaline is made from dopamine.
In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine-making cells of the substantia nigra die off.
Five dopamine receptors are distinguished, D1 to D5.
Arvid Carlsson received a Nobel Prize in 2000 for his dopamine research.

abschnitte.text: Dopamine is made from the amino acid **tyrosine**. The enzyme **tyrosine hydroxylase** first changes tyrosine, and in a second step dopamine arises. The body can also make tyrosine from phenylalanine. From dopamine, a further enzyme makes **noradrenaline**, and from that **adrenaline** can arise. All three belong to the **catecholamines**, because they contain a special ring with two hydroxyl groups.

As a **neurotransmitter**, dopamine passes signals from one nerve cell to the next. It docks onto **receptors**. In humans, five types are distinguished, **D1 to D5**. They are divided into a D1-like and a D2-like family. Depending on the receptor and brain region, dopamine acts in quite different ways.

Dopamine-making nerve cells in the **substantia nigra** in the midbrain control **movements** by way of the striatum. In **Parkinson’s disease**, these cells die off. Tremor, muscle stiffness and slowness of movement result. Dopamine itself cannot be given as a medicine, because it does not pass the **blood-brain barrier**. That is why **L-dopa** is given, which is turned into dopamine only in the brain.

Other dopaminergic nerve cells run from the midbrain to the **nucleus accumbens**. This **mesolimbic system** is closely linked with **reward** and **motivation**. It helps us to learn what is worthwhile. This reward system also plays an important part in **addiction**, though.

The Swedish researcher **Arvid Carlsson** showed in the **1950s** that dopamine is a messenger substance in its own right and is important for the control of movement. For this he received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** in **2000**. He shared the prize with Paul Greengard and Eric Kandel, who had researched other questions about nerve cells.

gewusst: In the past dopamine was thought to be only a precursor of noradrenaline, until its own role as a messenger substance was discovered.
Dopamine acts not only in the brain, but for example also on blood vessels and kidneys.

teile.einleitung: Fingernails are hard plates on the upper side of our fingertips. They protect the fingers and help us to grip small things.
wichtigste: Fingernails are made of horn, the substance keratin.
A person normally has 10 fingernails.
A fingernail grows only a few millimetres a month.
Fingernails grow faster than toenails.
Cutting does not hurt, because the front of the nail has no nerves.
On a nail you can tell apart the lunula and the cuticle.

abschnitte.text: Fingernails are made of **horn**. The technical term for this substance is **keratin**. Our hair and the outermost layer of skin are also made of keratin. A person normally has **10 fingernails**. They **protect** the sensitive fingertips and help to grip or scratch small things.

At the bottom of the fingernail you see a pale half-moon, the **lunula**. This is where the start of the nail plate lies, which is not yet fully hard. The thin skin at the lower edge is called the **cuticle**. It seals the gap so that no dirt or germs get in. That is why you should not tear it off.

The nail grows from a zone under the skin, the **nail root**. In a month, it grows only **a few millimetres**. **Fingernails** grow faster than **toenails**. The front part of the nail consists of dead cells and has **no nerves**. That is why cutting does not hurt.

It is best to cut fingernails with **nail scissors** or nail clippers. You do not cut too short, or the skin underneath can hurt. With a file you can smooth sharp edges. Clean nails are important, because dirt and germs easily collect under long nails.

gewusst: Cats have claws on their paws, which are also made of horn.
It takes several months for a whole fingernail to grow back once.

teile.einleitung: In diarrhoea the stool is watery and you have to go to the toilet often. Usually it is harmless and goes away by itself, but it is important to drink enough.
wichtigste: According to the WHO, you speak of diarrhoea from three watery stools a day.
The greatest danger is dehydration, especially in small children.
You should drink a lot and replace salts.
Noroviruses and rotaviruses are common triggers.
Thorough hand washing protects against infection.
When travelling the rule is: “Boil it, peel it or forget it”.

abschnitte.text: The **World Health Organization** (WHO) speaks of diarrhoea when you have watery stool **at least three times a day**. The intestine then takes up too little water or even gives off water. Common causes are **viruses** or **bacteria**, sometimes also spoiled food. Usually diarrhoea lasts only a few days.

In diarrhoea the body loses a lot of **water** and **salts**. The greatest danger is therefore **dehydration**. **Small children** especially can dry out quickly. It is important to drink a lot, best with a little salt and sugar. Special **rehydration solutions** from the pharmacy contain both in the right proportion. If a small child becomes very limp or no longer drinks, you must go to the doctor.

**Noroviruses** are very contagious and suddenly cause vomiting and diarrhoea, often in winter. Outbreaks are common in schools, hospitals and on ships. **Rotaviruses** affect mainly babies and small children and are among the most common causes of severe diarrhoea worldwide. Against rotaviruses there is an **oral vaccine**.

Many germs that cause diarrhoea are passed on by **dirty hands**. That is why **washing hands with soap** protects effectively, especially after the toilet and before eating. Anyone with diarrhoea does best to use a towel of their own. In this way the others in the family catch it less easily.

**Travellers’ diarrhoea** is the most common illness on trips to warm countries. Usually it is caused by bacteria in **water** or **food**. Helpful is the rule **“Boil it, peel it or forget it”**: boiling kills germs, and when peeling you remove the dirty skin. Raw, unpeeled food and **ice cubes** are risky.

gewusst: Very few noroviruses are enough to infect a person.
In Switzerland you can drink tap water almost everywhere without worry, but on many trips you cannot.

teile.einleitung: **Bile acids** are substances that the liver makes from cholesterol. They are an important part of bile and help to digest fat.
wichtigste: The liver makes bile acids from cholesterol.
The primary bile acids are cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid.
Gut bacteria convert them into secondary bile acids.
The liver joins bile acids with glycine or taurine.
About 95 per cent return through the enterohepatic circulation.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is used as a medicine against small gallstones.

abschnitte.text: The liver turns **cholesterol** into bile acids in several steps. Each step is controlled by an **enzyme**, a substance that speeds up chemical processes. For the body, this is an important way to get rid of cholesterol. Between meals, the bile is stored and thickened in the **gall bladder**.

The human liver makes two **primary bile acids**: **cholic acid** and **chenodeoxycholic acid**. In the gut, bacteria change these substances. This creates **secondary bile acids** such as deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid. So they are not made in the liver but only in the gut.

Before the liver releases the bile acids, it joins them with **glycine** or **taurine**. This process is called **conjugation**. It produces **bile salts**, which work better in the gut. They break fat up into tiny droplets so that enzymes can split it.

About **95 per cent** of the bile acids are taken up again in the lower small intestine. The blood carries them back to the liver. This route is called the **enterohepatic circulation**. Only a small remainder is lost in the stools. Through the nuclear receptor **FXR**, the bile acids slow down their own new production, which is a **negative feedback**.

The bile acid **ursodeoxycholic acid** is used as a medicine. It changes the make-up of the bile. With suitable small **cholesterol gallstones**, it can slowly dissolve them. The treatment, however, often takes many months.

gewusst: Ursodeoxycholic acid was first found in the bile of bears, hence the name: “ursus” means bear in Latin.
Because bile acids go round in a cycle, the body uses them several times a day.

teile.einleitung: Jealousy is a strong feeling that almost everyone knows. You are afraid that someone else will be favoured and that you will get less love or attention yourself.
wichtigste: Jealousy is the fear of being noticed or loved less than someone else.
Almost everyone feels jealous at some point, it is a normal feeling.
Jealousy is common between brothers and sisters, for example when a baby needs a lot of care.
Jealous children often want to show: I am still here too.
Talking about your own feelings helps most.
Being generous means being happy for others, it is the opposite of envy.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is jealous fears losing something important: a person's love, friendship or attention. Jealousy often comes together with anger, sadness or fear. Closely related is **envy**. You are envious when someone else has something you would like to have yourself. For strong envy there is the saying “green with envy”.

When a new **baby brother or sister** is born, the baby needs a lot of care. The parents then have less time for the older children. These children sometimes feel pushed aside and become jealous. Some children then behave like a baby again or get up to mischief. Behind this there is usually a wish for **attention**. Jealousy can also arise between older siblings or between friends.

Researchers have studied how **dogs** react when their human strokes a toy dog. Many dogs pushed in between and shoved the toy dog away. This suggests that dogs, too, can feel a kind of jealousy. Anyone with several pets often notices that they compete for cuddles.

Jealousy is unpleasant, but no reason to feel ashamed. What helps best is to **say how you feel**. If you talk about your feelings, you can find a solution together with others. Parents can, for example, deliberately spend time alone with each child. It is also important not to take anything away from others and not to hurt anyone.

The opposite of envy is **being generous**. Someone who is generous is happy for others when they get something nice or are good at something. This does not always work straight away. It helps to think about the good things you have yourself. If you are happy for others, you make others and yourself happy.

gewusst: The saying “green with envy” has been around for a very long time, and in English too, envy is described as being green.
In one study, jealous dogs pushed away a toy dog that their human was stroking.

teile.einleitung: The deltoid muscle is the strong muscle that rounds the shoulder. It moves the upper arm in many directions: forwards, sideways and backwards. It gets its name from its triangular shape.
wichtigste: The deltoid muscle is named after the Greek letter **delta**, which looks like a triangle.
It arises from the **collarbone** and the **shoulder blade**.
It attaches to the **upper arm bone**.
The middle part lifts the arm sideways.
The front part lifts the arm forwards, the rear part pulls it backwards.
It is supplied by the **axillary nerve** and is often used for vaccinations.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the Greek letter **delta**, which as a capital looks like a triangle (Δ). That is exactly what the muscle looks like when you see it from the side. It lies like a cap over the shoulder joint. That is why it gives the shoulder its round shape. You can feel it well when you lift your arm to the side.

A muscle is fixed to the bone at two places. The **origin** of the deltoid muscle lies on the **collarbone** and the **shoulder blade**. From there its fibres run downwards. They meet and attach about halfway down the **upper arm bone**. When the muscle contracts, it therefore moves the upper arm.

The deltoid muscle consists of three parts. The **front part** helps to lift the arm **forwards**. The **middle part** lifts the arm mainly **sideways**, until it is horizontal. The **rear part** pulls the raised arm **backwards**. Together they make the shoulder one of the most mobile joints of the body.

Every muscle needs a **nerve** that brings it commands from the brain. The deltoid muscle is supplied by the **axillary nerve**, in Latin **nervus axillaris**. If this nerve is injured, for example in a dislocated shoulder, it is harder to lift the arm sideways. After such an injury, doctors therefore also check the function of the nerve.

In young people and adults, a vaccination is often injected into the **deltoid muscle**. The muscle lies within easy reach on the upper arm, and no large blood vessels run directly under the skin there. Muscles have a good blood supply, so the vaccine reliably reaches the immune system. In babies, by contrast, the vaccination is usually given in the thigh.

gewusst: In strength training, the deltoid muscle counts as an important muscle for broad shoulders.
The deltoid muscle works closely with smaller muscles of the shoulder that keep the joint stable.

teile.einleitung: A defibrillator is a device that can end a dangerous heart rhythm with an electric shock. In a cardiac arrest every minute counts. That is why devices that lay people may also use now hang in many places.
wichtigste: A defibrillator ends a dangerous heart rhythm with an **electric shock**.
**AED** stands for automated external defibrillator.
It can end **ventricular fibrillation**.
People without medical training may also use an AED.
During the shock, nobody may touch the person.
In chest compressions you press about 5 to 6 centimetres deep, 100 to 120 times a minute.

abschnitte.text: Normally the heart contracts regularly and pumps blood through the body. In **ventricular fibrillation**, the heart muscle cells only twitch in confusion. The heart then no longer pumps blood, and the person collapses. A **defibrillator** gives a strong **electric shock**. This can end the confusion, so that the heart can beat in the right rhythm again.

**AED** stands for **automated external defibrillator**. It hangs, for example, in stations, schools, sports halls or shopping centres. Anyone may use it, even without medical training. The device gives clear **spoken instructions** and says step by step what to do. It checks the heart rhythm itself and gives a shock only if it is needed.

First you call the emergency number **144** and begin chest compressions. Then you open the AED and stick the **electrodes** on the **bare chest**, as shown in the pictures. The AED analyses the heart rhythm. While it gives a shock, **nobody may touch the person**, otherwise you get an electric shock yourself. After that the chest compressions carry on at once.

Until the device is ready, and afterwards too, **chest compressions** are very important. You press down hard with both hands in the middle of the chest. The rate is **100 to 120 times a minute**. In an adult you press the chest in **about 5 to 6 centimetres**. In this way some blood keeps flowing to the brain.

Some people have a high risk of dangerous heart rhythm disorders. They get an **implantable defibrillator**, which is placed under the skin. Thin wires usually lead to the heart. The device monitors the heartbeat around the clock. If it recognises ventricular fibrillation, it gives an electric shock by itself.

gewusst: The sooner a defibrillator is used, the greater the chance of survival.
You cannot use an AED wrongly: it gives a shock only if it recognises ventricular fibrillation.

teile.einleitung: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. The human body cannot make some of them itself. These **essential amino acids** have to be taken in with food.
wichtigste: According to the standard genetic code, **20** amino acids are built into proteins.
The body cannot make essential amino acids itself.
Glycine is not essential for humans.
Leucine, isoleucine and valine are called branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs).
The body makes the messenger substance serotonin from tryptophan.
Maize and beans complement each other in their amino acids.

abschnitte.text: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. According to the standard genetic code, **20** different amino acids are built into proteins in humans. The body can make many of them itself, for example **glycine**. Others it has to get from food. These are called **essential**, meaning indispensable.

For adults, eight amino acids are traditionally counted as essential: leucine, isoleucine, valine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan. **Histidine** is often counted too. **Leucine, isoleucine and valine** have a branched side chain and are therefore called branched-chain amino acids, **BCAAs** for short. **Threonine** has a hydroxyl group (-OH) in the side chain. **Methionine** contains sulphur.

Foods from plants do not always contain all the essential amino acids in good amounts. In **pulses** such as beans, for example, **methionine** is rather scarce. Maize, on the other hand, has too little lysine, which is plentiful in beans. If you eat **maize and beans** together, their amino acids complement each other. Combinations like this are common in many cuisines around the world.

From the essential amino acid **tryptophan**, the body makes the messenger substance **serotonin**, which plays an important role in the brain. People with the hereditary disease **phenylketonuria** cannot break down **phenylalanine** properly. They therefore have to limit this amino acid strongly in their food. Phenylalanine is also found, for example, in the sweetener aspartame, which is why some drinks carry a warning.

gewusst: Milk, eggs, meat and fish also contain all the essential amino acids in good amounts.
The term “essential” comes from the Latin word for being, and here means indispensable.

teile.einleitung: Pus is a thick, usually yellowish liquid that forms in some inflammations. It shows that the body is fighting hard against bacteria.
wichtigste: Pus consists of dead defence cells, germs and broken-down tissue.
Pus is usually yellowish to greenish and cloudy.
Common germs that cause pus are staphylococci.
An abscess is a pocket of pus in tissue that has newly broken down.
An empyema is pus in a body cavity that already exists.
A boil is a pus-filled inflammation of a hair follicle.
A pustule is a small blister of pus on the skin.

abschnitte.text: When bacteria get into the body, it sends **white blood cells** to defend it. Many of these defence cells die in the fight. Together with the germs and broken-down tissue, they form a thick liquid, **pus**. Pus is especially often caused by **staphylococci**. The most important germ in skin and wound infections with pus is Staphylococcus aureus.

Pus is usually **yellowish** to greenish and cloudy. The colour comes from the many cells. Certain white blood cells, the **neutrophil granulocytes**, contain the greenish enzyme **myeloperoxidase**. It helps to kill bacteria and turns the pus greenish.

An **abscess** is a walled-off collection of pus. Tissue breaks down, and a new cavity full of pus forms. In an **empyema**, on the other hand, pus collects in a body cavity that already exists, for example in a sinus or in the space around the lungs. Both often need medical treatment, and sometimes the pus is drained.

A **pustule** is a small blister of pus, as found for example in acne. A **papule**, on the other hand, is a small bump without pus. A **boil** forms when bacteria get into a hair follicle. A painful lump full of pus develops. You should not squeeze such spots, because the inflammation could otherwise spread.

gewusst: In the past, doctors often thought pus in wounds was a good sign of healing.
The word staphylococci comes from Greek and means roughly “little grape-like balls”, because under the microscope they look like bunches of grapes.

teile.einleitung: In rotational vertigo, everything seems to spin round in a circle, as after a ride on a merry-go-round. The cause very often lies in the balance organ in the inner ear.
wichtigste: In rotational vertigo the surroundings or your own body seem to spin.
The cause often lies in the balance organ in the inner ear.
Often the eyes twitch to and fro, which is called nystagmus.
Benign positional vertigo arises from displaced calcium crystals.
It can often be treated with targeted positioning manoeuvres.
Dancers fix their gaze on one point in pirouettes.

abschnitte.text: In **rotational vertigo**, the surroundings or your own body seem to spin, although you are standing still. Often nausea and unsteadiness when standing are added. Often the eyes twitch rhythmically to and fro. This eye tremor is called **nystagmus**. Doctors observe it to find the cause of the dizziness.

In the **inner ear**, next to the organ of hearing, lies the **balance organ**. It consists, among other things, of three **semicircular canals** that are filled with fluid, the **endolymph**. When you turn your head, the fluid moves and stimulates fine sensory cells. The **vestibular nerve** reports this to the brain. If these reports do not agree with what the eyes see, dizziness arises.

Very common is **benign positional vertigo**. In it tiny calcium crystals, the **otoliths**, get into a semicircular canal. When you turn over in bed or lie down, everything then spins for a short time. With targeted head and body movements, for example the **Epley manoeuvre**, the crystals are moved out of the canal again. After that the vertigo often disappears quickly.

In **Ménière’s disease**, endolymph presumably builds up in the inner ear. Typical are attacks with rotational vertigo, ringing in the ear (**tinnitus**) and poorer hearing. In **vestibular neuritis**, the vestibular nerve on one side is inflamed. This causes severe rotational vertigo for days, and hearing usually stays normal. More rarely, dizziness comes from the brain. In sudden, severe dizziness you should get medical help.

Ballet dancers turn very fast in **pirouettes**. So that they do not get dizzy, they use **“spotting”**: the gaze stays as long as possible on a fixed point, then the head turns quickly after. In this way the brain keeps getting a calm picture, and the dizziness becomes smaller.

gewusst: After a ride on a merry-go-round, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving for a short time, which is why everything spins afterwards.
The calcium crystals in the inner ear are so small that you can see them only under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: A clinical thermometer measures how warm the body is. This way you can tell whether someone has a fever.
wichtigste: A clinical thermometer is used to measure body temperature.
In Switzerland it shows the temperature in degrees Celsius.
Digital thermometers need a battery and beep when they are done.
In children, you can measure quickly with an ear thermometer.
Many forehead thermometers measure without touching the skin.
After measuring, you should clean the thermometer.

abschnitte.titel: What is a clinical thermometer for?
abschnitte.text: With a **clinical thermometer**, you measure body temperature. In Switzerland the reading is shown in **degrees Celsius**. Healthy people have about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees. If the temperature is clearly above that, you have a **fever**. With your hand on the forehead, you can only feel this roughly.

Today most clinical thermometers are **digital**. They need a small **battery** to work. At the front there is a sensor that measures the warmth. When the measurement is done, the device often **beeps** and the number appears on the small screen. In the past there were glass thermometers with mercury, a poisonous metal.

You can measure in different places, for example under the tongue or in the armpit. In children, a special **ear thermometer** is very quick. It measures the warmth in the ear canal with **infrared radiation**, that is invisible heat radiation. Many **forehead thermometers** work the same way and measure **without touching the skin**.

Before measuring, you should sit down quietly and should not have just had a hot bath. You read the instructions, because every device works a little differently. After measuring, you should **clean** the thermometer, for example with a damp cloth or a little disinfectant. This way you do not pass germs on to the next person.

gewusst: The Celsius scale is named after the Swedish scientist Anders Celsius.
An ear thermometer often needs only about a second for a measurement.

teile.einleitung: **Bile** is a liquid that is made in the liver. It helps with the digestion of fat and carries waste substances out of the body.
wichtigste: The liver makes about half a litre to one litre of bile every day.
Bile is yellowish to greenish.
Bile acids break fat up into small droplets.
The bile pigment bilirubin forms when the red blood pigment is broken down.
Most bile acids return to the liver after digestion.
Too much cholesterol in the bile can form gallstones.

abschnitte.text: The **liver** makes bile without a break, in adults about 0.5 to 1 litre a day. It flows away through fine ducts. Some of it is stored for a while in the **gall bladder**. When we eat, the bile reaches the small intestine. Fresh bile is coloured yellowish to greenish.

Fat does not dissolve in water. The **bile acids** break large drops of fat up into many tiny droplets. This creates a much larger surface. On it, the **enzymes**, that is, substances that break down food, can split the fat better. Without bile, the body would take up fat only poorly.

Old red blood cells are broken down. From their blood pigment **haemoglobin**, the yellow pigment **bilirubin** is formed. The liver releases it with the bile into the gut. There, gut bacteria turn it into brown substances, which is why stools are normally brown. If bile is missing in the gut, the stools become pale.

Most bile acids are not lost. At the end of the small intestine they are taken up again and carried with the blood to the liver. This route is called the **enterohepatic circulation**. This way the body can use the same bile acids several times.
