Bile also contains **cholesterol**. If there is too much of it, it can crystallise and form **gallstones**. If the bile cannot flow away or the liver is ill, bile pigment builds up in the blood. Then the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow. This is called **jaundice**.

gewusst: The body also gets rid of cholesterol through the bile.
When someone is very angry, they sometimes say that their bile is rising.

teile.einleitung: Friedrich Miescher was a Swiss doctor and researcher from Basel. In 1869 he discovered a substance in cell nuclei that we now call DNA, the genetic material of all living things.
wichtigste: Friedrich Miescher was born in Basel in 1844.
In 1869 in Tübingen he discovered the substance nuclein.
He obtained his first cell nuclei from pus on used wound dressings.
Nuclein contained a striking amount of phosphorus and so differed from proteins.
Later he was Professor of Physiology at the University of Basel.
He died in Davos in 1895.
In Basel, the Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Friedrich Miescher was born in **Basel** in **1844**. His father and his uncle were also doctors and professors. Miescher studied medicine but preferred to do research rather than treat the sick. That is why he went to **Tübingen** in Germany. There he worked in a chemistry laboratory housed in an old castle.

Miescher wanted to know what **cells** are made of. For that he needed a lot of white blood cells. He found them in the **pus** on used **wound dressings** from a hospital. From these cells he separated the **cell nuclei**. In **1869** he found a new substance in them and called it **nuclein**, after the Latin word for kernel.

Miescher examined the nuclein closely. It contained a striking amount of **phosphorus**. That clearly set it apart from **proteins**. Today we know that nuclein was mainly **DNA**. DNA is the **genetic material** in which the blueprints of all living things are stored. What exactly it does, however, was only found out many decades later.

Later Miescher returned to his home city. At the **University of Basel** he became Professor of **Physiology**, the study of the processes in the body. There he went on researching cell nuclei, among other things using salmon from the Rhine. He fell ill with tuberculosis and died in **1895** in **Davos** in the canton of Graubünden. In Basel, the **Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research** carries his name.

gewusst: The famous double helix of DNA was only described in 1953, more than 80 years after Miescher's discovery.
The word nucleic acid, which is part of the abbreviation DNA, goes back to Miescher's nuclein.

teile.einleitung: The vaccination rate, also called vaccination coverage, shows what percentage of a group has been vaccinated against a particular disease. It shows how well a population is protected against infectious diseases.
wichtigste: The vaccination rate is the share of a group that has received a particular vaccination.
For measles, the WHO recommends a rate of 95 per cent with two doses.
Switzerland measures vaccination coverage among 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds.
The entries in the vaccination record are what gets counted.
High rates also protect people who cannot be vaccinated.
Local gaps in vaccination can still lead to outbreaks.

abschnitte.text: The **vaccination rate** tells you what percentage of a group has received a particular vaccination. It is often measured separately by **age** and **vaccine dose**. Here is an example: at a school, 552 out of 600 teenagers have had two measles vaccinations. 552 divided by 600 gives 0.92. So the vaccination rate is **92 per cent**.

The Swiss **vaccination coverage monitoring** regularly examines the vaccination records of **2-, 8- and 16-year-olds** in the **cantons**. What is counted are the vaccinations and doses written down in the **vaccination record**, not the antibodies measured in the blood. The results are published by the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH). This shows where there are still gaps.

If almost everyone is immune, a germ rarely meets anyone it can infect. **Chains of infection** break. This also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as **babies** or people with a weakened immune system. This is called **herd protection**. Because measles is extremely contagious, the WHO says at least **95 per cent** of people need to be immune for this to work.

abschnitte.titel: Vaccinated does not always mean protected
abschnitte.text: No vaccine works for everyone who is vaccinated. Here is a calculation: in a municipality, **85 per cent** of the children are vaccinated, and the vaccine works for **95 per cent** of them. The protected share is then 0.85 times 0.95, which is 0.8075. That is **about 81 per cent** of all children. This is why a high vaccination rate is needed to get enough protection.

Even when the rate is high across the whole country, **measles outbreaks** can happen. Averages hide **local gaps in vaccination**. Where unvaccinated people are grouped together, for example in certain regions, schools or communities, the virus can still spread.

gewusst: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known.
In Switzerland, you can have your vaccination record checked at a pharmacy or by a doctor.

teile.einleitung: A hereditary disease is a disease that arises from a change in the genetic material and can be passed on from parents to children. Every person has most genes twice, one version from each parent. These versions are called **alleles**.
wichtigste: Cystic fibrosis is inherited in an **autosomal recessive** way, and the gene that is changed is **CFTR**.
Huntington's disease is inherited in an **autosomal dominant** way.
In Huntington's disease, a CAG repeat in the gene is lengthened.
Healthy carriers of a sickle-cell allele are better protected against malaria.
Phenylketonuria is treated with a diet low in phenylalanine.
If both parents are healthy carriers, a child falls ill with a probability of 25 per cent.

abschnitte.text: The genetic material, the **DNA**, lies in every cell. It contains genes, which work like blueprints for proteins. For most genes, a person has two alleles, one from the mother and one from the father. If an allele is changed, it can cause a disease. Whether this happens depends on how the disease is inherited.

In a **recessive** hereditary disease, you only fall ill if both alleles are changed. Someone who has only one changed allele is healthy and is called a **carrier**. If both parents are carriers, the risk for each child is **25 per cent**. One example is **cystic fibrosis**, in which the gene **CFTR** is changed. In it, the body makes thick mucus, mainly in the lungs.

In a **dominant** hereditary disease, one changed allele is enough. One example is **Huntington's disease**, a disease of the brain that usually begins only in adulthood. In the gene concerned, a short section, the **CAG repeat**, occurs far too many times in a row. The longer this repeat is, the earlier the disease often begins.

**Sickle-cell disease** distorts the red blood cells. But healthy carriers of a sickle-cell allele are better protected against **malaria**. That is why this allele is common in some regions of Africa. Some hereditary diseases can be treated well: in **phenylketonuria**, the body cannot break down the amino acid phenylalanine properly. With a diet low in phenylalanine, people affected can grow up healthy.

gewusst: In Switzerland, newborns are tested with a few drops of blood for several inherited diseases, including phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis.
A changed allele can be passed on over many generations without anyone falling ill.

teile.einleitung: An adult is a person who is fully grown and bears responsibility under the law. Between child and adult comes the time as a **teenager**. In Switzerland, you count as an adult at the age of 18.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, you come of age at **18 years**.
From 18 you may vote in federal votes.
You can get a learner's permit for a car from the age of 17.
An adult man in Switzerland is on average about 1.78 m tall.
Adults need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep, and schoolchildren more.
Many adult men grow a beard.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, you come of age at **18 years**. Then you can sign contracts yourself and have more responsibility. From 18 you may also take part in **federal votes** and elections. In the canton of Glarus, young people may already have a say from 16 in cantonal and municipal votes. Someone who is of age can decide many things for themselves.

From **17 years**, you can get a **learner's permit** for a car in Switzerland. With it you may practise with an accompanying person. Many adults work, earn money and pay taxes. Once they are in working life, they also pay into the old-age insurance (AVS). So freedom and duties go together.

Adults are **fully grown**, so they do not get any taller. An adult man in Switzerland is on average about **1.78 m** tall, and women are on average slightly shorter. Many adult men grow a **beard** on the face. In old age, the body keeps changing, for example the skin becomes more wrinkled.

Adults need about **7 to 9 hours** of sleep a night. A **schoolchild** needs more, because their body and brain are still growing and developing. Teenagers also need a lot of sleep. Someone who sleeps enough can concentrate better.

gewusst: Until 1996, you only came of age in Switzerland at 20.
Since 1991, Swiss citizens have been able to vote at federal level from 18 instead of 20.

teile.einleitung: Erythropoietin, **EPO** for short, is a hormone that stimulates the making of red blood cells. In adults it is made mainly in the **kidney**. EPO is known as a medicine, but unfortunately also as a banned doping substance.
wichtigste: In adults, EPO is made mainly in the kidney.
A lack of oxygen in the tissue increases its release.
EPO acts in the bone marrow on precursor cells of red blood cells.
It belongs to the **glycoprotein hormones**.
Genetically engineered EPO was approved as a medicine in the USA in 1989.
Too many red blood cells make the blood thick, which can lead to thrombosis.

abschnitte.text: Red blood cells carry oxygen around the body. To make sure enough of them are present, the **kidney** releases erythropoietin. The hormone travels with the blood to the **bone marrow**. There it acts mainly on the **precursor cells** of the red blood cells. These then divide more often and mature into new red blood cells.

The most important trigger for making EPO is a **lack of oxygen in the tissue**. In the **high mountains**, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, which means that less oxygen gets into the body with each breath. That is why EPO production goes up there, and after some time you have more red blood cells. Many endurance athletes therefore train at altitude. For discovering how cells sense oxygen, **Kaelin, Ratcliffe and Semenza** received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2019.

Chemically, EPO is a **glycoprotein hormone**, that is a protein with chains of sugar. Since it can be made by genetic engineering, it has been used as a medicine. In the USA it was first approved in **1989**. It helps, for example, people with severe kidney disease whose kidneys make too little EPO. In this way their anaemia is eased.

Because EPO raises the number of red blood cells and so **oxygen transport**, it is used illegally as a doping substance in endurance sport. This became well known through scandals in cycling, for example. Doping is unfair and dangerous. Too many red blood cells make the blood **thick**. This can cause **thrombosis**, that is blood clots in the vessels.

gewusst: The name erythropoietin comes from Greek and means roughly “making red”.
The blood of people who live in the high mountains for a long time often has more red blood cells.

teile.einleitung: The **palatine tonsils** sit on the left and right at the back of the throat. They belong to the defence system and spot germs early that get in through the mouth and nose.
wichtigste: A person has two palatine tonsils.
They lie at the sides at the back of the throat between the palatal arches.
They consist of lymphatic tissue of the defence system.
An inflammation of the tonsils is called tonsillitis or angina.
The removal of the tonsils is called tonsillectomy.
They belong to Waldeyer's ring.

abschnitte.text: The palatine tonsils lie at the point where the **mouth** passes into the **throat**. There is one on the left and one on the right, between the **palatal arches**. When the mouth is wide open, you can see them. Their technical name is **tonsils**, from the Latin word “tonsilla”.

The tonsils consist of **lymphatic tissue**, that is, tissue of the body's defence. They come into contact early with **germs** from the air we breathe and from food. This way they recognise bacteria and viruses and set off a defence. They are like guards at the entrance of the body.

Around the throat lies a ring of tonsils and defence tissue, **Waldeyer's ring**. It includes the palatine tonsils, the **pharyngeal tonsil** (adenoids), the **lingual tonsil** and further tissue. It is named after the anatomist **Wilhelm Waldeyer**. If the pharyngeal tonsil is enlarged in children, people informally speak of **polyps**, although these are not real polyps.

An inflammation of the palatine tonsils is called **tonsillitis**, in everyday speech a **sore throat** or **angina**. The throat hurts, swallowing is painful, and often a fever is added. Many cases of tonsillitis are triggered by **viruses**. A pus-forming inflammation often comes from **streptococci** of group A, a kind of bacteria.

abschnitte.titel: When the tonsils have to come out
abschnitte.text: With very frequent infections, the tonsils can be removed by an operation. This is called **tonsillectomy**. The ending “-ectomy” means cutting out. Today such an operation is weighed up carefully, because the tonsils have a job in the defence.

gewusst: The tonsils are called almonds in German because their shape reminds people of almond kernels.
The word angina comes from the Latin “angere”, which means to make narrow or to choke.

teile.einleitung: Diabetes mellitus type 2 is the most common form of sugar sickness. In it the body’s cells respond less well to the hormone insulin, and the blood sugar rises.
wichtigste: Around 90 per cent of all cases of diabetes are type 2.
At the start there is an insulin resistance of the cells.
A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/l or more, confirmed, counts as diabetes.
In the glucose tolerance test, an adult drinks 75 g of glucose.
Metformin is usually the first medicine in tablet form.
Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity.

abschnitte.text: In type 2 diabetes, **muscle, fat and liver cells** respond less well to **insulin**. This is called **insulin resistance**. At first the pancreas even makes more insulin to compensate. With time it wears out, and the blood sugar rises permanently. The part of the name **“mellitus”** comes from Latin and means honey-sweet.

According to the criteria of the **WHO**, a **fasting blood sugar** of **7.0 mmol/l** (126 mg/dl) or more counts as a sign of diabetes if a second measurement confirms it. In the **oral glucose tolerance test**, an adult drinks a solution with **75 g of glucose**. A value of **11.1 mmol/l** or more after two hours points to diabetes. Often the illness is discovered by chance at a check-up.

**Exercise** and weight loss are cornerstones of treatment. Working muscles take up glucose independently of insulin too and become **more sensitive to insulin**. A balanced diet with little sugar and enough fibre also helps. In some people the values can in this way be kept good for a long time without medicines.

If lifestyle is not enough, **metformin** is usually the first choice in tablet form. It mainly inhibits the **new formation of glucose in the liver** and improves insulin sensitivity. On its own it hardly causes any **hypoglycaemia**. Later, further medicines are often added, sometimes insulin too.

Diabetes that is badly controlled damages the small **blood vessels** over the years. Typical is **diabetic retinopathy**, a disease of the retina in the eye that can lead to blindness. The kidneys, nerves, heart and feet can suffer too. That is why regular check-ups with the doctor and the eye doctor are important.

gewusst: In the past type 2 was called “adult-onset diabetes”, but today more and more younger people fall ill too.
Type 2 often begins gradually and stays unnoticed for years.

teile.einleitung: The elbow joint connects the upper arm with the forearm. Three bones meet here, and the joint can not only bend and straighten but also rotate.
wichtigste: In the elbow joint, the upper arm bone, the ulna and the radius meet.
The triceps on the back of the upper arm straightens the arm.
In the elbow, the radius turns around the ulna.
A hook of bone on the ulna stops the arm overstretching.
In tennis elbow, the pain is on the outside of the elbow.
Small children should not be yanked up by their hands.

abschnitte.text: In the **elbow joint**, three bones meet: the **upper arm bone** and the two forearm bones, the **ulna** and the **radius**. It actually consists of three partial joints in one shared joint capsule. Between the upper arm and the ulna, the arm bends and straightens. In the joint between the ulna and the radius, the radius rotates. This is how you can turn your palm up or down.

The **biceps** on the front of the upper arm is mainly used for **bending**. The **triceps** lies at the back of the upper arm. When it contracts, the arm is **straightened** at the elbow. The two muscles work as opposites. You cannot stretch the arm far backwards: a **hook of bone** at the upper end of the ulna hits the upper arm bone and stops the movement.

In **tennis elbow**, tendons **on the outside of the elbow** are overloaded. This can also happen without tennis, for example from a lot of work with a computer mouse. In **small children**, a bone at the elbow can slip out of position if the arm is pulled hard. This hurts, and the child no longer wants to move the arm. That is why small children should not be yanked up by their hands or swung around.

In a fall, you often land on your elbows. When skateboarding, padded **elbow pads** therefore protect skin and joint as well as the helmet. At the elbow the **ulnar nerve** lies right under the skin. If you knock it, it tingles all the way to the little finger. This spot is popularly known as the funny bone.

gewusst: A dislocated elbow in small children is called “pronatio dolorosa” in medical language, and it can usually be put back quickly.
The elbow joint consists of three partial joints that sit in a single capsule.

teile.einleitung: The ulna, known in German as the Elle, is one of the two bones of the forearm. It lies on the little-finger side and forms the hard tip of the elbow at the top.
wichtigste: The ulna lies in the forearm on the side of the little finger.
Its Latin name is ulna.
The olecranon forms the tip of the elbow.
At the elbow, the ulna is the stronger forearm bone.
The ulna is slightly longer than the radius.
A membrane between the bones connects the ulna and the radius.
You can feel the head of the ulna as a bump at the wrist.

abschnitte.text: There are two bones in the forearm: the **ulna** and the **radius**. If you hold your palm facing forwards, the ulna lies on the inside, on the side of the **little finger**. The radius lies on the thumb side. The nerve that runs alongside it is named after it too: the **ulnar nerve**, or **Nervus ulnaris**.

The upper end of the ulna forms a strong projection, the **olecranon**. You can feel it when you lean on your elbow. Near the elbow, the ulna is thick and stronger than the radius. With a notch like a pair of tongs, it grips around the pulley of the **upper arm bone**. This is where the arm is bent and straightened.

The ulna runs from the elbow to the wrist. Because at the top the olecranon sticks out beyond the radius, it is slightly **longer** in an adult. Towards the wrist it becomes narrower. There the radius is the stronger bone. The lower end of the ulna is called the **head of the ulna**. It sticks out as a round bump on the little-finger side.

Between the ulna and the radius, a tight sheet of connective tissue is stretched along the whole length, the **interosseous membrane**. It holds the two bones together. It also passes forces from the radius to the ulna. When you turn your hand, the radius turns around the ulna, while the ulna stays almost in place.

gewusst: The ell, which has the same name in German as the ulna, used to be a unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertip.
The tingling when you knock your elbow comes from the ulnar nerve, which lies right under the skin there.

teile.einleitung: Iron is a trace element that the body needs only in small amounts, but it is essential. It is found mainly in the red pigment of the blood and helps to carry oxygen.
wichtigste: An adult has only about 3 to 5 grams of iron in the body.
Most of it is in the red blood pigment haemoglobin.
A serious lack of iron can lead to anaemia.
Iron is stored in the protein ferritin.
Vitamin C improves the absorption of iron from plants.
Black tea with a meal can reduce absorption.
Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum.

abschnitte.text: Iron is an important building block of **haemoglobin**, the red blood pigment. In the lungs, haemoglobin binds oxygen and carries it to all the cells. An adult has only about **3 to 5 grams** of iron, roughly as much as in a small nail. Even so, the body cannot do without it. It is also needed in muscles and in some enzymes.

Iron from food is absorbed mainly in the **duodenum**, the first part of the small intestine. The body absorbs only a small part of the iron in food. It is stored in the protein **ferritin**, mainly in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. A low ferritin level in the blood shows that the iron stores are empty.

If iron is missing, the body cannot make enough haemoglobin. This leads to **iron-deficiency anaemia**. People affected are often tired, pale and less able to perform. Iron deficiency is one of the most common nutrient deficiencies in the world. A doctor can check with a blood test whether someone has too little iron.

Iron is found in meat, but also in many foods from plants. Good sources are **pulses** such as lentils, as well as wholegrain foods, nuts and seeds. Cucumbers and apples, on the other hand, contain little iron. **Vitamin C** helps the gut absorb iron from plants better. A glass of orange juice with lentils therefore makes sense.

Some substances make it harder to absorb iron. The **tannins** in **black tea** bind iron in the gut. That is why it is better not to drink tea straight with iron-rich meals, but a little later. Coffee can also reduce absorption.

gewusst: The iron in blood is what makes blood red.
The body can hardly get rid of iron actively, and it controls the amount mainly through absorption in the gut.

teile.einleitung: Diabetes mellitus, often called sugar sickness, is an illness in which there is too much sugar in the blood. The reason is that the hormone insulin is missing or does not work properly.
wichtigste: In diabetes the blood sugar is permanently too high.
Insulin from the pancreas normally lowers the blood sugar.
Type 2 is the most common, at around nine in ten cases.
In type 1 the body hardly makes any insulin any more, and it has to be supplied from outside.
Great thirst and frequent urination are typical signs.
World Diabetes Day is every year on 14 November.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **diabetes** means roughly “flowing through”, the Latin **mellitus** means **honey-sweet**. In the past, doctors tested the urine of the sick and noticed that it tastes sweet. Hence the name “honey-sweet flowing through”. Today sugar is measured quite simply with a small device and a drop of blood.

From food, sugar gets into the blood. The cells need it as energy. The hormone **insulin** from the **pancreas** works like a key: it helps the sugar to get into the cells. If insulin is missing or does not work properly, the sugar stays in the blood. Then the kidneys excrete sugar with a lot of water. You have to go to the toilet often and have **great thirst**.

In **type 1**, the body hardly makes any insulin of its own. This form often begins in children and young people. Those affected supply insulin with a **syringe, pen or insulin pump**. In **type 2**, the most common form worldwide, the insulin no longer works properly. The risk rises through **lack of exercise** and severe **overweight**, and heredity plays a part too.

If the sugar is too high for a long time, fine **blood vessels** and **nerves** are damaged. Often affected are the **eyes, kidneys and nerves**. That is why eyes and kidneys are checked regularly in diabetes. The **feet** also need attention: if the nerves are damaged, you often no longer feel small wounds, and they heal badly.

Insulin was discovered in the 1920s in Canada, among others by **Frederick Banting**. For a long time it was obtained from the **pancreases of cattle and pigs** from slaughterhouses. Since the **1980s**, human insulin has been made by **genetic engineering**. In honour of Banting, whose birthday was on 14 November, this day is **World Diabetes Day**.

gewusst: With insulin, people with type 1 diabetes can today lead a perfectly normal life, play sport and travel.
Many people with type 2 do not notice their illness for a long time.

teile.einleitung: A double-blind study is a way of testing medicines and treatments fairly. Neither the participants nor the people treating them know who receives the real substance.
wichtigste: In a double-blind study, neither participants nor treating staff know the group allocation.
In a single-blind study, only the participants know nothing.
Allocation is random, which is called randomisation.
The randomised controlled trial counts as the gold standard.
In an emergency the blinding can be lifted, which is called unblinding.
In a triple-blind study, the people who analyse the results are blinded too.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who knows that they are getting a medicine often feels better just because of that. This is called the **placebo effect**. That is why in studies one group gets the active substance and another group a **placebo**, a dummy remedy without active substance. In a **double-blind study**, neither the **test subjects** nor the **treating professionals** know who gets what. In this way expectations on both sides do not distort the result.

In a **single-blind study**, the study staff know the allocation, but the participants do not. This protects against the placebo effect, but not against unconscious influence by the people treating. Anyone who knows who gets the real remedy judges symptoms differently without noticing. This is called **observer bias**. In a **triple-blind study**, even the people who **analyse the data** do not know the groups.

Who goes into which group is decided by chance. This is called **randomisation**. As a result, unknown influences such as age or way of life are also spread evenly over both groups. The **randomised controlled trial**, often carried out double-blind, avoids systematic errors best. That is why it counts as the **gold standard** of therapy research.

If severe side effects occur in a person, you have to know what they received. Then the blinding is lifted for them. This is called **unblinding**. In this way doctors can act correctly in an emergency. In Switzerland, studies with people are first checked by an **ethics committee**, and new medicines have to be approved by **Swissmedic**.

gewusst: Some placebos look so like the real medicine that no one can tell them apart.
Even sham treatments can have noticeable effects, which is why a comparison group is always needed.

teile.einleitung: Diabetes mellitus type 1 is an illness in which the pancreas can no longer make insulin. Without insulin, the sugar cannot get from the blood into the cells. Type 1 often begins in childhood or adolescence, and those affected have to supply insulin for the rest of their lives.
wichtigste: Diabetes type 1 is an autoimmune disease.
The immune system destroys the insulin-making cells of the pancreas.
Without insulin the blood sugar rises sharply.
Typical signs are great thirst, frequent urination and tiredness.
Those affected measure their blood sugar and inject insulin or wear an insulin pump.
Type 1 is neither contagious nor caused by sweets.
With good treatment, those affected can do almost everything, including sport.

abschnitte.text: Diabetes mellitus is the technical term for **sugar sickness**. In type 1, the body’s own immune system mistakenly attacks the beta cells in the pancreas. This is called an **autoimmune disease**. The beta cells are destroyed and can no longer make insulin.

**Insulin** is a hormone that works like a key. It opens the door of the cells so that sugar can get in from the blood. If insulin is missing, the sugar stays in the blood, and the cells go hungry. The body then breaks down fat, and harmful substances arise.

Typical signs are strong thirst and frequent urination. Many of those affected lose weight and are very tired. Without treatment, a dangerous acidification of the blood can occur, **ketoacidosis**. That is why you should go to the doctor quickly if you notice such signs.

People with type 1 have to supply insulin for the rest of their lives. In the past this was done only with syringes, today many use an **insulin pump**. Small sensors on the skin measure the blood sugar continuously and send the values to a phone. It is also important to estimate the carbohydrates in food.

Until about a hundred years ago, type 1 diabetes was fatal. In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Canada succeeded in obtaining insulin. In 1922 a child was treated successfully with it for the first time. For the discovery, the **Nobel Prize** was awarded in 1923.

In Switzerland, several thousand children and young people live with type 1 diabetes. They can go to school, play sport and go on trips like everyone else. Teachers and friends should know what to do in a **hypoglycaemia**. Then a little glucose or a sweet drink quickly helps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hormone that brings sugar from the blood into the cells.
An illness in which the immune system attacks the body itself.
An organ in the belly that makes insulin and digestive juices.
Too little sugar in the blood, you feel shaky and weak.

gewusst: The term diabetes mellitus means honey-sweet flowing through, because the urine of the sick was sweet.
World Diabetes Day on 14 November is the birthday of Frederick Banting.
Type 2 diabetes is a different illness and occurs mainly in adults.

teile.einleitung: Friendship is a special relationship between people who like and trust each other. Good friends make life nicer and even healthier.
wichtigste: Trust and honesty are part of a good friendship.
The UN International Day of Friendship is on 30 July.
Aristotle wrote that true friendship rests on mutual appreciation of character.
According to Robin Dunbar, a person can keep up about 150 stable relationships.
With closeness and trust, the “bonding hormone” oxytocin is released.
Good relationships promote health and well-being.

abschnitte.text: **Trust and honesty** are part of a good friendship. Friends listen to each other, help each other and are happy together. You do not always have to agree. What matters is that you respect each other and can be the way you are.

More than 2,000 years ago, the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** was already thinking about friendship. He distinguished friendships of usefulness, of pleasure and of true affection. A **true friendship**, he said, rests on **mutual appreciation of character**. In his view, such friendships last the longest.

The British researcher **Robin Dunbar** studied how many relationships a person can keep up. He arrived at **about 150** stable social relationships. This is called **Dunbar's number**. Very close friends, however, you usually only have a few. The **UN** has declared **30 July** the **International Day of Friendship**.

With closeness and trust, the body releases the hormone **oxytocin**. It is often called the “**bonding hormone**”. **Studies** show that good relationships promote **health and well-being**. Someone who has friends feels less alone and copes better with stress.

Even in good friendships there are sometimes arguments. A fair way is to say what bothers you using **“I” statements**, for example “I feel sad when you don't let me join in”. This way the other person does not feel attacked. You can often recognise an **unhealthy friendship** by the fact that you feel **constantly used or put down**. Then you are allowed to step back and talk to a person you trust.

gewusst: Animals such as chimpanzees, horses or dolphins also keep up close relationships with particular members of their species.
The International Day of Friendship was decided by the UN in 2011.

teile.einleitung: The **heel** is the back part of the foot. It carries a large share of our weight when we stand and walk. In it lies the **heel bone**, the largest bone of the foot.
wichtigste: The heel is at the back of the foot.
The largest bone in the foot is the **heel bone**.
In normal walking, the heel usually touches the ground first.
In new, hard shoes you often get a blister on the heel.
People who often go barefoot get thick hard skin on their heels.
“To be on someone's heels” means to follow them closely.

abschnitte.text: The heel forms the **back part of the foot**. In it lies the **heel bone**, the largest bone in the foot. The strong **Achilles tendon**, which leads to the calf muscles, is attached to the heel bone. Under the bone lies a thick pad of fat. It cushions every step like a pillow.

In normal walking, **the heel** usually touches the ground **first**. Then the foot rolls over the sole towards the toes. This spreads the weight evenly. When running fast, many people land more on the front of the foot. So the heel has to put up with a lot every day.

In **new, hard shoes**, the shoe often rubs on the heel. Then a **blister** soon forms. A plaster helps before it hurts. The raised part of the shoe under the heel is called the **heel**, too, in English also the heel of the shoe. People who often go **barefoot** get **thick hard skin** on their heels, which protects the skin.

The heel appears in sayings. “**To be on someone's heels**” means to follow them closely. In the **heel sit**, you kneel and sit on your own heels. This position is known from gymnastics and yoga. Also well known is the legend of the hero Achilles, whose heel was his only vulnerable spot.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the human body.
The expression “Achilles heel” for a weak point comes from the legend of Achilles.

teile.einleitung: Dialysis is a form of blood washing. It takes over the work of the kidneys when they hardly work any more, and removes waste substances and excess water from the blood.
wichtigste: A dialysis cleans the blood.
You need it when the kidneys hardly work any more.
The dialysis machine is often called an artificial kidney.
Many people go for haemodialysis about three times a week.
A fine membrane separates the blood from the rinsing fluid.
In peritoneal dialysis, the peritoneum serves as the filter.

abschnitte.text: Healthy **kidneys** filter the blood. They remove waste substances and excess water and make urine from them. In severe **kidney failure**, poisons and water collect in the body. Without treatment this would be life-threatening. Then a **dialysis** or a **kidney transplant**, that is, a donated new kidney, helps.

In **haemodialysis**, the blood flows through tubes out of the body into a machine, the **artificial kidney**. In it, a fine **membrane** with tiny pores separates the blood from a rinsing fluid. Small waste substances pass through, blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood. The cleaned blood flows back. Usually this is done **about three times a week** for four to five hours each time.

In **peritoneal dialysis**, rinsing fluid is filled into the abdominal cavity through a thin tube. The well-supplied **peritoneum** then acts as a filter. After some time the fluid with the waste substances is drained off again. This form can even be carried out **at home**.

Dialysis takes a lot of time and patience. Diseased kidneys often make almost no urine any more. That is why many of those affected have to pay close attention to **how much they drink**, because the water stays in the body until the next dialysis. There are also rules for eating, for example for salt and certain minerals.

The Dutch doctor **Willem Kolff** developed a dialysis machine during the **Second World War**. In **1945**, for the first time a person survived kidney failure thanks to his treatment. Since then the machines have become ever smaller, safer and better.

gewusst: A person can also live well with only one healthy kidney.
Every day the kidneys filter many times the whole amount of blood in the body.

teile.einleitung: Florence Nightingale was a British nurse. She is regarded as the founder of modern nursing, and she used numbers and diagrams to argue for better hygiene.
wichtigste: Florence Nightingale is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.
She was born in Florence in 1820 and named after the city.
In the Crimean War she nursed wounded soldiers in the hospital at Scutari.
Most of the soldiers there died of infections and epidemics.
With statistics and diagrams, she persuaded politicians to improve hygiene.
In 1858 she became the first woman to be admitted to the Royal Statistical Society.
On her birthday, 12 May, it is International Nurses Day.

abschnitte.text: Florence Nightingale was born on **12 May 1820** in **Florence**, while her British parents were travelling in Italy. She was given her first name from the city. She grew up in a rich family in England and learned a great deal, including mathematics. At that time, nursing was not seen as a suitable job for a woman from a good family. Florence wanted to help the sick all the same and trained as a nurse.

In the **Crimean War**, she travelled in 1854 with a group of nurses to **Scutari**, a district of present-day Istanbul. In the **military hospital** there, a hospital for soldiers, conditions were terrible. It was dirty, and there was a shortage of water, food and bandages. Most soldiers did not die of their wounds but of **infections and epidemics**. Nightingale made sure of cleanliness, fresh linen and better food.

At night, Florence Nightingale walked through the wards with a lamp and checked on the sick. That is why the soldiers called her “the Lady with the Lamp”. Newspapers in Britain wrote about her, and she became very famous. After the war, she founded a **nursing school** in London in 1860. There, nurses were trained according to fixed rules.

Florence Nightingale was very good at maths. She collected exact data on illnesses and deaths. With **statistics and diagrams**, she showed politicians that better **hygiene** saves lives. Her circular diagram is famous, and today it is often called the **rose diagram**. In 1858 she became the **first woman** to be admitted to the **Royal Statistical Society**, a scientific society for statistics.

Florence Nightingale died in London in **1910**. Her ideas shape nursing to this day: cleanliness, fresh air and good training. On her birthday, **12 May**, **International Nurses Day** is marked every year. It reminds us of the important work of nursing staff, including in Swiss hospitals and care homes.

gewusst: Florence Nightingale wrote thousands of letters and many books about nursing and health.
Her older sister was called Parthenope, after the old Greek name of the city of Naples, where she was born.

teile.einleitung: The tarsus, in German “root of the foot”, is the back part of the foot, between the lower leg and the middle of the foot. It consists of seven bones that carry our whole weight.
wichtigste: The tarsus consists of seven bones.
The largest tarsal bone is the heel bone.
Not a single muscle attaches to the talus.
The upper ankle joint mainly allows you to raise and lower the foot.
Between the talus and the heel bone lies the lower ankle joint.
A foot has 26 bones, not counting the sesamoid bones.

abschnitte.text: A human foot has **26 bones**, not counting the small **sesamoid bones**. It is divided into three parts: the **tarsus**, the **metatarsus** and the **toes**. The tarsus forms the back part, with the heel and the ankle area. It consists of **seven bones**. Together they carry our whole body weight when we stand and walk.

The largest bone of the tarsus is the **heel bone**, which forms the heel. On top of it lies the **talus**, whose German name means “jumping bone”. On the inner side, between the talus and the cuneiform bones, lies the **navicular**, which is named after a boat. On the outer edge of the foot sits the **cuboid**, which is named after its shape. In addition there are three **cuneiform bones**.

The **upper ankle joint** connects the lower leg with the talus. It mainly allows you to **raise and lower the foot**. The **lower ankle joint** lies between the **talus and the heel bone**. With it you can tilt the foot inwards and outwards, for example on uneven ground. When you twist your ankle, this area is often injured.

The **talus** has a special feature: **not a single muscle attaches** to it. It is held only by ligaments and passes the weight from the leg to the foot. The strong **Achilles tendon**, by contrast, attaches to the **heel bone**. There a painful **heel spur** can also form, a small bony projection. It often comes from overuse.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon on the heel bone is the strongest tendon in the human body.
Both feet together have roughly a quarter of all the bones in the body.

teile.einleitung: When something happens, the most important thing for children is to **get an adult** quickly. Adults can help better and call the emergency number. But children can also do a lot if they know how.
wichtigste: In an accident, as a child you first get an adult.
Before you help, you pay attention to your own safety.
On the playground, the teacher helps you.
You tell the adult what has happened and where.
If nobody is nearby, you call **144** yourself.
You should know your own home address by heart.

abschnitte.text: Before you help at the scene of an accident, you pay attention to **your own safety**. On a road with cars or when there is a fire, you are better off keeping your distance. If you get hurt yourself, you can no longer help anyone. After that the most important thing is: **get an adult**. Adults usually know better what to do.

Call out loudly and clearly, for example: “Help! Please come!” Speak to one particular person directly, and they will feel it is meant for them. On the playground, you fetch the **teacher**. Briefly tell the adult **what has happened and where**. That way they can act correctly straight away.

While an adult calls the emergency number, you stay **with the injured person**. You can talk to them and calm them. Say to them, for example: “**Help is on its way.**” Even that helps an injured person a lot. Only move the person if they are in danger.

If **no adult** is nearby, you call **144** yourself, which is the ambulance service in Switzerland. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade, and 112 works all over Europe. On the phone you say who you are, what has happened and where. That is why you should know your **home address by heart**. Only hang up when the person on the phone says so.

gewusst: Children can also call an emergency number, and it is never wrong if someone really needs help.
In Switzerland, you can call emergency numbers free of charge.

teile.einleitung: A cold is a mild illness of the nose and throat. It is caused by **viruses** and is very common, especially in winter. Usually it is over after about a week.
wichtigste: A cold is caused by **viruses**.
Typical signs are a runny nose, a cough and a sore throat.
Colds are especially common in winter.
A cold lasts about a week.
You sneeze into the **crook of your elbow** and wash your hands often.
Used tissues go in the bin.

abschnitte.text: With a cold, you often have a **runny nose**: your nose drips or is completely **blocked**. There is often a sore throat, a cough and tiredness as well. Sometimes you have a slight fever. After **about a week**, you usually feel well again. If you feel much worse or have a high fever, you go to the doctor.

Colds are caused by **viruses**, and there are many different ones. They spread through tiny droplets when sneezing, coughing and talking. They also reach the nose and mouth via the hands. In **winter**, colds are especially common because many people are indoors close together. Antibiotics do not help against viruses.

**Washing your hands** with soap helps a lot so that you are less likely to catch it. If you have to sneeze or cough, you do it into the **crook of your elbow** and not into your hand. A used paper tissue goes straight **in the bin**. After that you wash your hands. This also protects the others in your class.

What helps most against a cold is **rest** and plenty to drink, for example warm tea. A **nose spray with salt water** can clear a blocked nose. Sleep also helps the body fight the viruses. Fresh air in the room does you good as well.

gewusst: Adults catch a cold several times a year on average, and children even more often.
A cold is something different from flu, which is usually much more severe.

teile.einleitung: Joy is a lovely feeling that we sense in the whole body. We laugh, skip or sing when we are happy.
wichtigste: Feelings such as joy arise in the brain.
Endorphins are often called “happiness hormones”.
With great joy, the arms often shoot up into the air.
A feeling of deep contentment and joy is called happiness.
Animals also show joy: dogs wag their tails, cats purr.
Enough sleep helps you to be in a good mood in the morning.

abschnitte.text: Feelings such as **joy** arise in the **brain**. When something nice happens, it releases certain chemical messengers. **Endorphins** are often called “**happiness hormones**”. The substances dopamine and serotonin also play a part in a good mood. They make sure that we feel well and alive.

You can often see joy straight away. We **smile** or laugh out loud, and our eyes shine. With great joy, for example after a win, the **arms go up into the air**. Many people jump, clap or hug others. Someone in a good mood often **sings or whistles** quite by themselves.

Animals also show when they are doing well. A **dog wags its tail** when it is happy, for example when its person comes home. A **cat often purrs** when it is content. Some animals then also like to play especially much.

A feeling of deep contentment and joy is called **happiness**. Joy often comes suddenly, while happiness can last longer. Good friendships, exercise and time in nature all help. The body also needs **enough sleep** so that you are in a good mood in the morning.

Everybody is in a bad mood sometimes, and that is normal. Many children then find it helps to **play with friends**. Exercise in the fresh air, music or a chat can also lift your mood. Someone who is sad for a long time should talk about it with a person they trust.

gewusst: Laughing can be catching: when you hear others laugh, you often laugh along.
Even very small babies smile when they see familiar faces.

teile.einleitung: Ergonomics is the science of fitting work, tools and furniture to people. A good workplace protects your back, eyes and joints. This is true in the office, but also at a school desk or when doing homework.
wichtigste: The aim of ergonomics is to fit work to people.
The word comes from the Greek **ergon** (work) and **nomos** (law).
The top edge of the screen is roughly at eye level or slightly below.
When sitting, elbows and knees are at an angle of about 90 degrees.
For reading and writing, about 500 lux is recommended.
Changing position often is better than sitting still for hours.

abschnitte.text: The term is made up of the Greek words **ergon** for work and **nomos** for law. Ergonomics wants to **fit work to people**, not the other way round. To do this, people are measured precisely. This science of measuring the human body is called **anthropometry**. Its data are used to design chairs, tables, tools and even car seats.

When sitting at a desk, elbows and knees should form an angle of about **90 degrees**. The feet are flat on the floor, and the back is supported by the backrest. Even more important is **movement**: you should change position often and get up now and then. A desk you can stand at also helps.

The **top edge of the screen** is at eye level or slightly below. This keeps the neck relaxed. You place the screen **to the side of the window**, so that you look parallel to the window, so that nothing dazzles or reflects. For reading and writing work in an office, about **500 lux** of illumination is recommended. Lux is the unit for brightness at a workplace.

If you look at a screen for a long time, you blink less often and your eyes get tired. The **20-20-20 rule** helps here: every 20 minutes, you look at something about 6 metres away for 20 seconds. The number 20 comes from English-speaking countries, where the distance is measured as 20 feet. Short breaks and fresh air also do you good.

gewusst: Bicycles, computer mice and kitchen appliances are also designed according to ergonomic rules.
A desk that suits an adult is usually too high for a child.

teile.einleitung: An epidemic is an increase in cases of an infectious disease in a particular area and period. Then far more people fall ill than usual.
wichtigste: An epidemic is limited in place and time.
An endemic disease is present in a region all the time.
The reproduction number R shows how many people a sick person infects on average.
If R is greater than 1, cases rise.
Epidemiology studies how diseases spread.
In Switzerland, the Epidemics Act regulates the control of communicable diseases.
Doctors have to report certain diseases to the authorities.

abschnitte.text: In an **epidemic**, far more people than usual fall ill in a region within a short time. It is limited to one place. An **endemic** disease, on the other hand, is present in an area all the time, for example **malaria** in some tropical countries. The number of cases stays roughly the same. If a disease spreads over many countries and continents, it is called a **pandemic**.

The **reproduction number R** shows how many people a sick person infects on average. If R is greater than 1, cases increase. If R is less than 1, the epidemic declines. Here is an example: if one person infects 3 others and each of them infects 3 more, there are already **9** newly infected in the second round. This is how a disease can grow very fast.

**Epidemiology** is the science that studies how diseases spread in the population. It investigates how often diseases occur, who is affected and what causes lie behind them. One example of a large epidemic is the **Ebola** outbreak of 2014 to 2016 in **West Africa**. It mainly affected Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia and was the largest Ebola outbreak up to then.

In Switzerland, the **Epidemics Act** regulates how the Confederation and the cantons detect, monitor and fight infectious diseases. The version in force has applied since **2016**. For many infectious diseases there is a **duty to report**. Doctors and laboratories report cases to the health authorities of the canton and the Confederation. This allows the **cantonal medical officer** and the **FOPH** to detect outbreaks early and take measures.

gewusst: The word epidemic comes from Greek and means roughly “spread among the people”.
The Epidemics Act distinguishes a normal situation, a special situation and an extraordinary situation.

teile.einleitung: Everybody knows goosebumps: suddenly the little hairs stand up and the skin gets small bumps. This happens when we are cold, but also with fear or strong feelings. The name comes from the fact that the skin then looks like the skin of a plucked goose.
wichtigste: Goosebumps appear when tiny muscles at the hair roots contract.
The body hairs stand up as a result.
Goosebumps can appear in the cold and are meant to help keep warmth in.
Fear, music or being moved can also trigger goosebumps.
They are controlled without our noticing by the nervous system.
In animals with thick fur, raising the hairs warms much better than in humans.

abschnitte.text: With **goosebumps**, many small bumps form on the skin, and the little hairs stand on end. The skin then looks like the skin of a plucked goose. Experts also call this **piloerection**, which means raising of the hairs. It can appear all over the body or only on the arms.

At every hair root sits a tiny muscle, the **arrector pili muscle**. When it contracts, the hair stands up. At the same time, the skin around the hair is pushed upwards, and a little bump appears. You cannot control these muscles on purpose, because they are steered by the **autonomic nervous system**.

When you are cold, the body reacts with goosebumps in order to keep warmth in. In animals with fur, a cushion of air forms between the raised hairs, which warms well. In humans, the body hairs are very thin, so this helps only a little. Much more important for warming up in humans are **shivering** and warm clothes.

Fear, fright or excitement can also trigger goosebumps. Then the body releases the stress hormone **adrenaline**. Some people get goosebumps from lovely music or an exciting story. Researchers sometimes call this the feeling of chills, or “frisson”.

A cat that feels threatened bristles its fur and so looks bigger. Porcupines raise their quills in this way. Birds fluff up their feathers in the cold, for example sparrows in winter. Goosebumps in humans are a leftover from the time when our ancestors still had more body hair.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny muscle at the hair root that makes the hair stand up.
The part of the nervous system that works without our will.
A hormone that is released with fright or excitement.
The technical word for the raising of the hairs.

gewusst: Some people can trigger goosebumps on purpose, but that is very rare.
According to newer research, the arrector pili muscles also help to activate hair stem cells.
In German, goosebumps are called “Gänsehaut”, which means goose skin.

teile.einleitung: The endoplasmic reticulum, ER for short, is a large network of membranes inside the cell. It works like a factory in which proteins and fats are made.
wichtigste: The ER is directly connected to the outer nuclear membrane.
Ribosomes sit on the rough ER, which is why it looks grainy.
The rough ER makes membrane proteins and secreted proteins.
The smooth ER makes lipids such as phospholipids and steroids.
In liver cells, the smooth ER detoxifies foreign substances.
Transport vesicles take proteins to the Golgi apparatus.
Chaperones help new proteins fold correctly.

abschnitte.text: **Reticulum** means little net. The ER consists of branching tubes and flat sacs of membrane. It grows directly out of the **outer nuclear membrane**. Its inner space is connected with the space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope. There are two parts: the **rough ER** and the **smooth ER**.

Under the **electron microscope**, the rough ER looks grainy. On the outside of its membranes sit many **ribosomes**, the cell's protein factories. This is where **proteins** are made that are built into membranes or released from the cell. A **signal peptide** at the start of the growing chain makes sure the ribosome is steered to the ER membrane. A recognition particle, the SRP, helps with this.

A new protein chain has to find the right shape, or it will not work. Inside the rough ER, **chaperones** help with this, for example the protein BiP. They bind to unfolded chains and support correct folding. Misfolded proteins are sorted out and broken down. Finished proteins travel in pinched-off **membrane vesicles** to the **Golgi apparatus**.

The **smooth ER** has no ribosomes. It makes **lipids**, that is fats such as the phospholipids of membranes and **steroids**. In **liver cells** the smooth ER is especially extensive. There it contains enzymes that chemically change medicines and poisons. This makes them easier to get rid of. In muscle cells, a special form of the ER stores calcium.

gewusst: The ER can make up more than half of all the membranes of a cell.
If someone regularly takes certain medicines, the smooth ER in the liver cells can grow.

teile.einleitung: Disgust is a strong feeling that warns us about harmful things. When you feel disgusted, you want to get rid of something at once or not touch it at all.
wichtigste: Disgust protects against spoiled food that could make you ill.
When disgusted, people often say “Yuck” or “Ugh”.
Something disgusting in the mouth is usually spat out at once.
Strong disgust can lead to feeling sick and retching.
The nose often warns about spoiled food first.
Since 2017, some insects have been allowed as food in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Disgust** is one of the basic human feelings. It stops us from eating things that could make us ill. A typical sign is a twisted face with a wrinkled nose. People then say “**Yuck**” or “**Ugh**”. With strong disgust you can feel **sick**, and sometimes you even have to retch.

Spoiled food smells bad. That is why you often notice it first with your **nose**. Taste also warns you: if something tastes odd, you usually **spit** it out straight away. This stops inedible things from reaching the stomach. So disgust is a kind of shield for the body.

Most people feel disgusted by **mould**. Mould grows as a furry, fluffy coating, often green, white or black. Some moulds produce poisons. That is why you do not eat mouldy bread any more, not even if you only cut off the spot. Here, disgust protects us sensibly.

What disgusts you also depends on what you are used to. In many countries, people have eaten **insects** for a long time. In **Switzerland**, mealworms, crickets and migratory locusts have been allowed to be sold as food since **2017**. Even so, many people still find them disgusting. What counts as a delicacy in one country is disgusting to others.

gewusst: Small children hardly feel disgust yet, and they learn a lot of it only over time.
In 2017, Switzerland was one of the first countries in Europe to expressly allow insects as food.

teile.einleitung: The ellipsoid joint is a special type of joint in our body. It is also known as the egg joint because its joint head is elongated like an egg and sits in an oval socket.
wichtigste: In an ellipsoid joint, an egg-shaped joint head sits in an oval socket.
An ellipsoid joint allows movements around two axes.
Turning around its own axis is not possible.
Another name is the egg joint.
The joint between the radius and the wrist bones is an ellipsoid joint.
The upper joint of the head, between the skull and the first neck vertebra, is also an ellipsoid joint.

abschnitte.text: A joint connects two bones so that they can move. In an ellipsoid joint, the **joint head** is long and rounded, like an egg. It fits into an equally long **joint socket**. An ellipse is an oval, which is why the egg joint is also called an **ellipsoid joint**. The shape of a joint decides which movements are possible.

An ellipsoid joint allows movements around **two axes**. So you can move it forwards and backwards and to the side. Turning around its own axis, however, is not possible. The oval head only fits into the long socket in one position. If you turned it, it would jam and knock against the edge. A ball-and-socket joint such as the shoulder, on the other hand, can move in all directions.

The best-known ellipsoid joint is the **proximal wrist joint**. It connects the **radius** with the wrist bones. Three bones of the first row of wrist bones together form the egg-shaped head: the **scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum**. The socket is formed by the radius and a disc of cartilage. With this joint you can bend the hand up and down and tilt it towards the thumb side or the little-finger side.

abschnitte.titel: The upper joint of the head
abschnitte.text: There is also an ellipsoid joint between the head and the spine. The **upper joint of the head** connects the occipital bone of the skull with the first neck vertebra, the **atlas**. It is a paired joint, so there is one on the left and one on the right. With it you can mainly nod. Turning the head is done by another joint further down.

gewusst: The first neck vertebra is called the atlas, after a figure from Greek legend who carries the vault of the heavens.
The fact that the hand can still be turned is not due to the wrist joint, but to the radius rotating around the ulna in the forearm.

teile.einleitung: In a **fatty liver**, too much fat is stored in the liver. The medical term is **steatosis hepatis**. For a long time you do not notice anything, but without treatment it can harm the liver.
wichtigste: People usually speak of fatty liver when more than 5 per cent of the liver cells contain fat.
The fat is stored mainly as **triglycerides**.
Since 2023, the form linked to metabolism has been called **MASLD**.
When inflammation is added, it is called **steatohepatitis**.
The most important risk factors are being overweight and type 2 diabetes.
The most important treatment is losing weight through diet and exercise.

abschnitte.text: The liver is an important organ for metabolism. It processes nutrients and breaks down poisons. In a fatty liver, the liver cells store too much fat, mainly in the form of **triglycerides**. Usually people speak of a fatty liver when **more than 5 per cent** of the liver cells contain fat. The medical term is **steatosis hepatis**.

A fatty liver can be caused by too much **alcohol**. Today, however, the form linked to metabolism, which is not caused by alcohol, is more common. Since **2023** it has been called **MASLD**, which is an English abbreviation. It used to be called non-alcoholic fatty liver. Its most important risk factors are being **overweight** and **type 2 diabetes**.

A simple fatty liver often causes no symptoms. But if **inflammation** with damage to the cells is added, it is called **steatohepatitis**. Then the liver tissue can gradually change and become scarred. A serious late effect is **cirrhosis of the liver**, in which the liver can no longer do its jobs well. That is why it is important to spot a fatty liver early.

The most important treatment for a fatty liver linked to metabolism is **losing weight** through a healthy **diet** and plenty of **exercise**. Less sugar and fewer sweet drinks also help. You should also avoid alcohol. The good news: the liver can recover well if you change something early.

gewusst: The liver is the largest internal organ of the human body.
A fatty liver is often discovered by chance in an ultrasound examination.

teile.einleitung: People who are called **colour blind** usually still see colours. Most of them, however, confuse certain colours, especially red and green. Experts therefore often speak of **colour vision deficiency**.
wichtigste: Most so-called colour-blind people confuse certain colours.
**Red and green** are confused most often.
About 8 in 100 men in Europe have a red-green deficiency.
Men are affected much more often than women.
A red-green deficiency is usually inherited.
We see colours with the **cones** in the eye.

abschnitte.text: In the retina of the eye there are two kinds of sensory cells. The **cones** see colours, and the **rods** mostly see light and dark. There are three kinds of cones, each reacting especially to red, green or blue light. The brain makes all colours from their signals. The cones need **plenty of light**, which is why we see almost no colours at night.

In colour vision deficiency, one kind of cone works differently or is missing. **Red and green** are confused most often. In Europe, **about 8 in 100 men** have a red-green deficiency, and in women it is much rarer. The deficiency is usually **inherited**. The gene responsible lies on the X chromosome, which is why men are affected more often. True complete colour blindness is very rare.

Whether someone sees colours well is often tested with **pictures made of coloured dots**. A number is hidden in the dots, which you can only spot with good colour vision. The plates of the Japanese eye doctor Ishihara are well known. Many people only find out from such a test that they see colours differently. For some jobs, such as being a pilot, good colour vision is important.

People with colour vision deficiency usually find good solutions in everyday life. At **traffic lights**, they recognise the light by its **position**: red is at the top, green at the bottom. On maps or in games, extra patterns or symbols help. Many apps and games now offer a special colour mode.

gewusst: The English naturalist John Dalton described his own colour vision deficiency at the end of the 18th century.
Many animals see colours quite differently from us, and bees, for example, can also see ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: When we breathe in, we bring fresh air into the lungs. The most important helper is a muscle you cannot see: the diaphragm.
wichtigste: When you breathe in, the lungs fill with air.
The diaphragm below the lungs is the most important breathing muscle.
The lungs sit in the chest and are protected by the ribs.
The left lung is smaller because the heart needs room there.
In the end, the air reaches tiny air sacs called alveoli.
We breathe in through the nose and mouth.

abschnitte.text: Air enters the body through the **nose** or the **mouth**. In the nose it is warmed, moistened and cleaned of dust. Then it flows through the throat into the **windpipe**. This divides into two branches, the bronchi. They branch out like a tree into ever finer tubes.

The **lungs** fill almost the whole **chest**. The ribs protect them on all sides. They consist of two lobes. The left one is slightly smaller, because the **heart** lies more on the left side and needs room. At the end of the finest tubes sit millions of tiny **alveoli**. This is where the blood takes up oxygen.

The **diaphragm** is a flat, dome-shaped muscle below the lungs. When you breathe in, it tightens and becomes flatter. This makes more room in the chest, and air flows in. Muscles between the ribs also help by lifting the chest. When you breathe out, the muscles relax and the air flows out again.

Put one hand on your tummy and breathe in deeply. You can feel your **tummy bulge outwards**. The diaphragm lowers and pushes the organs of the abdomen down and forwards. This is called **abdominal breathing**. Calm, deep breathing can help you relax.

gewusst: At rest, a person breathes in about 12 to 20 times a minute.
The surface of all the alveoli together is roughly as big as half a tennis court.

teile.einleitung: In **sign language**, you speak with your hands, face and body. You see the language instead of hearing it. Deaf people above all use it.
wichtigste: Sign language uses hands, face and body.
Deaf people above all speak sign language.
There are many different sign languages in the world.
In Switzerland there are three sign languages.
Names are spelled with the finger alphabet.
International Day of Sign Languages is on 23 September.

abschnitte.text: In sign language, words are shown with **hand signs**, the **signs**. In addition there are movements of the body and the **facial expression**. Sign languages are full languages with their own vocabulary and their own **grammar**. You can talk about anything in them, just as in spoken language.

The face is part of the grammar. With the eyebrows, for example, you show that you are asking a **question**. **Feelings** such as joy or anger can also be seen in the face. That is why people look at each other closely when signing.

There is not just one sign language but **many**. Usually each country has its own. In Switzerland there are **three**: German-Swiss, French and Italian sign language. They belong to the language regions of the country.

For names or rare words there is the **finger alphabet**. In it, every letter has its own hand sign. This way you can show a word letter by letter. Many people also have their own **name sign**, a short sign for their name.

**Sign language interpreters** translate between spoken language and sign language. On television you often see them in a small picture at the edge. The United Nations have declared **23 September** the International Day of Sign Languages. It draws attention to these languages.

gewusst: The sign languages in Germany and in German-speaking Switzerland are not exactly the same, even though German is spoken in both.
American Sign Language is related to French Sign Language, not to British Sign Language.

teile.einleitung: Whispering means speaking very quietly. You whisper when other people should not be disturbed or when something is meant to stay secret.
wichtigste: When whispering, you speak very quietly.
The vocal cords do not vibrate in whispering as they do in normal speech.
In a library you whisper so as not to disturb others.
With a secret, you often hold your hand in front of your mouth.
In the game “Chinese whispers”, a word is passed on in a whisper.
In a noisy room, it helps to move closer to the whispering person.

abschnitte.text: In normal speech, the **vocal cords** in the larynx **vibrate** and make a sound. In **whispering**, they do not vibrate in this way. They stay a little open, and the air rushes through. Mouth, tongue and lips shape the words out of the rushing sound. That is why whispering sounds breathy and is much quieter.

You whisper so as **not to disturb others**. In a **library**, in the cinema or in a church, this is usual. At home you often whisper when a **baby is sleeping**. In the woods, too, many people whisper so as not to scare away animals. This is a way of being considerate to others.

Someone who whispers something **into your ear** wants **others not to hear it**. Often they hold **a hand in front of the mouth**. This way nobody sees the lips, and the sound goes straight to the ear. If the room is loud, it helps to go **closer** to the whispering person. Quiet sounds quickly become weaker with distance.

In **Chinese whispers**, everyone sits in a row or in a circle. The first child whispers a word into the next child's ear. The word is passed on from ear to ear. At the end, the last child says out loud what they heard. Often a completely different, funny word has come out.

gewusst: People who are hoarse often whisper, but whispering can strain the voice too.
Under a round dome, you can sometimes hear a whisper on the opposite wall, which is called a whispering gallery.

teile.einleitung: A touch box is a box that you reach into without looking inside. You have to guess what is in it using only your sense of touch.
wichtigste: With a touch box, you feel things without seeing them.
For this you mainly need your hands.
A pine cone feels rough and scaly.
A cotton wool ball is soft and fluffy, and a metal spoon smooth and cool.
A walnut is hard with a wrinkled shell.
Nothing pointed belongs inside, so that nobody gets hurt.

abschnitte.text: A **touch box** is a box with a hole in the side. Often a piece of cloth hangs in front of it so that you cannot see inside. You reach in and **feel things without seeing them**. Then you guess what it is. You can also make a touch box very simply from a cloth or a cloth bag.

With the touch box, you mainly need **your hands**. In the skin, especially on the **fingertips**, there are many small **touch receptors**. They sense whether something is soft or hard, smooth or rough, warm or cool. The brain puts the clues together and recognises the object. Because you cannot see anything, you pay much closer attention to touch.

A **pine cone** feels **rough and scaly**. A **cotton wool ball** is **soft and fluffy**. A **metal spoon** feels **smooth and cool** because metal quickly carries away the warmth of the hand. A **walnut** you recognise by the fact that it is **hard** and has a **wrinkled shell**. A **sponge** is soft, has many holes and soaks up water.

**Nothing pointed** or sharp belongs in a touch box, for example no needles, knives or pieces of broken glass. Otherwise someone could **get hurt**, because you cannot see what you are touching. Very small things are also dangerous for small children, because they could swallow them. It is best to choose firm, clean objects from nature and around the house.

gewusst: With your fingertips you can feel bumps thinner than a hair.
A metal spoon and a wooden spoon in the same room have almost the same temperature, yet the metal spoon still feels colder.

teile.einleitung: Diffusion is the spreading of particles through their own random movement. It makes substances spread out evenly by themselves, and it is vital for the body.
wichtigste: Diffusion arises from the disordered thermal movement of the particles.
There is a net flow from high to low concentration.
At a higher temperature, diffusion is faster.
Oxygen can diffuse directly through the cell membrane.
Glucose gets into many cells by facilitated diffusion.
Double the distance means about four times the diffusion time.

abschnitte.text: All particles, because of their **thermal energy**, constantly move to and fro at random. This is called **Brownian motion**. If you put a tea bag into water, the colour spreads out by itself with time. Simply, more particles travel from the place of high **concentration** to the place of low concentration than the other way round. The result is a **net flow**.

If the concentration is the same everywhere, the movement does not stop. The particles keep moving, but equal numbers in both directions, so there is **no net flow** any more. The physiologist **Adolf Fick** described this in 1855 in **Fick’s first law**: the steeper the **concentration gradient**, the more substance flows per unit of time. At a **higher temperature** the particles move faster, and diffusion proceeds more quickly.

Every cell is surrounded by a **membrane** made of a fat-like double layer. Small, nonpolar molecules such as **oxygen** and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through it. **Ions** and large polar molecules need **transport proteins**. In this way **glucose** gets into many cells by way of GLUT transporters. This **facilitated diffusion** follows the concentration gradient and needs no energy in the form of ATP.

In the lung, oxygen gets from the **air sacs** into the blood by diffusion. The amount that diffuses rises with the **exchange surface**. The many small sacs together create a surface of roughly **100 square metres**. In addition, the wall between air and blood is extremely thin.

The time that particles need for a distance grows with the **square of the distance**. Double the distance therefore means about **four times the time**. That is why diffusion is efficient only over very short distances. For long routes in the body, the **blood circulation** is needed, which actively transports substances.

gewusst: In the years around 1855 Adolf Fick was a professor in Zurich.
You smell the scent of a perfume across a room partly because the scent particles spread by diffusion and air movement.

teile.einleitung: Electroencephalography, EEG for short, measures the electrical activity of the brain. For this, electrodes are stuck to the scalp, and the brain currents are recorded as wavy lines.
wichtigste: Hans Berger recorded the first EEG of a human in Jena in 1924.
The signals at the scalp are only a few microvolts strong.
Alpha waves show relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed.
Beta waves appear during concentrated activity.
Delta waves below 4 Hz are typical of deep sleep.
The electrodes are arranged according to the 10-20 system.
The EEG is especially important for diagnosing epilepsy.

abschnitte.text: In 1924, the German psychiatrist **Hans Berger** recorded the brain currents of a human for the first time, in **Jena**. He published his results in 1929 and introduced the name **electroencephalogram**. The word comes from Greek: “enkephalos” means brain, “graphein” means to write. Today the EEG is a standard test in hospitals.

Nerve cells work with small electric currents. The EEG signal comes mainly from the **pyramidal cells** of the cerebral cortex. Many of these cells, lined up in parallel, produce currents at their contact points at the same time. Their sum can be measured at the scalp. The signals are only a few to about a hundred **microvolts** strong, so sensitive amplifiers are needed.

Depending on the state, the EEG shows different waves. **Alpha waves** of about 8 to 13 Hz appear in calm wakefulness with the eyes closed. When you open your eyes, they become weaker. **Beta waves** of about 13 to 30 Hz show an active, alert brain. **Delta waves** below 4 Hz are slow and tall and mark **deep sleep**.

For an EEG, electrodes are placed on the scalp, often with a cap. Their positions follow the international **10-20 system**. The electrodes lie at distances of 10 or 20 per cent of certain lines across the head. This makes measurements comparable for different head sizes. The test does not hurt.

abschnitte.titel: What the EEG is needed for
abschnitte.text: The EEG is especially important in **epilepsy**. There it often shows typical spikes and steep waves. This makes it possible to work out the type of seizure and the place in the brain where the seizures start. The EEG also helps in **sleep medicine** and in cases of unconsciousness.

gewusst: Hans Berger worked on his method for years before he published it.
The brain is never completely silent even in sleep, and the EEG then simply shows other waves.

teile.einleitung: On the fingertips, every person has a pattern of fine lines. This pattern is unique, which is why people can be recognised by their fingerprint.
wichtigste: Nobody has exactly the same fingerprint as you.
A fingerprint shows fine lines of the skin.
The pattern forms before birth and stays the same for life.
Typical patterns are arch, loop and whorl.
The police look for fingerprints at crime scenes.
Since 2010, two fingerprints have been stored in the chip of the Swiss passport.

abschnitte.text: If you look at your fingertips with a magnifying glass, you see many **fine lines**. They are called **papillary ridges**. They help with gripping and feeling. If you press a finger on a smooth surface, a print of this pattern is left behind. The reason is sweat and skin oil on the skin.

The pattern forms **before birth**, months before a baby comes into the world. After that it stays **the same** for life, and the finger just gets bigger. No person has exactly the same fingerprint as another, not even identical twins. Typical basic forms are the **arch**, the **loop** and the **whorl**. The loop is the most common.
