Because fingerprints are unique, the **police** look for them at a crime scene. With fine powder and a brush, they make invisible prints visible. Then they compare the marks with stored prints. This method is called **fingerprinting** (dactyloscopy) and has been used for over a hundred years.

Many **mobile phones** can be unlocked with a fingerprint, without having to type in a number. A sensor recognises the pattern in a short time. In the Swiss **passport**, two fingerprints have been stored in the chip since **2010**. This makes it possible to check at controls whether the passport really belongs to the person.

You can make your own fingerprint clearly visible by pressing your finger on an **ink pad**. Then you carefully roll it on a sheet of white paper. With a magnifying glass, you can then work out your pattern. Compare it with the prints of your family, and you will find differences.

gewusst: Koalas have fingerprints that are very similar to those of humans.
Toes also have a line pattern of their own.

teile.einleitung: Imagination is the ability to think up things in your head that perhaps do not exist at all. With imagination we invent stories, games and pictures. It helps with learning, solving problems and playing.
wichtigste: Imagination means thinking up things in your head.
The **unicorn** exists only in the imagination.
The mermaid is a mythical creature, half human and half fish.
A **fairy tale** is an invented story with witches, fairies and magic.
Many children have an **imaginary friend**.
In **role play**, you pretend to be someone else.

abschnitte.text: Imagination means that we can **picture things in our heads**. These can be places, creatures or whole worlds. You need it especially when **making up stories**, painting and playing. Inventors and scientists also need imagination to think up new things. So imagination is not only important for children.

Some animals and creatures exist **only in the imagination**. The **unicorn** is a horse with a horn on its forehead. The **mermaid** is half human and half fish. Dragons and fairies also appear in many stories. Such invented creatures are called **mythical creatures**.

Many legends are also told in Switzerland. According to legend, **dragons** are said to have lived on **Pilatus** near Lucerne. One story tells of a dragon stone that is said to come from a dragon. Legends like this used to be passed on by word of mouth. Today you can read them in books.

A **fairy tale** is an invented story with witches, fairies and magic. In **role play**, you pretend to be someone else, for example a knight or a cook. Many children also have an **imaginary friend** that they only make up. This is completely normal and shows how much imagination they have. With imagination you can travel anywhere in your thoughts.

gewusst: The Lucerne dragon stone is now kept in the Natural History Museum in Lucerne.
More than 200 years ago, the Brothers Grimm collected many fairy tales and wrote them down.

teile.einleitung: Wrinkles are **lines and furrows in the skin**. They appear mainly with age, because the skin becomes less elastic. Wrinkles are completely natural and part of life.
wichtigste: Wrinkles are lines and furrows in the skin.
In old age, the skin becomes less elastic and gets wrinkles.
A lot of sun without protection makes the skin wrinkle sooner.
Fine wrinkles at the corner of the eye are also called **crow's feet**.
Vertical wrinkles between the eyebrows are called **frown lines**.
After a long bath, your fingers go wrinkly.

abschnitte.text: Young skin is firm and elastic, and it springs back at once after being stretched. With age, the skin becomes **less elastic** and thinner. It can then store less water and forms wrinkles. That is why an 80-year-old usually has many more wrinkles in the face than a child. Smoking and **a lot of sun without protection** also make the skin wrinkle sooner.

Many wrinkles appear where we often move the skin. Someone who laughs a lot gets fine wrinkles at the outer corner of the eye. These are also called **crow's feet**. The vertical wrinkles between the eyebrows are called **frown lines**, because you pull the skin together there when you frown. So a face tells a little of a person's life.

After **a long bath**, fingers and toes go wrinkly. These are not real wrinkles and they soon disappear again. Researchers think that the body controls this through the nerves. Wrinkly fingers might help you grip wet things better.

The **elephant** is known for its thick, wrinkled skin. In the many folds and furrows, water stays for longer. This helps the elephant cool down in the heat. Some breeds of dog also have many skin folds.

gewusst: Sun cream and shade protect the skin not only from sunburn but also from early wrinkles.
The skin is the largest organ of the human body.

teile.einleitung: Iron deficiency means that the body has too little iron. You need iron mainly to make haemoglobin, the red blood pigment. If it is missing, you often feel weak and tired.
wichtigste: Iron is a trace element that the body has to take in with food.
The body needs iron mainly to make haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.
Iron deficiency is the most common nutrient deficiency in the world.
Typical signs are tiredness, paleness and problems concentrating.
Meat, pulses and wholegrain foods provide iron.
Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods.

abschnitte.text: Iron is a **trace element** that the body needs only in small amounts. An adult has only about 3 to 5 grams of iron in the whole body. If you get too little over a longer time, the iron stores run empty. This is called **iron deficiency**.

abschnitte.titel: What does the body need iron for?
abschnitte.text: Most of the iron is in the **haemoglobin** of the red blood cells. Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and carries it to all parts of the body. Muscles and many enzymes also need iron. Without enough iron, the cells get too little oxygen.

Typical signs are tiredness, paleness and reduced performance. Some people have brittle nails, hair loss or cracked corners of the mouth. If the deficiency is severe, it leads to **anaemia**. Only a blood test can show whether there is an iron deficiency.

Girls and women are especially often affected, because they lose iron during their monthly period. Teenagers who are growing and pregnant women also need more iron. People who eat a vegetarian or vegan diet should pay attention to iron-rich foods. Endurance athletes can also have a higher need.

A lot of iron that the body can use well is found in **meat** and fish. Plant sources are lentils, beans, oat flakes, millet, nuts and pumpkin seeds. A glass of orange juice or some pepper with the meal improves absorption, because vitamin C helps. Black tea and coffee with the meal slow it down.

If a deficiency is found, the doctor often prescribes **iron tablets**. In severe cases, iron can also be given through a drip. In Switzerland, iron infusions are used fairly often. You should only take iron supplements on a doctor's advice, because too much iron is also harmful.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mineral that the body needs only in very small amounts.
The red blood pigment that carries oxygen.
A lack of red blood pigment in the blood.
A storage protein for iron, whose level can be measured in the blood.

gewusst: Spinach contains less iron than was long claimed, and the body can absorb it from spinach only poorly.
Iron in the blood is the reason why blood tastes slightly metallic.
According to the World Health Organization, hundreds of millions of people around the world are affected by anaemia.

teile.einleitung: The small intestine is the longest organ of digestion. Here the food is broken down completely and the nutrients get into the blood. Although it is called the small intestine, it is a real powerhouse of your body.
wichtigste: The small intestine lies between the stomach and the large intestine.
In an adult it is about 4 to 6 metres long.
Its main task is to take nutrients from the food.
It consists of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
Millions of tiny intestinal villi enlarge its surface enormously.
Bile and pancreatic juice help it with digestion.

abschnitte.text: The small intestine joins the stomach and ends at the **large intestine**. It lies folded in many loops in the belly. In an adult it is about 4 to 6 metres long, but only about 3 centimetres thick. It consists of three parts: the **duodenum**, the jejunum and the ileum.

In the duodenum, digestive juices are added to the food pulp. Bile from the liver helps to break down fats. The juice of the **pancreas** contains enzymes for proteins, fats and carbohydrates. In this way the food is broken into tiny building blocks.

The inner wall of the small intestine is covered with folds and tiny outgrowths, the **intestinal villi**. They look like a velvety carpet. Through them the surface becomes huge, according to recent measurements about 30 to 40 square metres. Over this surface, sugars, protein building blocks, fats and vitamins pass into the blood and the lymph.

Muscles in the wall of the intestine contract in waves. This **peristalsis** pushes the food pulp slowly onwards. At the same time it is well mixed. The passage through the small intestine takes a few hours.

Fibre from vegetables, fruit and wholegrain keeps the intestine going. Drinking enough is also important. In **coeliac disease**, the small intestine cannot tolerate the sticky protein gluten. Those affected have to do without wheat, rye and barley.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny finger-like outgrowths that take up nutrients.
The first section of the small intestine directly after the stomach.
Wave-like muscle movement that pushes the food pulp onwards.
A fluid from the liver that helps in digesting fat.

gewusst: The German word for the duodenum, “Zwölffingerdarm”, means twelve-finger gut, because it is about as long as twelve fingers side by side.
In the living body the small intestine is shorter because of muscle tension than after death.

teile.einleitung: The large intestine is the last part of the digestive tract. It takes water and mineral salts from the contents of the intestine and so forms the stool.
wichtigste: The large intestine of an adult is about 1.5 metres long.
It frames the loops of the small intestine.
The first section at the bottom right is called the caecum.
The longest part is the colon.
The ileocaecal valve prevents the contents of the intestine from flowing back into the small intestine.
The large intestine mainly takes up water and mineral salts.

abschnitte.text: In an adult the large intestine measures around **1.5 metres**. It is much shorter, but thicker than the small intestine. Like a **frame** it runs around the loops of the small intestine: it begins at the bottom right and ends in the middle of the pelvis. Its wall forms many sac-like bulges, the **haustra**. They give it its typically segmented appearance.

The start is the sac-shaped **caecum** at the bottom right of the belly. There the small intestine opens into it. The **ileocaecal valve** at this point prevents contents with many bacteria from flowing back. Then follows the **colon**: it rises on the right, runs across under the stomach and descends on the left. At the end lies the **rectum**, which leads to the anus.

Most nutrients have already been taken up by the small intestine. The large intestine takes back mainly **water** and **mineral salts** such as sodium. In this way the liquid contents of the intestine slowly become firmer. In the large intestine there also live countless **gut bacteria**. They break down remains of the food, for example fibre, and are important for health.

On the caecum hangs a small appendage, the **appendix**. In the so-called “Blinddarmentzündung”, in English appendicitis, it is almost always the appendix that is inflamed. It is then often removed in an operation. To examine the large intestine, a **colonoscopy** is done: a flexible tube with a small camera is inserted. In this way inflammation or growths can be recognised.

gewusst: The ileocaecal valve is named after Caspar Bauhin, a doctor and botanist from Basel.
The caecum is called “Blinddarm”, blind gut, in German because it ends blindly like a dead end.

teile.einleitung: Stretching is a simple exercise in which you gently pull muscles longer. Anyone who stretches regularly becomes more flexible. What matters is to do it right: calmly, without bouncing and without pain.
wichtigste: Regular stretching makes you more **flexible**.
You hold a stretch **calmly and without bouncing**.
Stretching should **pull lightly**, but not hurt.
You hold a stretch for about **15 to 30 seconds**.
It is best to stretch when the muscles are **warm**.
In **rhythmic gymnastics** you have to be especially flexible.

abschnitte.text: In stretching you slowly bring a muscle into a long position. Then you hold this position **calmly and without bouncing**. The feeling should be a **light pull**, but not pain. You hold a stretch for about **15 to 30 seconds**. While doing so you keep breathing calmly and do not hold your breath.

Cold muscles are stiff. That is why in training it is best to stretch **when the muscles are warm**, for example after running in or at the end of a PE lesson. Even a few minutes of hopping, running or arm circles warm the muscles. Then they can be stretched more easily and more safely.

For the **calf**, you put one leg far back and press the heel to the floor. For the **front of the thigh**, you stand on one leg and pull the other foot towards your bottom. Anyone who sits with straight legs and reaches for the toes stretches mainly the **back of the legs**. With each exercise you then do the other side.

In some sports you have to be **especially flexible**. These include **rhythmic gymnastics**, artistic gymnastics and ballet. There they practise stretching every day. But in football, swimming or climbing too, good flexibility helps. Anyone who stretches regularly can move more freely and easily.

You should never stretch with force or a swing. Jerky bouncing can overload a muscle. If something really hurts, you stop and stretch less far. Every body is different: some people are naturally more flexible than others. All that matters is that you improve slowly.

gewusst: Children are usually more flexible than adults.
Cats and dogs, too, stretch out at length after sleeping.

teile.einleitung: A bedtime routine is a fixed sequence of steps before sleeping that is the same every evening. It helps the body become calm and fall asleep more easily.
wichtigste: You do a bedtime routine the same way every evening.
This lets the body notice that bedtime is coming soon.
Brushing your teeth is part of it every evening.
A calm bedtime story relaxes you, while wild games keep you awake.
Fixed bedtimes help the body clock.
A lullaby is a calm song for falling asleep.

abschnitte.text: A **routine** is something you always do the same way. If you repeat the same steps every evening, the body gets used to it. It then knows: soon it will be time to sleep. Fixed **bedtimes** also help. The **body clock** then makes sure you get tired at the right time every evening.

Before sleeping you brush your **teeth**, so that they stay clean overnight. Many people then put on their pyjamas and go to the toilet once more. After that comes something calm, for example a **bedtime story**. At the end you say “Good night” to each other. What matters is that the sequence is similar every evening.

A **lullaby** is a calm song for falling asleep. In the past it was sung while rocking the baby in the cradle. A well-known one is, for example, “Weisst du, wie viel Sternlein stehen” (“Do you know how many little stars there are”). Reading aloud or listening to a story is also relaxing. Exciting films and wild games, on the other hand, tend to keep you awake.

An old tip is **counting sheep**. Counting evenly is boring and is supposed to make you tired. A glass of **warm milk** suits the evening well, because it contains no **caffeine**. Drinks with caffeine, such as cola or black tea, can keep you awake. Screens just before bedtime also often make it harder to fall asleep.

gewusst: The German word for lullaby, Wiegenlied, comes from Wiege, a rocking baby's cot.
Many adults also have bedtime routines, for example reading a few pages.

teile.einleitung: Everybody knows yawning: you open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply. We yawn when we are tired or bored, and often also when we see someone else yawn.
wichtigste: When yawning, you open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply.
A yawn lasts about 6 seconds.
We often yawn when we are tired or bored.
Yawning is catching.
Many animals yawn too, for example lions and cats.
Out of politeness, you hold your hand in front of your mouth.

abschnitte.text: When **yawning**, we open our mouth wide and breathe in deeply. Then we slowly breathe out again. Often we screw up our eyes as we do so, and sometimes tears even come. A yawn lasts on average about **6 seconds**. After waking up, many people yawn and **stretch** their arms and legs.

We yawn especially often when we are **tired**, that is, in the evening before sleep and in the morning after waking up. **Boredom** also makes us yawn, for example during long waits. Exactly why we yawn is not yet fully understood. Researchers have different explanations, and one of them is that yawning helps you to wake up.

Yawning is **catching**. When you see someone yawn, you often have to yawn yourself. Sometimes it is even enough to read about yawning or to think about it. Perhaps you are yawning right now? With people you know well, yawning is often especially catching.

It is not only humans who yawn. Many **vertebrates** do it too, for example **lions**, cats, dogs and monkeys. When lions yawn, you can see their big teeth. Birds and fish can also show a kind of yawning.

In our culture it is seen as **polite** to hold your **hand in front of your mouth** when yawning. This way the other person does not have to look into your open mouth. Someone who keeps yawning in class or during a conversation quickly seems bored, even if they are only tired.

gewusst: Even reading about yawning can make you yawn.
Dogs sometimes yawn too when their person yawns.

teile.einleitung: **112** is the European emergency number. With this number you can get help in an emergency all over Europe. It is especially handy when you are abroad on holiday.
wichtigste: The emergency number **112** works all over Europe.
You can also dial 112 in Switzerland.
The European emergency number has three digits.
In Switzerland, 112 connects you to an emergency call centre.
You can dial 112 for any emergency, including on a mobile phone.
In the USA, the number 911 is the main one.

abschnitte.text: Every country has its own emergency numbers, and they are hard to remember on holiday. That is why there is the **European emergency number 112**. It works in all countries of the European Union and in many other countries in Europe. The number has only **three digits** and is easy to remember. So even **abroad** you know at once whom you can call.

In **Switzerland** too, 112 works, even though it is not part of the EU. Whoever dials it reaches an **emergency call centre**, which sends the help that is needed. In addition, Switzerland has the well-known numbers: **117** for the police, **118** for the fire brigade and **144** for the ambulance service. Rega, the Swiss Air Rescue, can be reached on 1414. So you can choose, but 112 is never wrong.

You can call 112 from a landline and also **with a mobile phone**. The call is free. You can dial 112 for **any emergency**: for accidents, fire or when someone is in danger. On the phone you calmly say who you are, what has happened and where. Then you wait until the person at the call centre asks questions.

Outside Europe, other numbers often apply. In the **USA** and Canada, you mainly dial **911**. Anyone travelling far therefore checks beforehand which number applies at the holiday destination. An emergency call is only for real emergencies. Someone who calls without a reason blocks the line for people who urgently need help.

gewusst: The number 112 was agreed by the European Community in 1991 as a single emergency number.
11 February is European Emergency Number Day, because the date is written as 11.2.

teile.einleitung: Emulsification means that large drops of fat are broken up into many tiny droplets. In the small intestine this is an important step in the digestion of fat, because fat does not mix with water by itself.
wichtigste: An emulsion is a fine spread of two liquids that do not mix.
In emulsification, large drops of fat break up into many small ones.
Bile salts are amphiphilic, they have a water-loving and a fat-loving part.
The muscle movements of the stomach and gut also help.
Emulsification does not split any chemical bonds.
Smaller droplets give the enzymes a larger surface to work on.
Micelles carry the fat building blocks to the gut wall.

abschnitte.text: Oil and water do not mix. If you shake them, though, fine droplets of one liquid form in the other. Such a spread is called an **emulsion**. **Milk** is an example: in it, tiny droplets of fat float in water. Mayonnaise is also an emulsion. Substances that keep an emulsion stable are called **emulsifiers**.

In the small intestine, the **bile salts** take on the role of emulsifiers. They are **amphiphilic**: one side loves water, the other loves fat. That is why they settle at the boundary between fat and water. **Lecithin** from the bile is also amphiphilic and helps. In addition, the **stomach and gut** knead and mix the food pulp vigorously. These forces break the drops of fat up further.

Emulsification itself does **not split any chemical bonds**. Even so, it speeds up digestion a great deal. Fat-splitting **enzymes**, the lipases, can only work on the surface of the droplets. Many small droplets together have a much larger **surface** than one large drop. So the enzymes find many more places to attack.

The enzymes break the fat down into fatty acids and **monoacylglycerols**. With the bile salts and lecithin, these form tiny globules, the **micelles**. They carry the fat building blocks through the watery layer to the gut cell. Detergent-like molecules only form micelles above a certain amount, the **critical micelle concentration**. Below that, the molecules exist singly.

gewusst: Soap and washing-up liquid also work as emulsifiers: they lift fat from the plate by breaking it into small droplets.
Most of the bile salts are absorbed again in the gut and reused several times a day.

teile.einleitung: The strawberry is a popular fruit that ripens in early summer. The plant grows low to the ground and belongs to the **rose family**. Strawberries are sweet, juicy and healthy.
wichtigste: The strawberry belongs to the **rose family**.
The little seeds sit on the outside of the fruit.
Strawberries contain a lot of **vitamin C**.
The plant makes long shoots, the **runners**.
Small **wild strawberries** grow in the woods.
You wash strawberries first and only then pull off the green leaves.

abschnitte.text: The strawberry plant grows **low to the ground** and has leaves with three parts. In spring it bears white flowers. It belongs to the **rose family**, just like the apple, cherry and raspberry. The plant likes to spread with long shoots, the **runners**. Where a runner touches the ground, roots grow and a new plant forms.

The small yellow **seeds** sit on the outside of the red fruit. For botanists, these seeds are the real fruits, and they are called achenes. The red, juicy flesh is an enlarged flower base. That is why the strawberry is called an **aggregate fruit**. In everyday speech, we still simply say berry.

In the woods grow the small **wild strawberries**, which taste very aromatic. The large strawberries from the garden and the field are called garden strawberries. In Switzerland, strawberries are harvested mainly from May to July. On some farms you can even pick them yourself.

Even a handful of strawberries contains plenty of **vitamin C**. It is best to wash them briefly and pull off the green leaves **only afterwards**. That way no water gets into the fruit, and it stays aromatic. Strawberries are delicate and go soft quickly. What you do not eat straight away, you store somewhere **cool**, for example in the fridge.

gewusst: Botanically, the strawberry is not a berry at all but an aggregate fruit.
The garden strawberry came from wild American species that were crossed in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The franchise, which is like an excess, is the amount that people in Switzerland pay towards their health costs themselves each year before the health insurer pays. Anyone who chooses a high franchise pays a lower premium in return.
wichtigste: The franchise applies for one calendar year at a time.
The standard franchise for adults is 300 francs.
Adults can choose a franchise of up to 2,500 francs.
For children up to 18, the standard franchise is 0 francs, and up to 600 francs can be chosen.
Young adults aged 19 to 25 have the same levels as adults.
A higher franchise lowers the monthly premium.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, everyone must have **basic insurance** with a health insurer. For this you pay a **premium** every month. The **franchise** is the amount that you pay yourself per **calendar year** towards doctor, hospital and medicine costs. Only when the franchise is used up does the health insurer pay. On 1 January everything starts again from the beginning.

For **adults**, the standard franchise is **300 francs**. You can also choose a higher level, and the highest is **2,500 francs**. For **children up to 18**, the standard franchise is **0 francs**, and up to **600 francs** can be chosen. **Young adults aged 19 to 25** have the same levels as adults. These amounts have applied for many years, including in 2025.

A person has a franchise of **2,500 francs**. Over the whole year, they have doctor's bills of **1,800 francs**. Because the costs stay below the franchise, they pay everything themselves. The basic insurance pays **0 francs**. If the costs were higher than the franchise, the insurer would take over the rest, minus a small share, the **co-payment**.

The **higher** the franchise, the **lower** the monthly premium. A high franchise is therefore typically worth it for **healthy people** with low health costs. Someone who often has to see the doctor or needs medicines regularly is usually better off with a low franchise. You should put enough money aside to be able to pay the franchise in an emergency. You can change the franchise for the start of each new year.

gewusst: The word franchise comes from French and originally means “freedom” or “exemption”.
Besides the franchise, you usually pay 10 per cent of further costs as a co-payment, but only up to a fixed maximum per year.

teile.einleitung: Fish is a healthy food. It provides protein, valuable fats and vitamins that our body needs.
wichtigste: Oily fish such as salmon and herring contain a lot of vitamin D.
The body needs vitamin D for strong bones and teeth.
Sea fish provide healthy omega-3 fatty acids and iodine.
Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods such as fish.
Eating fish once or twice a week is often recommended.
In many Swiss lakes, perch is caught.

abschnitte.text: Oily sea fish such as **salmon**, **herring** or mackerel contain **omega-3 fatty acids**. These are healthy fats that the body cannot make itself. They are important for the heart, brain and eyes, among other things. Salmon is pink and often rich in fat. Its colour comes from pigments in small crustaceans that it eats.

Oily fish contain especially a lot of **vitamin D**. The body needs it for **strong bones and teeth**. The skin also makes vitamin D itself with sunlight, but in winter this is often not enough. Fish also provides **vitamin B12**. This vitamin is found almost only in food from animals, that is in meat, fish, eggs and dairy products.

Sea fish also provide **iodine**. The body needs iodine for the **thyroid gland**, a small organ in the neck. In Switzerland, the soil contains little iodine. That is why iodine has been added to table salt for many decades. This way everyone gets enough of it.

In many Swiss lakes, **perch** is caught, called “Egli” in Swiss German. Perch fillets are a popular dish. Whitefish and trout also come from Swiss waters. For a healthy diet, it is often recommended to eat fish **once or twice a week**.

When eating fish, you have to be especially careful of **bones**. These are the fine bones of the fish. You eat slowly and chew well, and then you find them in time. Fillets usually have fewer bones than whole fish.

gewusst: Many sea fish do not taste salty, even though they live in salt water.
The perch has spiny dorsal fins, so you have to handle it carefully.

teile.einleitung: Tick-borne encephalitis, known as TBE for short, is an illness that is mostly passed on by tick bites. A virus causes it, and you can be vaccinated against it. In German it is called “early summer meningoencephalitis”.
wichtigste: TBE stands for tick-borne encephalitis, or early summer meningoencephalitis in German.
The illness is caused by a virus.
It is mostly passed on by tick bites, rarely through raw, unpasteurised milk.
TBE can inflame the membranes around the brain and the brain itself.
There is no medicine against the virus, but there is a vaccine.
For the basic course of vaccination, 3 doses are needed.
The FOPH recommends the vaccination for the whole of Switzerland except Ticino (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: **TBE** stands for **tick-borne encephalitis**. The long German name, early summer meningoencephalitis, describes what happens: **meningitis** is an inflammation of the **membranes around the brain**, and **encephalitis** an inflammation of the **brain**. A **virus** triggers the illness. Many people who are infected notice nothing at all or have only mild, flu-like symptoms. In some people, however, a serious illness develops.

The TBE virus is mostly passed on by the bite of a **tick**. Ticks live in woods, at the edge of woods and in tall grass. They are active mainly from spring to autumn, which is why the German name says “early summer”. **Rarely**, you can also catch it from **raw, unpasteurised milk** from goats, sheep or cows. TBE is not passed from person to person.

There is **no medicine against the virus** itself. Doctors can only ease the symptoms, for example fever and headaches. In serious cases, patients have to be cared for in hospital. That is why it is especially important to protect yourself against infection.

There is an effective **vaccination** against TBE. For the **basic course**, **3 doses** are needed, a few months apart. Later, the protection is topped up after several years. The Federal Office of Public Health **FOPH** recommends the vaccination for **the whole of Switzerland except Ticino** (as of 2025). From what age children are vaccinated is something you discuss with the paediatrician.

When you go into the woods, it is best to wear long trousers and closed shoes. Light-coloured clothes help you to spot ticks more quickly. A **tick repellent** on skin and clothes keeps many ticks away. After the outing, you check the whole body for ticks. If you find a tick, you remove it quickly with tick tweezers or ordinary tweezers.

gewusst: Ticks do not jump from trees, they mostly wait on grasses and bushes.
Ticks can also pass on other illnesses, such as Lyme disease, for which there is no vaccination.

teile.einleitung: Nutrition means everything we eat and drink in order to live and stay healthy. Food provides energy and building materials for the body. A balanced diet helps you grow, concentrate and stay fit.
wichtigste: The three main nutrients, carbohydrates, fats and proteins, provide energy.
Fat provides the most energy per gram, about 9 kilocalories.
Carbohydrates and proteins each provide about 4 kilocalories per gram.
Vitamins and minerals are vital in small amounts.
A severe lack of vitamin C leads to scurvy.
The body makes vitamin D in the skin with the help of sunlight.
On the bottom level of the Swiss food pyramid are unsweetened drinks.

abschnitte.text: **Nutrition** is taking in the food that the body needs for energy, growth and health. The body uses the food during digestion. The energy in food is measured in **kilocalories** or kilojoules. Children need different amounts of energy depending on their age and how much they move.

**Carbohydrates** from bread, pasta, potatoes or rice are the most important source of energy. Fats provide the most energy, about 9 kilocalories per gram. Proteins from milk, eggs, meat or pulses are building materials for muscles and organs. Here is an example: 25 grams of carbohydrates provide about 100 kilocalories.

The body needs **vitamins** only in small amounts, but without them it becomes ill. If vitamin C is missing for a long time, scurvy results, a disease that many sailors used to suffer from. The skin makes vitamin D with the help of sunlight. Minerals such as calcium and iron are important for bones and blood.

The **Swiss food pyramid** shows how much of what you should eat. At the very bottom are unsweetened drinks such as water, and you should drink the most of these. Above them come vegetables and fruit, then cereal products and potatoes. At the very top are sweets, salty foods and alcohol, which are meant only in small amounts.

Five portions of vegetables and fruit a day, in different colours, are recommended. Wholegrain products keep you full for longer than white flour. Sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar and should be drunk rarely. Regular meals and eating without a screen help you listen to your body.

What we eat also has consequences for the environment. Seasonal and regional products often have shorter transport routes. Producing meat needs more land and water than producing vegetables. In addition, a lot of food is thrown away in Switzerland, which can be avoided with good planning.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in food that the body needs to live.
A unit of measurement for the energy in food.
A vital substance that the body usually cannot make itself.
Indigestible parts of plants that support digestion.

gewusst: In the 18th century, the sailor James Cook protected his crew from scurvy with sauerkraut.
The human body is about 60 per cent water.
The Swiss food pyramid is published by the Swiss Society for Nutrition.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Commission for Vaccination, FCV for short, advises the Confederation on all questions about vaccinations. Together with the Federal Office of Public Health, it draws up the vaccination recommendations for Switzerland.
wichtigste: The FCV is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation.
Its members are chosen by the Federal Council.
It draws up vaccination recommendations and advises the FOPH and the Federal Council.
It is not the FCV but Swissmedic that may approve vaccines.
Recommended vaccinations are mostly paid for by basic health insurance.
In Germany, the STIKO has a similar role.

abschnitte.text: The FCV is an **extra-parliamentary commission**. Commissions of this kind advise the **Federal Council** and the **federal administration** with expert knowledge from outside. The FCV is appointed by the Federal Council, and its members are **experts** from medicine and healthcare. It deals with all questions about vaccinations.

The FCV assesses **scientific data** and, together with the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH), draws up **vaccination recommendations**. In doing so it weighs up how common and how serious a disease is, that is, the **disease burden**. It also checks how well and how safely a vaccine works, whether the vaccination can be put into practice and what it costs. The recommendations are set out in the **Swiss vaccination schedule**.

Whether a vaccine may be sold at all is decided not by the FCV but by **Swissmedic**. This authority checks **quality, safety and effectiveness** and grants the **approval**. Only after that does the question arise of whether, and for whom, a vaccination is recommended. That is the work of the FCV and the FOPH.

For many **recommended vaccinations**, the **compulsory health insurance**, the basic insurance, covers the costs. The condition is that they are listed in the **Health Insurance Benefits Ordinance**. **Travel vaccinations** are mostly not covered. So the FCV's recommendations also affect what families have to pay for themselves.

Other countries also have expert bodies like this. In **Germany**, the **Standing Committee on Vaccination** (STIKO) at the Robert Koch Institute publishes the vaccination recommendations. In the **USA**, the **Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices** (ACIP) advises the health authority CDC. There, approval is granted by the **FDA**, much like Swissmedic in Switzerland.

gewusst: The Swiss vaccination schedule is revised regularly when new scientific findings become available.
A vaccination recommendation is not compulsory: in Switzerland, people usually decide for themselves whether to be vaccinated.

teile.einleitung: Stretching exercises make muscles and joints more flexible. There are different ways of stretching, depending on whether you hold a position or move in a controlled way. Which way suits also depends on what you are planning to do afterwards.
wichtigste: In **static stretching** you hold a position calmly for a few seconds.
In **dynamic stretching** you make controlled, swinging movements.
A proper stretch feels like a **light pull**.
When stretching you **keep breathing calmly**.
Jerky bouncing can injure muscles.
Before a sprint you tend to stretch dynamically.

abschnitte.text: In **static stretching** you slowly bring the muscle into a stretched position. You then hold this position **calmly for a few seconds**, often 15 to 30 seconds. You should feel a **light pull**, but no pain. This way suits well after training or in a separate flexibility session.

In **dynamic stretching** you move **in a controlled and swinging way**, for example with **leg swings** forwards and backwards. The movement slowly becomes larger, but always stays controlled. In this way the muscles are stretched and warmed up at the same time. Many sportspeople do this when running in.

Before a **sprint** or a jump, you tend to stretch dynamically rather than statically for a long time. The reason: **holding** a stretch **for long** can briefly lower **explosive strength**. The muscle then reacts a little less explosively for a while. Dynamic stretching, by contrast, prepares it well for fast movements.

If you pull the **heel towards your bottom** while standing, you stretch the **front thigh muscle**. For the **calf muscle**, you go into a lunge position, lean on a wall with your hands and keep the back heel on the floor. In both exercises you keep your back straight. Afterwards you change sides.

When stretching you should **keep breathing calmly** and not hold your breath. This helps the muscles to relax. You should not stretch with **jerky bouncing**, because this **can injure muscles**. Anyone who practises slowly and regularly becomes more flexible with time.

gewusst: Many sports clubs no longer do long static stretching before training, but a dynamic warm-up.
How flexible someone is also depends on the joints and on the connective tissue, not only on the muscles.

teile.einleitung: The story of human evolution tells how our ancestors developed over millions of years. At the start were ape-like creatures in Africa, and at the end the human of today, Homo sapiens. Fossils such as the famous skeleton Lucy help us understand this story.
wichtigste: Humans and chimpanzees share common ancestors who lived about 6 to 7 million years ago.
Walking upright developed as one of the earliest human features.
Lucy is a partial skeleton of an Australopithecus afarensis found in Ethiopia in 1974.
According to current knowledge, Homo sapiens arose in Africa.
The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old.
Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago.
Many people today carry a small piece of Neanderthal DNA.

abschnitte.text: Humans are not descended from chimpanzees, but both have **common ancestors**. These lived about 6 to 7 million years ago in Africa. From then on, the lines developed separately. The science of how humans came about is called **palaeoanthropology**.

One of the first typically human features was **walking upright**. It developed long before the large brain. The early human relatives of the genus **Australopithecus** were already walking on two legs over three million years ago. The famous skeleton **Lucy** was found in Ethiopia in 1974 and is about 3.2 million years old.

About 2.5 million years ago, the first members of the genus Homo appeared, such as **Homo habilis**. They made simple stone tools. Later came Homo erectus, who was the first to leave Africa and who used fire. The brain became larger and larger over time.

Modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, arose in Africa. The oldest known fossils come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 300,000 years old. Later Homo sapiens spread all over the world. It reached Europe over 40,000 years ago.

The **Neanderthal** lived in Europe and western Asia and was well adapted to the cold. It is named after a valley near Düsseldorf, where bones were found in 1856. About 40,000 years ago it died out. Because Neanderthals and Homo sapiens sometimes mixed, many people today carry one to two per cent Neanderthal DNA.

People also lived in Switzerland during the Ice Age. In caves such as the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein, traces from the Old Stone Age were found. Much later, pile-dwelling settlements were built on Lake Neuchâtel and other lakes. Since 2011, prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Petrified remains or traces of living things from earlier times.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
The scientific name of humans today, meaning wise human.
A genus of early human relatives that walked upright and lived in Africa.

gewusst: The skeleton Lucy was named after the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”, which was playing during the dig.
The Swedish scientist Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022 for decoding the Neanderthal genome.
On the Indonesian island of Flores lived a species of human only about one metre tall, Homo floresiensis.

teile.einleitung: The energy balance compares how much energy the body takes in with food and how much it uses. If it is not in balance over a longer time, body weight changes.
wichtigste: The basis is the first law of thermodynamics: energy is not lost.
In a positive energy balance, more is taken in than used, and the surplus is stored mainly as fat.
In adults who are not very active, the basal metabolic rate makes up about 60 to 70 per cent.
Total energy expenditure is basal metabolic rate times the PAL value.
Indirect calorimetry measures oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide output.
When only carbohydrates are burned, the respiratory quotient is 1.0.
After a long, strong cut in calories, the basal metabolic rate usually falls.

abschnitte.text: The energy balance is based on the **first law of thermodynamics**. It says that energy is not lost, only converted. So energy that is taken in is used up, stored or given off as heat. In a **positive energy balance**, more is taken in than used. The surplus is stored mainly as **fat**, and weight goes up. In a negative balance, the body draws on its stores.

The **basal metabolic rate** is the energy the body needs in complete rest, for example for the heart, breathing and the brain. In adults who are not very active, it makes up about **60 to 70 per cent** of the total expenditure. Movement and digestion share the rest. **Total energy expenditure** is calculated with the **PAL value**, which shows physical activity. Example: 1600 kcal times 1.5 gives 2400 kcal per day.

In **indirect calorimetry**, **oxygen consumption** and **carbon dioxide output** are measured, for example with a breathing mask. From this you can work out how much energy the body uses. The **respiratory quotient** is the ratio of carbon dioxide given off to oxygen taken in. When only carbohydrates are burned, it is **1.0**, and for fat it is lower.

If someone takes in 500 kcal less than they use every day for a week, the deficit is 7 times 500, which is **3500 kcal**. The body covers it mainly from its stores. With a long and strong **cut in calories**, however, the body adapts. The basal metabolic rate **falls**, partly because body mass is lost. This makes further weight loss harder.

gewusst: The brain uses about a fifth of the energy of the basal metabolic rate, although it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight.
One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules, and in Switzerland both figures are shown on packaging.

teile.einleitung: A pressure bandage is an important first aid measure. It presses together a heavily bleeding wound on an arm or leg, so that less blood escapes.
wichtigste: A pressure bandage slows heavy bleeding.
First you press directly on the wound, best with gloves.
A sterile wound dressing goes directly on the wound.
Over it, a pressure pad presses in a targeted way on the bleeding place.
If the bandage bleeds through, you put a second one over it.
Blue, cold or tingling fingers show that it is too tight.

abschnitte.text: Before treating a bleeding wound, you put on **disposable gloves** if possible. They protect you from germs in the blood and the wound from dirt. They belong in every car first aid kit. The first measure is **direct pressure**: you press firmly on the wound with a compress or a clean cloth. At the same time you call for help, in Switzerland by the number **144**.

A pressure bandage has three parts. Directly on the wound goes a **sterile wound dressing**, that is, a germ-free compress. Over it you lay the **pressure pad**, for example an unopened **bandage packet**. It presses in a targeted way on the injured blood vessels. At the end a **bandage** is wrapped firmly round everything, so that the pad stays in place.

An injured arm you also hold **up**, above the height of the heart. Then less blood flows into the wound, and the bleeding becomes weaker. The injured person should preferably sit or lie down, because they can get dizzy with heavy blood loss.

If the first bandage bleeds through, you leave it in place and put a **second pressure bandage** over it. If you took the first one off, it would disturb the **blood clotting** that is just starting. It is also important that the bandage is not too tight. If **fingers or toes turn blue, cold** or **tingle**, the blood supply is disturbed. Then you have to loosen it a little.

gewusst: In Switzerland a first aid course is compulsory before you get the learner’s licence for a car.
An unopened bandage packet is well suited as a pressure pad, because it is firm and clean.

teile.einleitung: In a peanut allergy, the body's defence system reacts too strongly to proteins from peanuts. Even tiny amounts can cause serious symptoms. That is why people affected have to be very careful with what they eat.
wichtigste: Even tiny amounts of peanut can cause severe reactions.
In most people, a peanut allergy lasts for life.
In Switzerland, peanuts have to be highlighted in the list of ingredients.
“May contain traces” means: small amounts can get in during production.
**Lupin** can also cause reactions in people with a peanut allergy.
Peanut is especially often found in **satay sauce**.

abschnitte.text: The **immune system** protects us from germs. In an allergy, however, it mistakes harmless substances for dangerous ones. In a peanut allergy, these are certain **proteins** in the peanut. By the way, the peanut is not a true nut but a **legume**, like beans and peas. That is why lupin, another legume, can also cause reactions because of similar proteins.

Peanut allergy is especially feared because **tiny amounts** are enough. Itching, a rash, swollen lips, tummy ache or difficulty breathing are possible. In the worst case there is an **anaphylactic shock**, which is life-threatening. Many people affected therefore carry an emergency kit with an adrenaline auto-injector. In a severe reaction, you call 144 at once. Unlike some other allergies, it usually does **not** go away by itself.

In Switzerland, allergens such as peanuts have to be **highlighted** in the list of ingredients, for example in bold print. This makes them quicker to spot. The notice “May contain traces of peanuts” means that small amounts can get in during production. For very sensitive people, even this is dangerous. Peanut is often found in satay sauce, in Asian dishes, in muesli bars and in chocolate.

The most important protection is to avoid peanuts. In some children, however, sensitivity can be lowered under **medical supervision**. They are given tiny, slowly increasing amounts of peanut protein. In this way the body gradually gets used to it. You must never try this alone at home.

gewusst: The peanut does not grow on a tree: its pods ripen underground.
Botanically, the peanut is related to beans and peas.

teile.einleitung: Thirst is the feeling that tells us: the body needs water. Because we lose water every day, we also have to drink every day.
wichtigste: More than half of the body is made of water.
We lose water when we sweat, breathe and go to the toilet.
On hot days and during sport, you need to drink especially much.
Pale yellow urine usually shows that you are drinking enough.
If you drink too little, you get tired and may get a headache.
A person can only survive a few days without water.

abschnitte.text: The human body is made of **more than half water**. In children the share is slightly higher than in older people. Water carries nutrients in the blood, helps with digestion and cools the body. A person can last a long time without food, but **only a few days** without drinking.

The body gives off water when we **sweat**, **breathe** and go to the **toilet**. That is why you have to drink every day. On **hot days** and during **sport** you sweat especially much. Then the body needs more water. The brain notices when water is missing and speaks up with the feeling of **thirst**.

**Water** quenches thirst best. In Switzerland, **tap water** is clean drinking water and is checked regularly. In many towns and cities there are also fountains with drinking water. **Sugary drinks**, on the other hand, contain a lot of **sugar**. That harms the teeth, and they are less good at stopping thirst than water.

The colour of your urine often shows whether you are drinking enough. If it is **pale yellow**, everything is usually fine. If it is **dark yellow**, you should drink more. If you drink too little, you get **tired** and may get a **headache**. Thinking and concentrating also become harder. That is why a water bottle at school is a good idea.

gewusst: Fruit and vegetables such as cucumbers or melons are also mostly made of water.
If you feel thirsty, you have often already gone a little too long without drinking.

teile.einleitung: Disinfectants are agents that kill germs such as bacteria and many viruses. They are needed for hands, for wounds and for surfaces, especially where sick people have to be protected.
wichtigste: Disinfectants kill germs.
Hand disinfectant often contains a lot of alcohol.
The alcohol evaporates quickly, so the hands soon dry again.
In hospital, hands are disinfected especially often.
On wounds, a special wound disinfectant is the right choice.
You must never drink disinfectant or get it in your eyes.

abschnitte.text: On the skin and on objects live countless **germs**. Most are harmless, but some can cause illness or make a wound **inflamed**. To disinfect means to reduce these germs so much that they are no longer dangerous. This is not the same as cleaning: in cleaning you mainly remove dirt, in disinfecting you kill germs.

Many **hand disinfectants** contain a high proportion of **alcohol**. The alcohol destroys the shell of many germs. You rub the agent thoroughly onto all parts of the hands, also between the fingers and onto the fingertips. Because alcohol **evaporates** very quickly in the air, the hands are dry after a short time, and the smell too soon becomes weaker.

For small wounds there are special **wound disinfectants**. They are made so that they are gentle on the delicate skin. Even so, it can **sting** briefly on an open wound, but this soon passes. Cleaning agents for surfaces never belong on a wound. For large or deep wounds you need a doctor.

In **hospital** there are many sick and weakened people. So that germs are not carried from one room to the next, nurses and doctors disinfect their hands very often, for example before and after every contact with patients. Instruments and surfaces are also disinfected regularly. At many entrances there are dispensers that visitors should use too.

Disinfectant is meant only for the skin or for objects. **If drunk it is poisonous** and very dangerous. In the **eyes** it irritates strongly, so you take good care when using it. Because many agents contain alcohol, they can also be flammable. That is why you keep them tightly closed and out of the reach of small children.

gewusst: As early as 1847 in Vienna, the doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed that thorough disinfection of the hands prevents many illnesses.
Against ordinary everyday germs, thorough hand washing with soap is usually enough at home.
